title: Task2Hand: A Contact-Grounded Skill for Parametric Dexterous-Hand Morphology Design
authors: Haoyang Wang,Weibo Gao,Zhengxiong Li,Lingfeng Tao
abstract: Dexterous hand design demands repeated expert work across geometry, robot-description code, collision debugging, grasp initialization, and policy training. We present Task2Hand, a Skill: a specification package that turns a functional manipulation brief into a parameterized hand model and routes every candidate through cost-ordered contact, dynamics, and learning gates. Each gate returns a status and an evidence record; on failure, the Skill records the earliest blocker, revises one bounded parameter group, and reruns the cheaper gates. The agent generates, validates, and trains autonomously within declared bounds, and escalates trade-offs, plateaus, and conflicting evidence to a human who sets the next design direction. An evidence-driven design trajectory for bidirectional in-hand manipulation yielded SAGE Hand (Skill-Aware Generative Embodiment): four fingers, 16 actuated DoF, an integrated guiding palm, compact roots, cylindrical tips, and a collision-cleared opposable thumb. Under a matched training protocol, SAGE Hand reaches 45.6% task success on a hexagonal prism against 37.3% for the LEAP hand, and 70.8% on a bicolor cylinder against 51.6%. Dense simulated tactile input more than halves the cylinder drop rate. In a controlled iteration study, the Skill path preserves capture at 164/165 trials while the path without the Skill degrades to 14/165, confirming that the gates act as a regression guard during refinement. Accepted candidates pack with URDF/MJCF, metrics, checkpoints, and a provenance manifest.

title: Real-time neuromorphic audio and vision perception for autonomous robotic applications: Integration and experimental evaluation on a rover platform
authors: Guillem Fustier-Castillo,Ruben Ribes-Serrano,Javier Naranjo-Alcazar,Vicent Ortiz-Castello,Pedro Zuccarello
abstract:
Neuromorphic sensing and computing offer a promising alternative to conventional
deep learning pipelines for mobile robots, where perception must run continuously
under tight latency and energy constraints. However, most neuromorphic solutions
are still evaluated offline or on isolated benchmarks, and their integration into
complete robotic systems remains largely unexplored. In this technical report, a
four-wheel rover platform is presented that combines three real-time perception
pipelines: a classical audio tagging pipeline based on Pretrained Audio Neural
Networks (PANNs) running on an NVIDIA Jetson GPU, a neuromorphic audio pipeline in
which a spiking neural network (SNN) is deployed on the SynSense Xylo Audio 2 chip,
and a neuromorphic vision pipeline in which events from an event-based camera are
processed by the SpikeYOLO spiking detector for traffic cone detection. On the Xylo
chip, the whole processing chain—from the microphone signal to the classification
of low- and high-pitched sounds—is performed on-chip, while the host only
configures the device and reads the output neurons. All models are deployed as
containerised services and integrated through ROS 2, and a configurable action
dispatcher maps the detected classes to robot behaviours, closing the loop between
perception and actuation. The platform is demonstrated in a proof-of-concept
scenario in which the robot reacts to sound classes detected by both audio
pipelines and detects traffic cones with the event camera, showing the feasibility
of integrating neuromorphic hardware into a multimodal robotic platform operating in
real time.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots must perceive their environment continuously and react to
it within short time frames, while relying on embedded computing platforms with
limited energy budgets. Deep learning has become the standard approach for robotic
perception, and edge devices such as the NVIDIA Jetson family make it possible to
run convolutional neural networks (CNNs) close to the sensors, reducing the
dependence on network connectivity, the latency of the response and the
transmission of raw data [1]. In the audio domain, recent
studies have shown that audio tagging models can be deployed on resource-constrained
devices, although their inference time and thermal behaviour strongly depend on the
selected architecture and the deployment conditions [2, 3]. These constraints are even more critical in battery
powered robots, where perception competes for energy with locomotion and the
remaining onboard systems.

Neuromorphic computing addresses these limitations by taking inspiration from the
way biological neural systems process information. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs)
process information through discrete spike events instead of continuous-valued
activations, which enables sparse and event-driven computation with high energy
efficiency [4, 5]. This paradigm
is complemented by neuromorphic sensors, such as event-based cameras, which
generate spike-like outputs directly [6], and by dedicated
neuromorphic processors that execute SNNs at very low power. These properties make
neuromorphic systems particularly attractive for always-on perception in mobile
robotics. Nevertheless, most neuromorphic audio and vision solutions are evaluated
offline or on isolated benchmarks [7, 8], and their
integration into complete robotic platforms operating in closed loop remains
largely unexplored.

In this technical report, the integration of neuromorphic audio and vision
perception into a four-wheel rover platform is presented. The robot combines three
real-time perception pipelines: (i) a classical audio tagging pipeline based on
PANNs [9] running on the GPU of an NVIDIA Jetson device, (ii) a
neuromorphic audio pipeline based on an SNN deployed on the SynSense Xylo Audio 2
chip, in which the audio signal is processed entirely on-chip, and (iii) a
neuromorphic vision pipeline in which the output of an event-based camera is
processed by the SpikeYOLO spiking detector [10] to detect traffic
cones. Running classical and neuromorphic pipelines on the same platform allows
both approaches to be compared under the same operating conditions, while
providing the robot with complementary perception capabilities.

The main contributions of this work are the following:

A multimodal rover platform that integrates conventional and neuromorphic
sensors and processors, including an NVIDIA Jetson device, a SynSense Xylo
Audio 2 development kit and an event-based camera.

The closed-loop integration of the Xylo Audio 2 neuromorphic chip into the
robot, from the deployment of a trained SNN on the hardware to the execution of
robot actions triggered by its predictions.

An event-based vision pipeline that feeds the SpikeYOLO spiking detector
with event representations built in real time from the camera stream.

A modular and containerised software architecture, in which each model is
exposed as an independent service and integrated through ROS 2, so that models
can be replaced without modifying the robot software.

A proof-of-concept demonstration in which the robot detects sound classes
with both the classical and the neuromorphic audio pipelines and translates them
into actions, while detecting traffic cones with the event camera.

The remainder of this report is organized as follows. Section 2
introduces SNNs, neuromorphic hardware and sensors, and reviews related work.
Section 3 describes the robotic platform, and
Section 4 presents the software architecture that integrates
the perception pipelines with the robot. Sections 5,
6 and 7 detail the classical audio, neuromorphic audio
and neuromorphic vision pipelines, respectively. Section 8
describes the proof-of-concept demonstration, Section 9
discusses the
current limitations and future work, and Section  concludes the
report.

1. A multimodal rover platform that integrates conventional and neuromorphic
sensors and processors, including an NVIDIA Jetson device, a SynSense Xylo
Audio 2 development kit and an event-based camera.

2. The closed-loop integration of the Xylo Audio 2 neuromorphic chip into the
robot, from the deployment of a trained SNN on the hardware to the execution of
robot actions triggered by its predictions.

3. An event-based vision pipeline that feeds the SpikeYOLO spiking detector
with event representations built in real time from the camera stream.

4. A modular and containerised software architecture, in which each model is
exposed as an independent service and integrated through ROS 2, so that models
can be replaced without modifying the robot software.

5. A proof-of-concept demonstration in which the robot detects sound classes
with both the classical and the neuromorphic audio pipelines and translates them
into actions, while detecting traffic cones with the event camera.

title: What Must a Model Tell a Planner? Outcome Interfaces for Risk-Aware Planning After Robot Damage
authors: Hassan Iqbal,Krishna Kumar
abstract:
When a robot is damaged, it must decide which routes it can still afford, and the amount of risk it may accept can change from one mission to the next.
We argue that whether a learned model helps such a robot depends on its decision interface, that is, on what the model hands to the planner.
A decision policy tells the planner what to do, whereas an outcome model, a kind of world model, predicts the consequences of each route.
We study simulated Unitree Go2 quadrupeds and H1 humanoids with weakened motors, added payloads, or reduced foot friction.
We compare four interfaces.
The first is a decision policy, and the second is the same policy trained with fixed penalties for infeasible routes.
The third is an outcome model that predicts each route’s feasibility and travel time.
The fourth, which we call a capability contract, is an outcome model that predicts the robot’s chance of success and its travel time on each terrain and composes them along a route.
All share the same collected experience, matched tuning and risk calibration, and an uncertainty guard.
Two comparatively low-risk probes let the capability contract rank hazardous terrains about as well as four new trials on every hazard.
At a calibrated 5% limit on selecting empirically infeasible routes, outcome models cut declined missions from about 32% to 7–8% on Go2 and from 57% to 35–36% on H1 compared with the plain policy.
Fixed penalties narrow this gap, but the best penalty changes with the risk target.
Predicting outcomes lets the planner preserve missions by changing routes as risk requirements tighten.
introduction:
Consider a quadruped whose front-left knee has lost half of its torque.
Its planner can send it up a short flight of stairs, along a mixed path with a single obstacle, or around a long detour over gentle slopes, and the robot can always stop and ask for help.
The terrain and available routes have not changed, but the robot’s chances of completing them have.
Testing the hazards by trial would invite the falls the planner exists to prevent.
The acceptable risk may change from one mission to another, with stricter requirements near people than during a survey.
If the preferred route becomes unacceptable, the planner must still decide which alternative the damaged robot can attempt.

Policies map observations to choices [3, 23, 10], while world models predict consequences that can inform those choices [7, 8].
We study their decision interface, what the learned component hands to the planner.
A decision policy scores routes, while an outcome model estimates feasibility or success probability and travel time.
Confidence that a route is preferred is not the same as the probability that the robot can complete it.

Tightening the risk target reveals a practical difference between the evaluated rules (Fig. 1).
The decision policy accepts its preferred route or falls back, whereas the outcome planners can select another qualifying route.
We compare four interfaces on damaged Go2 and H1 robots with matched learning and calibration.

Damage recovery uses Gaussian process predictions to search for compensatory behaviors [4], while adaptive locomotion learns how to act under changed dynamics [11, 14].
Whereas these methods improve how the robot moves, we assess where its existing controller can still succeed.
Related assessment methods use competence estimates to decide when autonomy should defer to human assistance [2], or predict perception performance from experience to avoid failure [6].
Our Gaussian process instead learns across damaged robots how responses on easier terrain predict the probability of successful traversal and travel time on hazards.
This relationship lets two comparatively low-risk probes assess a new robot without retesting every hazard.
We evaluate the resulting hazard ranking and the trials and falls required to obtain it against direct hazard retesting.

Model-free RL can learn locomotion without an explicit transition model [18], while model-based RL can combine policy proposals with predicted rollouts [9, 22].
These approaches establish that learned policies and outcome predictions can play complementary roles.
We ask what a route planner gains when information about physical execution remains explicit rather than being compressed into a route choice.
Navigation methods already incorporate deployment instructions [16, 20], and conformal planners calibrate uncertain predictions or decisions [13, 5, 12, 17].
With shared locomotion, experience, and risk calibration, we compare filtering a learned route choice with reevaluating alternatives from route or terrain predictions.
This comparison measures the missions retained as risk targets change and tests whether predictions for individual terrains help when missions recombine them.

title: Interactive Semi-Parametric On-Track Learning for Vehicle Dynamics in Autonomous Racing
authors: Jungbin Kim,Youngim Nam,Cheolhyeon Kwon
abstract:
Autonomous racing requires an accurate vehicle dynamics model near the limits of handling, yet a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics inevitably remains.
To reduce this mismatch, existing methods learn from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions, by adapting the physical parameters of the nominal model or by learning a residual that captures the remaining mismatch.
However, these on-track learning methods typically handle either the physical parameters or the residual separately, which restricts their ability to resolve the mismatch.
To address this limitation, we propose an interactive semi-parametric learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual under a single shared prediction-error objective.
Since updating one changes the learning target of the other, they are recursively updated in turn, each guided by the other’s latest update.
Each update is then accepted only if it does not increase the shared objective, so that the objective is guaranteed to be non-increasing and convergent over the recursion.
Numerical simulations and hardware experiments show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines.
Compared with the nominal model, it reduces the one-step prediction errors of lateral velocity and yaw rate by 90.0% and 81.6% in simulation and by 54.0% and 59.4% on hardware.
introduction:
In autonomous racing, a vehicle must complete a track as quickly as possible while operating near the limits of handling [1].
Doing so requires a controller built on an accurate dynamics model, yet the actual vehicle dynamics are hard to identify.
For instance, physical parameters, such as tire friction, vary with operating conditions, and complex nonlinear effects, such as lateral load transfer, are difficult to capture accurately [2].
Traditionally, such parameters are obtained through steady-state calibration performed before racing [3, 4], but the resulting values may not remain valid during racing.
With off-track calibration alone, these factors inevitably cause a mismatch between the nominal and actual dynamics (see Fig. 1(a)), motivating efforts to learn vehicle dynamics from on-track data, i.e., data collected while the vehicle drives on the track under racing conditions.

One common approach is parametric learning, which identifies the physical parameters of a dynamics model [5, 6].
While this approach can mitigate the mismatch caused by inaccurate parameter values, its effectiveness is inherently constrained by the underlying model structure (see Fig. 1(b)).
For computational efficiency, most studies rely on simplified models that fail to capture complex nonlinear effects, regardless of parameter accuracy [7, 8].
Increasing model fidelity can address this limitation, but the additional parameters make reliable identification difficult with limited on-track data [9].

Instead, nonparametric learning retains a simplified parametric model and captures the unmodeled dynamics as a residual, yielding a semi-parametric dynamics model [10, 11].
This residual is commonly learned using Gaussian process (GP) regression due to its flexibility in modeling nonlinear functions.
However, standard GP regression scales poorly with dataset size, making its use challenging in real-time control.
Sparse approximations address this issue using a small set of inducing points [12], but they often fail to capture localized variations in the residual [13] (see Fig. 1(c)).
This difficulty is further compounded because the underlying parametric model is not updated, leaving the sparse GP to compensate for the entire mismatch.
In essence, existing dynamics learning methods in racing typically pursue either parametric learning of the physical parameters or nonparametric learning of the residual in isolation, leaving part of the mismatch unresolved.

A straightforward approach to combining parametric and nonparametric learning is to apply them sequentially, i.e., to adapt the parametric model first and then train the residual model on what remains unmatched.
However, the two models are mutually dependent, so this sequential learning can lead to biased estimates on both sides.
In this case, the parameters are distorted to compensate for the unmodeled dynamics, and the residual model then learns from this distorted parametric model [14].
Re-adapting the parameters using the learned residual, in turn, changes the residual target and can leave the residual model outdated [15].
For robot manipulators, a few studies have addressed this dependence by analytically adjusting the residual model according to parameter updates [15] or by estimating both models in a single regression [14].
Both approaches, however, exploit the linearity of rigid-body dynamics in the inertial parameters, limiting their direct extension to nonlinearly parameterized vehicle dynamics.

To address these challenges, this paper proposes an interactive framework for semi-parametric learning from on-track data in autonomous racing.
The framework learns both the physical parameters and the residual model under a single shared objective, namely the prediction error of the resulting semi-parametric model.
Since the nonlinear parameterization of the dynamics and the nonparametric nature of the residual model make this objective difficult to minimize directly, the two models are recursively updated in turn.
In doing so, each model guides the other with its latest update, accounting for their mutual dependence.
As a result, neither model has to compensate for the part of the mismatch that the other can explain, unlike when each is learned in isolation.

Specifically, once the data are collected, the physical parameters are adapted via nonlinear least-squares (NLS) optimization [7] given the current residual model.
The residual model is then learned via sparse GP regression [16] on residual targets recomputed from the adapted parameters.
Each parameter update in this recursion shifts the residual targets by an amount that depends on the parameter change.
The sparse GP must therefore be updated by a matching amount, without increasing the shared prediction-error objective.
To this end, we introduce an adaptive learning rate and prediction-error-based model selection.
Since neither model update is allowed to increase the shared objective, the objective is provably non-increasing and convergent over the recursion.
Given the same limited on-track data, the resulting model achieves higher prediction accuracy than either model learned alone.
The overall contributions are summarized as follows:

A semi-parametric dynamics learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual model from on-track data in autonomous racing;

An interactive recursive learning scheme in which the two models guide each other’s updates under a shared objective, accounting for their mutual dependence;

A sparse GP learning strategy in which an adaptive learning rate scales each GP update with the parameter change, and prediction-error-based model selection ensures that the objective is non-increasing and convergent over the recursion; and

Evaluation through numerical simulations and real-world autonomous racing experiments, demonstrating improved dynamics prediction accuracy and lap time.

1. A semi-parametric dynamics learning framework that learns both the physical parameters and the residual model from on-track data in autonomous racing;

2. An interactive recursive learning scheme in which the two models guide each other’s updates under a shared objective, accounting for their mutual dependence;

3. A sparse GP learning strategy in which an adaptive learning rate scales each GP update with the parameter change, and prediction-error-based model selection ensures that the objective is non-increasing and convergent over the recursion; and

4. Evaluation through numerical simulations and real-world autonomous racing experiments, demonstrating improved dynamics prediction accuracy and lap time.

title: Humanoid robots for safety-critical electrical switching: A perception-informed runtime constraint filter
authors: Songyang Liu,Yu Hou,Yuqing Hu,Shuai Li
abstract: Humanoid robots can reduce personnel exposure in electrical switching, but safe control is challenging because the tool must reach a target switch next to similar devices, where an imprecise operator command can contact a non-target switch. This study proposes a runtime safety filter that checks each operator command during virtual-reality teleoperation of a humanoid robot. The filter integrates a scene model estimated from the robot’s head camera and a target-conditioned control barrier function quadratic program that keeps the tool away from the non-target switch while passing safe commands unchanged. In real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, with six rounds at each of two standing positions, target operations succeed in all ten rounds with an unchanged target and no non-target actuation. A simulation study achieves 9/9 safe completions, compared with 5/9 for raw teleoperation, demonstrating the feasibility of the method for humanoid switching operations.
introduction:
Electrical substations are critical infrastructure in modern power systems, where
transmission and distribution equipment must be switched, isolated, restored, and
verified to maintain grid reliability. Although a switching action may appear to
be a simple physical operation, such as opening or closing a disconnect switch,
breaker, or switchgear handle, power-system switching is a safety-critical
procedure performed near equipment that is or may be energized. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) requires
safety-related work practices to prevent electric shock and other injuries when
employees work on or near energized equipment or circuits; exposed live parts
shall generally be de-energized before work is performed unless de-energization
is infeasible or introduces additional hazards, and only qualified persons may
work on energized equipment under appropriate precautions
(Occupational Safety and Health Administration, 2024). These requirements indicate that switching is not merely
a manipulation problem, but a hazardous intervention task involving electrical
risk, procedural control, and human safety (Fig. 1, left). Utility switching manuals further show that switching must be executed as an
authorized and verified sequence rather than as an isolated device actuation.
The Snohomish County Public Utility District switching and clearance manual
establishes the authority, responsibilities, and procedures for system operation,
clearance, and switching, and states that system operators issue orders to open
and close switches, place or remove safety cards, and de-energize or clear
equipment (Snohomish County Public Utility District No. 1, 2026). Similarly, the Platte River Power
Authority power-system switching procedure requires the switchman to carry the
switching program, verify the device identification nameplate and location,
recheck the correct sequence, operate the device, and verify that the device has
moved to the desired position (Platte River Power Authority, 2021). These procedures
highlight that electrical safety switching requires not only physical manipulation,
but also perception, target identification, communication, operator supervision,
and post-operation verification (Fig. 2). This work addresses the physical operation step of this workflow.

Robots have increasingly been introduced into substations to reduce human
exposure and improve inspection efficiency. Existing substation robots are
commonly designed for autonomous patrol, visual inspection, thermal imaging,
gauge reading, and anomaly detection. Recent work on substation inspection
robots focuses on navigation, multi-sensor fusion, obstacle perception, and
route-based inspection in complex substation environments
(Yang et al., 2025). Industrial deployments of mobile and quadruped
robots similarly emphasize routine visual and thermal inspection of
transformers, breakers, and other assets (Avangrid, 2024). These
systems are valuable for monitoring and condition assessment, but they do not
fully address contact-rich switching operations that require human-scale
reachability, accurate end-effector alignment, controlled force interaction, and
verification of a mechanical state change on legacy equipment. In contrast,
device-specific remote switching or racking systems can reduce human exposure
for particular switchgear, but they often require pre-installed hardware,
compatible equipment, or task-specific adaptation.

This motivates the use of humanoid robots for safety switching. The goal
is not to claim that humanoids are universally superior to wheeled robots,
quadrupeds, fixed manipulators, or specialized remote actuators. Rather, the
motivation is that many electrical facilities and operating procedures are
designed around human morphology and human tool use. Switch handles, access
holes, cabinet layouts, doors, stairs, narrow passages, and hot-stick-style
interfaces implicitly assume human reach, posture, bimanual operation, and
visual confirmation. Humanoid robots provide a human-scale body, arms, mobile
base, and whole-body redundancy that can potentially reuse existing
human-centered infrastructure with less environmental modification. This
advantage is particularly relevant when the target facility is not redesigned
for automation and when the robot must act as a remote physical avatar in a
workspace originally intended for human operators. A fixed or rail-mounted arm can operate a known device reliably, but it must be installed at each panel and reaches only the devices within its workspace. A mobile manipulator avoids this installation, yet its base and arm height are usually chosen for a particular task, and stairs, doorways and raised thresholds in older facilities can restrict where it can go. A humanoid can, in principle, walk to a panel, stand where a worker would stand and use the same handles and tools. The method proposed in this paper, however, does not depend on the humanoid form: it filters the arm command and could be placed on another manipulator. What the humanoid adds to the safety problem is that the robot stands at a different place each time it approaches a panel, so the position of the neighboring devices relative to the arm changes from one visit to the next and cannot be fixed by a one-off calibration. For this reason, the constraints in this work are rebuilt from the robot’s own head camera at its current standing position.

Using robots can reduce human exposure to electrical hazards, but it does not eliminate the hazards themselves. Human workers near energized equipment rely on arc-rated clothing and insulated tools, and a robot near the same equipment would also need protection, since its sensors, motors and onboard computers can be damaged by an arc or disturbed by electromagnetic fields. This study focuses on the motion of the robot relative to neighboring devices, and protection of the robot itself is discussed in our Discussion section.
Fig. 1 (right) shows the humanoid used in this study at a pair of neighboring safety switches.

Safety-switch operation is not only a precision-control problem. Its main safety challenge comes from intentional contact with a selected switch in a confined workspace, next to neighboring devices of the same type, with limited operator visibility and imperfect or delayed teleoperation commands. The robot must be allowed to contact the target switch with its designated tool or finger, while its arms, hands, torso and tool stay clear of the cabinet and neighboring switches, and which device counts as the target changes with the operator’s selection. A safety layer for this task therefore has to correct unsafe operator commands continuously, adapt its constraints to the selected target, and stop inward motion toward a non-target device in a way that an unchanged operator command cannot restart.

In this paper, we present a runtime safety filter for virtual-reality (VR) teleoperation of a humanoid robot on neighboring safety switches. Here, runtime means that our filter operates inside the control loop while the robot is being teleoperated: in every control cycle, it checks the operator’s command against the scene model before the command is sent to the robot, and modifies the command only when it would bring the tool too close to a non-target device. This differs from approaches that plan a safe motion in advance or train safe behavior offline. An operator commands the robot’s arms through a PICO headset, and an existing retargeting and whole-body control stack generates the nominal command. Instead of replacing this stack with a task-specific learned policy, we insert a minimum-intervention filter between its upper-body command and the robot. A scene model estimated from the robot’s head red-green-blue-depth (RGB-D) camera defines the constraints, and the operator’s choice of target decides which objects they apply to. Safe commands pass through unchanged, and at the boundary the arm returns to its initial pose and waits for re-authorization. No reinforcement- or imitation-learning training is required. We evaluate the filter on a physical Unitree G1 operating two wall-mounted safety switches. Separately, in a MuJoCo pushbutton task, we extend it with part-region contact permissions and phase-dependent motion directions, and compare it with raw teleoperation and two ablations.

We make the following contributions:

We propose a target-conditioned runtime safety filter for humanoid teleoperation, which uses an onboard RGB-D scene model to keep the tool away from non-target devices while leaving the selected target reachable, passes safe commands unchanged, and adds part-region and phase constraints in simulation.

We conduct experiments on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot (10/12 operator-reported target operations, no non-target actuation) and in a paired simulation study (9/9 safe completions versus 5/9 for raw teleoperation), to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

1. We propose a target-conditioned runtime safety filter for humanoid teleoperation, which uses an onboard RGB-D scene model to keep the tool away from non-target devices while leaving the selected target reachable, passes safe commands unchanged, and adds part-region and phase constraints in simulation.

2. We conduct experiments on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot (10/12 operator-reported target operations, no non-target actuation) and in a paired simulation study (9/9 safe completions versus 5/9 for raw teleoperation), to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method.

title: BRINA: Bottom-Referenced Inertial Navigation with AKAZE, a Sonar SLAM for Autonomous Marine Vehicles
authors: Adolfo Damiano Cafaro,Patrizio Mariani,Roberto Galeazzi
abstract: Forward-looking sonar (FLS) provides reliable underwater perception where optical sensing is limited, but its use for navigation is hindered by the unobserved elevation of each return. As a result, motion estimated directly from sonar images suffers from an unknown metric scale that is commonly resolved using a Doppler velocity log (DVL). We present Brina (Bottom-Referenced Inertial Navigation with AKAZE), a sonar–inertial SLAM system for marine vehicles that uses the FLS as its only exteroceptive sensor. Brina estimates the sonar altitude from the first seabed return in each beam and uses it to project matched features onto the seabed, providing metric odometry without a DVL. We further derive a bound relating the remaining scale error to seabed tilt and slope variability. The method is evaluated in simulation with an autonomous underwater vehicle, and in field experiments with uncrewed surface vehicles over ten missions, using two FLS systems under different operating conditions.
introduction:
Marine vehicles surveying the seabed and inspecting critical infrastructure require reliable localisation when external positioning is unavailable or untrusted. For uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs), GNSS can be degraded by multipath and shadowing near harbour structures, or falsified by spoofing [1, 2]. LiDAR SLAM provides an alternative near quays and bridges, but depends on sufficient above-water structure [3], which open water may not provide. For autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs), GNSS is unavailable while submerged, and visual odometry can be degraded by turbidity, poor illumination and limited visibility [4]. These limitations motivate navigation using onboard observations of the underwater environment.

Forward-looking sonar (FLS) provides acoustic imagery for inspection and mapping in conditions that challenge optical sensing [5]. Using these observations for odometry, however, requires accounting for their geometry. An FLS measures metric slant range and bearing but does not resolve elevation within its vertical beam. Consequently, interpreting image displacement as horizontal motion can introduce feature-dependent scale errors: the conversion depends on the unknown position of each return within the beam. Previous methods address this geometry through planar approximations, additional navigation sensors or multiview estimation [6, 7, 8, 9]. Here, we investigate how the seabed return itself can constrain feature projection and how departures from the assumed seabed geometry affect the estimated motion.

We present Brina (Bottom-Referenced Inertial Navigation with AKAZE), a sonar–inertial SLAM system for marine vehicles using the FLS as its only exteroceptive sensor. Under a locally horizontal seabed model, the range
of the first seabed return, termed the seabed edge, provides an altitude estimate using the known beam geometry and IMU-estimated roll and pitch. This altitude is used to project static seabed features into
horizontal coordinates before motion estimation. The resulting odometry is fused with IMU preintegration and loop closures in a factor graph. The sonar observations also support 3-D seabed mapping. The approach
targets seabed-observing survey motion on surface and underwater platforms.

The main contributions are:

Brina, a sonar–inertial SLAM system that combines seabed-edge altitude estimation, ground-projected AKAZE odometry with adaptive keyframe selection, and loop closures using sonar mosaics and seabed submaps.

An analysis of the elevation-induced scale error. We identify motion conditions under which inertial measurements cannot separate scale from accelerometer bias, and derive a model and bound relating the remaining odometry error to seabed tilt and slope variability.

Extensive simulation and experimental results: evaluation with an AUV in simulation over ten seabeds spanning tilt and roughness, and with USVs in ten field missions at six sites. The field trials use a BlueView at two frequencies and an Oculus in calm water and waves. Together, these evaluations assess the error model, trajectory accuracy and loop closures.

Acoustic navigation.
Sonar-based navigation encompasses several sensing geometries and sensor combinations. Imaging-sonar SLAM has fused acoustic constraints with odometry from a Doppler velocity log (DVL) and an IMU [7], while camera–sonar methods use acoustic measurements to recover monocular scale [10]. Side-scan sonar correspondences have constrained AUV trajectories through loop closures added to dead reckoning [11]. Multibeam echosounder bathymetry has also supported SLAM with an IMU and no DVL [12]. These approaches establish acoustic observations as navigation measurements, while differing in the geometry measured and the additional information required.

FLS odometry and elevation.
Image-registration methods support FLS mosaicking [6], while multiview formulations estimate motion and scene structure while accounting for sonar degeneracies [8]. Franchi et al. [13] also demonstrate DVL-free navigation by estimating velocity from FLS imagery within an adaptive navigation filter. Our focus is the seabed reference used to correct feature projection before registration and the scale error that remains when the seabed departs from that reference.

Seabed projection and the seabed edge.
The closest geometric precedent is Henson and Zakharov [14], who estimate attitude and trajectory using a planar scene model. Their extension estimates pitch and altitude from the first and last illuminated points, assuming a flat scene and known vertical beamwidth. Brina combines the seabed edge with IMU attitude, avoiding the need to detect the far boundary of the footprint. It integrates this altitude estimate into sonar–inertial SLAM and quantifies how seabed geometry affects odometric scale. Compared with previous sonar-plane odometry [9], it replaces a fixed image-to-motion conversion with altitude-dependent ground projection.

Section II introduces the measurement model and scale problem; Section III presents the system and error analysis; Section IV reports the experiments; and Section V concludes.

title: Generalist Action Critic: Harnessing Frontier Models in Autonomous Driving
authors: Yun Yan,Shizhi Hu,Zhichao Li,Yang Guan,Shiqi Liu,Jiaxin Gao,Xiangteng Zhang,Wenbo Ding,Jiuhua Zhao,Hui Guo,Xintao Yan,Keqiang Li,Shengbo Eben Li
abstract: Frontier models have demonstrated remarkable general-purpose reasoning capabilities, opening new possibilities for intelligent decision making in the physical world. In autonomous driving, many recent approaches seek to leverage these capabilities through additional adaptation for action output, particularly in scenarios where existing models underperform. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a zero-shot framework that combines frontier models’ general-purpose reasoning with the planning competence of specialized driving models through an inference-time harness. In GAC, specialized planners generate multiple candidate trajectories and make an initial selection, while a frozen frontier model serves as an action critic that assesses the selected trajectory against scene evidence and either retains it or reselects from the available candidates. The harness combines camera images with spatial overlays, provides driving context and reasoning principles through textual instructions, and regulates the information available at each stage to support trajectory assessment and reselection. On HUGSIM, GAC raises DrivoR’s HD-Score to 43.2, achieving state-of-the-art performance among methods trained without additional simulation data. GAC also consistently improves closed-loop driving safety across three planners, with relative HD-Score gains of up to 32.1%. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 further reveal how GAC improves planning performance by correcting up to 52.13% of eligible unsafe trajectory selections while introducing new failures in only 0.67% of originally high-quality selections. These results demonstrate the potential of harnessing frontier models to improve driving safety through inference-time cooperation with specialized planners.
introduction:
Recent advances in artificial intelligence have significantly expanded the capabilities of general-purpose models. From language understanding and generation to multimodal reasoning, complex problem solving, and tool use, frontier models are breaking traditional boundaries in the range of tasks that general-purpose AI can perform [2, 3]. This progress has now reached the physical world, with recent studies demonstrating GPT-6 Astra’s strong spatial reasoning and decision-making capabilities in robotic manipulation, navigation, and other embodied AI tasks [4, 5].

Autonomous driving is a representative domain of embodied AI, requiring systems to connect scene understanding with driving decisions and vehicle control [6, 7, 1, 8]. Existing approaches organize these capabilities through different architectures, including planning-oriented end-to-end (E2E) [9, 1, 10, 11], vision-language-action (VLA) [12, 13, 14, 15], and world–action models (WAM) [16, 17], as illustrated in Figure 1. Despite their different architectures, these paradigms have largely advanced through task-specific training and adaptation. As frontier models continue to advance, a key question is how to directly leverage their general-purpose reasoning capabilities to improve driving decisions.

Multi-candidate planning provides a concrete setting for exploring this question. The inherently multimodal nature of driving behavior has motivated a growing shift from predicting a single trajectory toward generating multiple candidate trajectories [18, 19]. Effective candidate selection is therefore essential to realizing the full potential of multimodal planning. Yet existing planners do not always select the best available trajectories, leaving a gap between candidate generation and selection [20]. Frontier models’ strong spatial reasoning offers a promising way to address this gap.

To this end, we introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a new paradigm for autonomous driving that combines general-purpose frontier models with specialized driving planners through inference-time cooperation. Rather than adapting frontier models for driving action output, GAC directly employs them as action critics to assess and improve the decisions of specialized driving systems. In this work, we instantiate GAC for multi-candidate trajectory planning, where the critic evaluates the planner’s initial selection and reselects from the available candidates when needed. Effective trajectory assessment requires understanding how candidate trajectories interact with the surrounding environment and determining whether they are safe and appropriate for the driving situation. We therefore develop an evidence-grounded inference harness that integrates layered visual representations with a structured reasoning context to support selective decision revision. We envision GAC as a step toward a new generation of autonomous driving paradigms, where advances in general-purpose intelligence and specialized planning can jointly shape future driving systems.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a new paradigm for autonomous driving that enables zero-shot, inference-time cooperation between general-purpose frontier models and specialized driving planners.

We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a new paradigm for autonomous driving that enables zero-shot, inference-time cooperation between general-purpose frontier models and specialized driving planners.

We develop an evidence-grounded inference harness that integrates layered visual representations, a structured reasoning context, and selective decision revision to support trajectory evaluation based on scene evidence.

We demonstrate GAC’s effectiveness across three driving planners on HUGSIM and NAVSIM v1. GAC improves HD-Score by up to 32.1%, increases DrivoR’s HD-Score to 43.2 on the full HUGSIM benchmark, and recovers up to 52.13% of eligible zero-score failures.

1. We introduce Generalist Action Critic (GAC), a new paradigm for autonomous driving that enables zero-shot, inference-time cooperation between general-purpose frontier models and specialized driving planners.

2. We develop an evidence-grounded inference harness that integrates layered visual representations, a structured reasoning context, and selective decision revision to support trajectory evaluation based on scene evidence.

title: EvoTER: Evolving Embodied Agents via Tool-Use Experience and Reflection
authors: Yingting Zhou,Yuyin Zhou,Yongliang Wang,Haoran Li,Dongbin Zhao
abstract:
Long-horizon embodied tasks require agents to ground instructions in changing observations, coordinate heterogeneous tools, and recover from failures that can propagate through downstream operations.
Although existing LLM-based agents retain experience and refine reusable skills, successful local repairs do not by themselves establish complete-task gains over the current shared procedure library.
We present EvoTER, an experience-driven framework that enables embodied agents to self-evolve tool-use skills without updating model parameters.
EvoTER operates through a three-role evolution loop: Explorer records tool-use trajectories;
Diagnoser distills successful and failed executions into skills for tool selection,
parameter computation, postcondition checks, and recovery;
and Validator retains candidate revisions only when they improve complete-task success in fresh sessions.
In simulation, EvoTER improves overall task success from a pre-evolution baseline of 53.60%53.60\% to 80.40%80.40\%. In real-world experiments, simulation initialization reduces the attempts required to acquire short-horizon skills, while continued real-world evolution improves long-horizon success from 20%20\% to 80%80\%–100%100\% across tasks and enables the evolving skill library to incorporate new tool functionality introduced after simulation development.
Project website: https://evoter-project.github.io/.
introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) enable embodied agents to translate natural-language instructions into executable programs over robotic APIs [1, 2]. By interleaving reasoning, tool calls, and execution feedback, LLM-based agents coordinate perception, planning, and control for multi-step tasks [3]. Integrating pretrained visuomotor policies, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, further extends this repertoire by combining learned manipulation behaviors with conventional robotic tools [4].
However, reliable long-horizon execution remains challenging, as errors in perception, tool coordination, and physical interaction can propagate across dependent steps.

These challenges motivate four complementary capabilities for reusable tool-use procedures: (i) Grounding: deriving tool arguments from current observations [1]; (ii) Composition: coordinating heterogeneous tools as subtasks and scene conditions change [4]; (iii) Verification: checking physical outcomes and recovering from execution deviations [5]; and (iv) Adaptability: supporting reuse and refinement under changing physical conditions and tool interfaces [6]. These capabilities interact during execution, complicating procedure reuse across changing task states and environments.

Existing agents exploit execution feedback at different levels: closed-loop agents use it for execution and recovery [3, 5], but such corrections do not necessarily yield reusable knowledge. Memory-guided agents retain experience [7, 4], while self-improving systems revise reusable skills [6, 8]. In tool-use settings, such revisions can modify tool selection, state-dependent parameter computation, sequencing, and recovery. Recent approaches assess revisions in different ways: transfer studies validate memory or stack updates before frozen target evaluation [9, 10],
whereas feedback-driven systems use execution and regression checks during refinement [6, 8].
However, successful repairs or regression checks do not necessarily establish complete-task gains over the current shared library, as local changes may affect downstream operations. This issue becomes particularly relevant after sim-to-real transfer, where physical feedback can reveal new failures and motivate further revisions. With model parameters and tool implementations fixed within each evolution phase,
we ask: How can agents select revisions based on complete-task gains over the current library to continually evolve reusable tool-use procedure libraries for long-horizon tasks across simulation and real-world refinement?

To address this question, EvoTER evolves a persistent library of reusable, observation-grounded tool-use skills through feedback-driven revision and comparative complete-task acceptance. These skills support heterogeneous tool composition, postcondition checks, and recovery. The evolution loop comprises three roles sharing a frozen multimodal LLM: Explorer collects execution trajectories, Diagnoser identifies failures and proposes revisions, and Validator compares candidate and current libraries on matched complete-task runs. Only revisions improving aggregate complete-task validation success over the current library are retained. Model parameters, tool implementations, and evaluation settings remain fixed per evolution phase for controlled comparisons. Privileged simulation feedback may aid diagnosis, while skill execution and validation rollouts use only deployment-available observations and tools. Validated simulation skills initialize real-world evolution, where physical feedback triggers further revision-and-acceptance cycles. In simulation, EvoTER achieves a 26.8026.80 percentage-point gain in overall task success over its pre-evolution baseline. On real robots, simulation initialization reduces short-horizon skill-acquisition attempts, while continued evolution adapts long-horizon procedures to real-world conditions and tool interfaces. Our contributions are as follows:

We propose EvoTER, a framework organizing tool invocation, composition, outcome checks, and recovery into reusable, observation-grounded skills for long-horizon tasks without updating model parameters.

We introduce an Explorer–Diagnoser–Validator loop that turns execution and simulation data into skills for real-world use, selects revisions by task-success gains, and continues evolving skills from real-world feedback.

We demonstrate superior performance in simulation, and real-world experiments further confirm that simulation-initialized skills reduce development attempts while continued evolution supports long-horizon execution.

1. We propose EvoTER, a framework organizing tool invocation, composition, outcome checks, and recovery into reusable, observation-grounded skills for long-horizon tasks without updating model parameters.

2. We introduce an Explorer–Diagnoser–Validator loop that turns execution and simulation data into skills for real-world use, selects revisions by task-success gains, and continues evolving skills from real-world feedback.

3. We demonstrate superior performance in simulation, and real-world experiments further confirm that simulation-initialized skills reduce development attempts while continued evolution supports long-horizon execution.

2. 是否属于 World Model：是 + 理由：EvoTER的核心在于通过记录和分析工具使用的轨迹，学习如何在不同的环境和任务状态下进行工具调用和技能修正。这种对未来状态和观察的预测与评估符合World Model的定义，尤其是在进行技能进化和验证时。

3. 是否属于 VLA：是 + 理由：论文中提到的LLM（大型语言模型）使得具身智能体能够将自然语言指令转化为可执行的机器人技能，这表明输入包含视觉和语言信息，输出是机器人动作，因此符合VLA的定义。

4. 是否属于 Humanoid Loco-manipulation：否 + 理由：尽管论文涉及工具使用和技能进化，但没有明确提到使用人形机器人（humanoid）进行联合的运动和操控控制。任务的描述更侧重于工具的使用和技能的进化，而不是具体的人形机器人运动和操控。

5. 最终标签总结：
   - World Model: 是
   - VLA: 是
   - Humanoid Loco-manipulation: 否

6. 如果有歧义，请说明最容易混淆的点：
   最容易混淆的点在于EvoTER框架中提到的工具使用和技能进化可能让人联想到复杂的运动和操控任务，但实际上并未明确涉及人形机器人的整体协调控制，因此在Humanoid Loco-manipulation的分类上存在一定的模糊性。

title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zhenxuan Fan,Zhuoya Wang,Yuqian Yuan,Wenqiao Zhang,Juncheng Li,Jun Xiao,Siliang Tang,Yueting Zhuang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
abstract:
Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer
a promising approach to robotic manipulation,
yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization,
uncertain failure attribution, and limited
reuse of execution experience.
We propose Embodied-Harness, a
dual-agent framework that improves manipulation
by refining the execution harness without updating
model parameters.
The Actor interacts with the environment through
a robot-control interface, while the Reflector
converts execution evidence into reusable
operational guidance.
Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution
context and long-term experiential knowledge
to support execution and reflection.
Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis
in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness
Self-Improvement refines operational guidance
across successive attempts.
Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench
demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness
in generalization under environmental variations,
spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and
memory-dependent manipulation.
Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%,
76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks,
respectively.
Real-world evaluation further yields an average
success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks.
These results highlight the potential of
Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation
through experience-driven harness self-improvement.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation is a fundamental capability of
embodied intelligence Billard and Kragic (2019); Kroemer et al. (2021); Duan et al. (2022), enabling robots to interact
with the physical world and perform diverse tasks
across household assistance Li et al. (2023); Fu et al. (2025), industrial manufacturing Narang et al. (2022); Tang et al. (2023),
and healthcare Dupont et al. (2021); Kim et al. (2025a).
Developing general manipulation capabilities
is essential for enabling versatile and autonomous
robotic operation in real-world environments,
representing a critical step toward general
embodied intelligence (GEI) Firoozi et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025a); Team et al. (2025).

Towards this goal, different paradigms have emerged
for robotic manipulation.
End-to-end frameworks, including vision-language-action
(VLA) models Zitkovich et al. (2023); Kim et al. (2025b); NVIDIA et al. (2025); Black et al. (2025a); Shukor et al. (2025); Zheng et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026) and world-action models (WAMs) Hu et al. (2025a); Bi et al. (2026); Kim et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026a); Ye et al. (2026); Yuan et al. (2026), have
demonstrated remarkable progress in learning robotic
policies from multimodal inputs.
However, these approaches often rely on large-scale
robotic datasets, face challenges in generalizing
to unseen environments O’Neill et al. (2024); Khazatsky et al. (2024); Ma et al. (2026), and struggle with reliable
long-horizon manipulation Mees et al. (2022); Liu et al. (2023a); Fan et al. (2026).
In contrast, agentic frameworks leverage the reasoning
and planning capabilities of vision-language models
(VLMs) to decompose complex tasks and coordinate
robot actions ichter et al. (2023); Liang et al. (2023); Huang et al. (2023a); Wang et al. (2026a).
Such frameworks support flexible action planning and
feedback-driven execution, offering a promising
alternative without requiring task-specific updates
to the underlying model parameters Huang et al. (2023b); Duan et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2026).

Despite these advantages, agentic frameworks still face
several challenges in achieving reliable robotic
manipulation.
(i) Inadequate Memory Organization.
Many real-world manipulation tasks are inherently
long-horizon, requiring agents to track task progress
and detailed execution histories while retaining
experience across attempts and tasks Park et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2024); Zhang et al. (2025a); Chen et al. (2026a).
Managing such information across different temporal
scales and levels of granularity remains challenging.
(ii) Uncertain Failure Attribution.
Manipulation failures may stem from inaccurate action
grounding, unsatisfied preconditions, or violated
state constraints Liu et al. (2023b); Duan et al. (2025b); Xia et al. (2025).
However, execution feedback often reveals only
observable outcomes rather than underlying causes,
making it difficult to identify critical errors
and derive reliable operational guidance.
(iii) Limited Self-Improvement Capability.
Even when agents identify execution errors and
extract useful insights, these reflections may remain
isolated from subsequent executions.
Without mechanisms to accumulate, validate, and
refine operational guidance across attempts,
agents may repeatedly encounter similar failures Shinn et al. (2023); Zhao et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024).

To address these challenges, we propose
Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework
for robotic manipulation that enables recursive
harness self-improvement through accumulated
execution experience (Fig. ).
The framework comprises two complementary roles,
an Actor and a Reflector.
The Actor interacts with the environment through
control interfaces, while the Reflector analyzes
execution trajectories and environmental feedback
to improve subsequent task execution.
Specifically, Embodied-Harness incorporates three
complementary mechanisms:
(i) Hierarchical Memory Architecture
organizes short-term execution context and long-term
experiential knowledge across different temporal scales;
(ii) Evidence-based Experience Reflection
identifies potential failure causes from execution
evidence and derives actionable operational guidance;
and (iii) Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
refines the execution harness using accumulated
guidance, with subsequent execution feedback
informing further reflection and refinement.
Together, these mechanisms enable continual
improvement in robotic manipulation without updating
the underlying model parameters.

We evaluate Embodied-Harness on three robotic
manipulation benchmarks, RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA,
and RMBench, covering generalization under
environmental variations, fine-grained spatial
reasoning, long-horizon procedural planning, and
memory-dependent manipulation.
Embodied-Harness outperforms baselines spanning
VLA models, WAMs, and agentic frameworks,
achieving average success rates of 82.4%,
76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks,
respectively.
Real-world evaluation further yields an average
success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation
tasks.
Ablation studies and further analyses
support the effectiveness of the proposed
components and illustrate how accumulated
experience enables more reliable manipulation.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose Embodied-Harness, an experience-driven
dual-agent framework that improves robotic
manipulation through complementary execution
and reflection without updating model parameters.

We design a Hierarchical Memory Architecture
that integrates short-term working memory and
long-term experiential memory to support coherent
task execution and effective experience reuse.

We introduce Evidence-based Experience
Reflection and Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
to derive actionable guidance from execution
feedback and refine the harness across
successive attempts.

We conduct extensive experiments on three
robotic manipulation benchmarks and real-world
tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of
Embodied-Harness across diverse manipulation
settings.

1. We propose Embodied-Harness, an experience-driven
dual-agent framework that improves robotic
manipulation through complementary execution
and reflection without updating model parameters.

2. We design a Hierarchical Memory Architecture
that integrates short-term working memory and
long-term experiential memory to support coherent
task execution and effective experience reuse.

3. We introduce Evidence-based Experience
Reflection and Recursive Harness Self-Improvement
to derive actionable guidance from execution
feedback and refine the harness across
successive attempts.

4. We conduct extensive experiments on three
robotic manipulation benchmarks and real-world
tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of
Embodied-Harness across diverse manipulation
settings.

title: Trust What Repeats: Capped World-Model Policy Gradients for Humanoid Motion Tracking
authors: Xuzhe Dang,Stefan Edelkamp
abstract:
Training a humanoid motion tracker by backpropagating imagined returns through a learned world model is fast, because
the model gives a first-order policy gradient. We ask how much of that gradient holds in the simulator. On a tracker
for the Unitree G1, the 0.5%0.5\% of imagined rollouts with the largest gradients carry 22%22\% of the summed gradient
norm, yet neither a second rollout from the same state nor the simulator confirms them. When the actions are moved
along the model’s gradient, the simulator returns 94%94\% of the predicted change in return where the gradient norm is
below the batch median, 48%48\% between 33 and 1010 times the median, and 1%1\% above 3030 times; the part of a
gradient that either check confirms stops growing at a few times the median. We therefore cap each rollout’s
action-gradient norm at 1010 times the batch median, draw imagination starts in proportion to their predicted gradient
norm so that the cap removes less, and reset episodes where the world model and critic predict the lowest return.
Trained on 223 hours of motion and tested on 353 motions that no actor performed in training, the method raises the
normalized return of SuperMimic, the baseline it builds on, from 0.9530.953 to 0.9670.967 and the lowest 1%1\% of test clips
from 0.650.65 to 0.760.76, halves the test clips that fall persistently, from 1515–1818 to 77–1010, and reaches the
baseline’s final return in 40%40\% of the baseline’s iterations and half its training time. On LAFAN1, trained and
evaluated on the same clips as prior work, it reaches 0.9350.935 against 0.9060.906.
introduction:
A general motion tracker turns a library of human motion into a single policy that a humanoid can run: given the
next frames of a reference, the policy outputs joint targets that make the robot follow it. Such trackers are the
low-level layer under teleoperation, motion generation and learned skills, and their quality is set by how many
motions they follow without falling and by how long they take to train. With model-free reinforcement learning the
second number is large: trackers for libraries of a hundred hours and more are trained for days on many
GPUs [1, 2, 3].

SuperMimic [4] changed that. It fits a world model to the simulator’s transitions and improves the
policy by backpropagating the imagined return through the model, a first-order gradient that needs no likelihood
ratio and no exploration in action space. The authors report the return of a strong model-free tracker after hours
on one GPU. The price of a first-order gradient is known from differentiable simulation: through contact and over
long horizons the gradient of a rollout can be large, wrong, or both [5, 6, 7], and a model that is
accurate in its predictions need not be accurate in its derivatives.

This paper measures that price for motion tracking and removes most of it. It rests on two measurements on a
trained tracker.

A few rollouts carry the gradient. Among imagined rollouts, the 0.5%0.5\% whose action-gradient norm GG
exceeds 3030 times the batch median hold 22%22\% of the summed norm and 99%99\% of the summed squared norm, while
88%88\% of rollouts lie below 33 times the median. Heavy tails of this kind are known for gradients through
simulators [7] and were reported for humanoid tracking in concurrent
work [8]; what has not been asked is whether the tail is signal.

The large gradients are not backed. We roll the same start state out twice under independent sensor noise
and ask how much of one rollout’s gradient the other reproduces; and we set the simulator to states from the replay
buffer, step it along the model’s gradient, and ask how much of the predicted change of the return appears. The two
tests agree (Fig. 1). Up to about 33 times the median, both confirm most of a gradient’s norm. Beyond
that the confirmed part stops growing: from 55 times on, both confirm about 33 to 44 times the median whatever
the norm, and the simulator returns 48%48\% of the
model’s predicted change between 33 and 1010 times the median, 12%12\% between 1010 and 3030 times and 1%1\% above.

The part of a rollout’s gradient that both tests confirm is thus roughly min⁡(G,k⋅med⁡G)\min(G,k\cdot\operatorname{med}G), with med⁡G\operatorname{med}G
the batch median and kk a few units, and we make that the update rule: the norm of each rollout’s action gradient
is capped at k=10k=10 times the batch median. The cap acts as a trust region on the model’s derivative, set per
rollout and measured against the batch’s own median. Two further changes go with it. Start states whose gradients
the cap would cut are drawn more often and weighted down, which leaves the expected gradient unchanged and gives
the cap less to remove. And episodes are reset where the world model and critic predict the lowest return, ranked
over the whole library every 2,000 iterations, which directs data to the motions the policy cannot yet follow and
finds them without first visiting them.

We evaluate on a split that no tracker of this kind has reported, to our knowledge: BONES-SEED retargeted to the
Unitree G1, divided by motion, so that no test motion was performed by any actor in training. On 11,828 test clips of 353 unseen motions and three seeds, the method raises the
normalized return from 0.9530.953 to 0.9670.967, the lowest 1%1\% of clips from 0.650.65 to 0.760.76, and halves the clips
that fall in at least half of the last six snapshots (Fig. 4). It passes the baseline’s final test return at 10,00010{,}000 of 25,00025{,}000
iterations, after 1.21.2 hours against 2.42.4 to 2.62.6. The cap is what raises the mean and the model-ranked resets
what raise the tail; the start draw adds little at this scale. Doubling the baseline’s learning rate gives it about a third of the
method’s gain at 15,00015{,}000 iterations and none of the drop in failing clips. On LAFAN1, the motion set on which this line of work reports results, the method reaches 0.9350.935
against 0.9060.906 and passes the baseline’s final return at 7,6007{,}600 to 9,6009{,}600 of 15,00015{,}000 iterations.

Our contributions are:

two tests of a world model’s policy gradient, one against a redraw of the same start and one against the
simulator, and the finding that both level off at a few times the batch median of the gradient norm;

an update built on that finding: a cap on each rollout’s action-gradient norm, a start distribution drawn
by gradient norm, which reduces what the cap removes without adding bias but adds little once the resets are
model-ranked, and a reset distribution for motion tracking that is
ranked by the world model and critic instead of by visits;

an evaluation of world-model motion tracking on motions unseen in training, with ablations of each part, on
two versions of the Unitree G1, and a comparison on LAFAN1.

1. two tests of a world model’s policy gradient, one against a redraw of the same start and one against the
simulator, and the finding that both level off at a few times the batch median of the gradient norm;

2. an update built on that finding: a cap on each rollout’s action-gradient norm, a start distribution drawn
by gradient norm, which reduces what the cap removes without adding bias but adds little once the resets are
model-ranked, and a reset distribution for motion tracking that is
ranked by the world model and critic instead of by visits;

3. an evaluation of world-model motion tracking on motions unseen in training, with ablations of each part, on
two versions of the Unitree G1, and a comparison on LAFAN1.

title: SOAR: Training-Free Rank-Consistent Rollout Compression for Latent World Model Planning
authors: Anqi Li,Kai Liu,Linghe Kong,Yulun Zhang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: including supplementary material. Anqi Li and Kai Liu contributed equally
abstract:
Latent world models plan by rolling out hundreds of candidate action sequences through a transformer predictor, so a single decision can take tens of seconds.
Existing accelerations prune spatial tokens as in vision-language models, yet a sampling-based planner uses predicted costs only to rank candidates, so a rollout can be compressed freely as long as the ranking survives.
We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression to each planning decision.
At every decision, SOAR probes a few candidates under several token budgets and keeps the smallest budget that preserves their ranking, so it compresses as far as the current decision allows, without task labels.
A closed-loop study of more than 80,000 episodes fixes the rest of the rollout: the first step, which alone reads a real observation, stays exact, and the context frame is cached rather than recomputed.
On seven navigation and manipulation tasks with frozen checkpoints, SOAR matches dense-level planning success at 2.3×2.3\times speedup and retains 98% at 2.5×2.5\times.
Our code is available at https://github.com/starrywiki/SOAR.
introduction:
Latent world models [20, 2, 14] plan by imagination.
At every decision, the cross-entropy method (CEM) [12] samples hundreds of action sequences, rolls each one out autoregressively through a transformer predictor over a dense grid of patch features, and keeps the candidates with the lowest predicted cost.
With the original budget, one planning call of the released JEPA-WM [14] takes 20–50 seconds on an H100 and recurs at each replanning step.

The natural remedy, and the one recent work has adopted, is token reduction.
Sparse Imagination [5], DDP-WM [18], Scope-WM [11] and CostGrad [16] all decide which spatial tokens the predictor should process in full.
This framing is inherited from vision-language models [3, 4, 15, 1], where an image is encoded once and the kept tokens must preserve its content.
A planner differs in what it consumes.
A vision-language model consumes the tokens themselves, whereas CEM consumes only an ordering: it keeps the KK lowest-cost candidates and discards the costs.
A cheaper rollout is therefore exactly as good as the dense one whenever it selects the same elites, however much its predicted features differ.
This changes the question.
Token selection asks which tokens best preserve a frame; a planner asks which computation, if removed, reorders the candidates.
Because the predictor consumes its own outputs, the answer need not be spatial: an error at the first step is inherited by every later prediction and by the cost; one at the last step is not.

We therefore take the candidate ranking as the criterion and ask along which axis a latent world-model rollout can be reduced without reordering the candidates.
We prune along four axes at comparable compute—space, the context frame, the rollout step and predictor depth—using frozen released checkpoints, the original planner budget, and more than 80,000 closed-loop episodes on seven navigation and manipulation tasks.
Three findings emerge, and together they determine the design of our method.

Which tokens matters little. At a 50% budget, rules from vision-language models are near or below random selection, and planning-aware selectors stop 5 to 8 points below the dense model, within a few points of a fixed checkerboard, as shown in Sec. 4.1.

When matters: the first step anchors the ranking. Step 0 is the only step that reads the real observation. Computing it in full and compressing only later steps recovers 5.4 points lost to spatial pruning, while spending comparable compute on the last step instead drops success to 0.66 of dense, as shown in Sec. 4.2.

Context must be kept but not recomputed. After step 0, half of the predictor’s work recomputes the previous frame only to provide keys and values. Dropping that frame is free on navigation and pushing but costs 12 to 43 points on robot-arm reaching; reusing its cached keys and values removes the trade-off and matches dense success at a 1.76×1.76\times speedup without knowing the task, as demonstrated in Secs. 4.3 and 6.

The findings also reveal that tasks differ in what they need: halving the spatial positions costs Push-T 27% of its dense successes but leaves MetaWorld Reach unchanged, whereas dropping the context frame does the opposite, as illustrated in Fig. 3b.
Once the context is cached, the only remaining question is how far the newest frame can be compressed, which varies across tasks and individual decisions.

We propose SOAR, a training-free method that adapts rollout compression online, choosing at every decision how much computation the candidate ranking needs.
At each decision, SOAR rolls out 16 candidates of the first CEM population under three nested token budgets and selects the smallest budget whose Spearman rank correlation with the full budget reaches a threshold, so each decision is compressed as far as its ranking allows.
This adaptive choice is affordable because the findings fix everything else: SOAR computes the first step in full and reads the context frame from a cache, which leaves a single scalar per decision, the token budget of the newest frame.
The probe adds 1–2% to the planning time and requires neither task labels nor training.
Without being told the task, SOAR compresses most on MetaWorld and RoboCasa, least on Maze, and differently across decisions on Push-T and Wall, as shown in . It reaches dense-level success at a 2.3×2.3\times speedup, whereas every cheaper fixed budget loses successes on tasks that need spatial detail, as detailed in Sec. 6.

Online criterion. We recast rollout compression for sampling-based planning as preserving the elite ranking rather than the predicted features, as established by Proposition 1, and show that this criterion is cheap enough to check at every decision: 16 probe candidates, 1–2% of the planning time.
Diagnosis. In a closed-loop study along four axes at comparable compute on frozen released checkpoints, we find that spatial selection saturates regardless of the selector, that the first step anchors the ranking, that the context frame must be kept but not recomputed, and that tasks fail along different axes, so no fixed budget is safe for all of them.
Method. SOAR keeps what the diagnosis shows must stay exact and lets the ranking decide the rest, reaching dense-level success at a 2.3×2.3\times speedup and 98% of it at 2.5×2.5\times with no training and no task label, while avoiding the task-specific failures of cheaper fixed budgets.

2. When matters: the first step anchors the ranking. Step 0 is the only step that reads the real observation. Computing it in full and compressing only later steps recovers 5.4 points lost to spatial pruning, while spending comparable compute on the last step instead drops success to 0.66 of dense, as shown in Sec. 4.2.

3. Context must be kept but not recomputed. After step 0, half of the predictor’s work recomputes the previous frame only to provide keys and values. Dropping that frame is free on navigation and pushing but costs 12 to 43 points on robot-arm reaching; reusing its cached keys and values removes the trade-off and matches dense success at a 1.76×1.76\times speedup without knowing the task, as demonstrated in Secs. 4.3 and 6.
