title: Seeing Is Not Steering: Where Verifiable Reasoning Can Enter an End-to-End Driving Planner
authors: Gautam Kumar Jain,Atharva Mahindrakar,Shubham Phoolari,Ignacio Alvarez,Carsten Markgraf,Constanze Hungar,Christoph Lauer,Julian Staehler
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Driving models that reason may describe a hazard correctly while choosing their path for other reasons. We study where scene reasoning can enter an end-to-end planner so its influence can be checked. We freeze Drive-JEPA and use a fine-tuned vision-language model to state scene facts. Although fine-tuning improves fact accuracy, the two learned components we test show no detectable benefit from reading them. A rule-based fact check instead rejects or shortens paths that contradict the facts, linking each intervention to a stated fact. On the frozen planner alone, it gains 2.4 EPDMS points on navhard. Its 2.0-point margin over a control that changes the same frames without consulting facts remains statistically uncertain. A diagnostic using exact facts from maps and annotations yields a 3.6-point margin over its corresponding control, with a 95% confidence interval above zero. Separately, a path scorer and plan memory that read no stated facts raise navhard from 41.2 to 51.8. Bounding travel distance using the reasoner’s facts adds 0.3 there and reduces navtest by 2.0. The fact check makes each intervention auditable, while the driving value of the reasoner’s facts remains unresolved.
introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) can state useful facts about a driving scene, such as the traffic light, the vehicle ahead, or the free road. A driving planner, however, is judged by the path it drives, not by what a VLM says. A fact may be correct and still be ignored, while a trajectory may improve for reasons unrelated to that fact. We therefore ask whether the facts stated by a VLM actually influence a planner’s decisions, and whether that influence improves driving.

This is hard to establish when reasoning is part of the policy itself. A fluent chain of thought need not be the reason for an answer [1, 2], vision-language-action models can show a gap between stated reasoning and action [3], and learning to reason does not necessarily improve driving [4]. A benchmark score alone also cannot reveal which fact, if any, caused a better trajectory.

We study this reasoning-to-action gap using Drive-JEPA [5], an end-to-end planner that proposes and scores candidate paths. It performs strongly on navtest but drops substantially on navhard [6], which also evaluates counterfactual states reached by the planner’s own trajectories. We keep Drive-JEPA frozen so that any behavioral change comes from components added around it.

Our approach separates seeing from steering (Fig. 1). An offline Cosmos-Reason2-8B reasoner [7], fine-tuned for driving, writes a structured fact sheet describing scene attributes such as the traffic light and stop line, vehicle ahead, free distance, adjacent lanes, and surrounding road users. We test two interfaces: learned components can consume these facts as inputs, or an explicit fact check can remove or shorten candidate paths that violate them.

The fact check makes every intervention traceable to a stated fact. To test whether the gain comes from factual content rather than from changing the path itself, we compare against shuffled facts from another scene and a matched control that changes the same frames without using a fact.

We also build a stronger base system around the frozen planner using a learned path scorer and plan memory, neither of which reads the facts. The full system then adds the reasoner’s free-distance constraint. This lets us ask not only whether reasoning helps, but where: on scenes where the frozen planner already fails, or on rare scene types.

Our contributions are:

A controlled test of stated facts. We test whether facts are correct, whether they change the driven path, and whether that change improves the score, using shuffled and matched controls.

A controlled test of stated facts. We test whether facts are correct, whether they change the driven path, and whether that change improves the score, using shuffled and matched controls.

A verifiable reasoning-to-action interface. On navhard, the explicit fact check scores 2.4 EPDMS above no check and 3.5 above shuffled facts. Its 2.0-point margin over the matched control includes zero. With exact facts, used only as a diagnostic, the margin is 3.6 points. The two learned components we tried did not benefit from the same facts.

A stronger frozen-planner system. The path scorer and plan memory raise Drive-JEPA from 41.2 to 51.8 EPDMS on navhard. Adding the free-distance bound gives 52.2 on navhard, within noise of the base system, and lowers navtest from 90.2 to 88.2.

Hard, not rare. The free-distance bound helps mainly where the frozen planner already fails and hurts where it does not. We find no additional benefit on rare scene types, where the reasoner’s facts are also less accurate.

These results separate reading reasoning from acting on it: explicit constraints make reasoning interventions auditable, but their benefit depends on where and how they are applied.

Its 2.0-point margin over the matched control includes zero. With exact facts, used only as a diagnostic, the margin is 3.6 points. The two learned components we tried did not benefit from the same facts.

title: Synthesizing Expressive Human-Object Interactions via Test-time Latent Adaptation
authors: Zijing Wu,Yiping Li,ZhiPeng Yu,Yuzhou Zheng,Ziyazhuo Wang,Binghui Zuo,Yangang Wang
abstract: In reality, when interacting with an object whose physical properties are unknown, humans sometimes go through an iterative adaptation process: they probe, over-exert, stagger, and adjust, rather than achieving a successful interaction on the first attempt. We argue that this adaptation process itself is an expressive aspect of human-object interaction, yet it has been largely overlooked in human motion synthesis. Both kinematic data-driven methods and physics-based controllers tend to produce flawlessly executed motions: the former lack sufficient data for learning fine-grained adaptation behaviors, while the latter, optimized through reinforcement learning (RL), are trained toward robust, deterministic behaviors by conditioning on privileged object dynamics. To synthesize such expressive motions, we propose a test-time latent adaptation framework called ExpHOI (Expressive Human-Object Interaction), which is built upon an RL-trained physics-based control policy. During policy training, we encode diverse object dynamics contexts into a structured latent space. At test time, we use Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) to perform iterative latent optimization for a given object with unknown physical properties. During this process, temporary mismatches between the latent code and the true object dynamics turn latent optimization into an expressive progression from tentative, error-prone trials to proficient interaction. Adaptation behaviors inevitably come with occasional failures, so a high-level planner is introduced to handle failed cases to maintain full, consistent animations. We demonstrate our framework’s effectiveness on a large-object transportation task, where such adaptation is especially pronounced. To train our framework, we introduce a mass-diverse object dataset with rich physical-property annotations. Across carrying and push-pull, our method pairs over 90% success with markedly higher posture diversity, and is rated the most lifelike in our user study on animation liveliness.
introduction:
In reality, humans often misjudge an object’s weight, mass distribution, or friction, so the interaction involves probing, over-exerting, staggering, sometimes failing, and then adjusting. This effortful adaptation is itself an expressive and valuable form of character animation, yet it has gone largely overlooked in computer animation. The probing and adaptation that arise under such physical uncertainty are among the scarcest and hardest-to-synthesize aspects of physical human–object interaction. We call this expressive exertion.

Existing methods struggle to produce such adaptive behavior, for three reasons. First, kinematic data-driven methods [1, 25, 22, 10, 20] are inherently constrained by training data. Their generated motions are biased toward the distribution of training datasets [30]. Motion capture of people straining under unknown or off-center loads is scarce, leading the learned models to produce only rigid, generic successful behaviors without expressive adaptive dynamics. Second, existing physics and RL-based controllers inherently generate optimal dynamics through reinforcement learning [5, 14, 6, 16, 24]. During interaction, the character is always equipped with full physical parameter knowledge, and tends to output the reward-optimal torques. This optimal control results in stiff motion and cannot simulate the hesitant, uncertain behaviors humans would show when underestimating or overestimating the object’s mass or friction. Third, hand-crafting such adaptive interaction via keyframes is inefficient. For instance, animating a character that underestimates a box’s weight, overstrains, staggers, and readjusts its push demands extensive manual work. Meanwhile, this workflow easily compromises the physical consistency of generated movements.

To tackle these limitations, we take our cue from how people cope. Confronting an unfamiliar object, a person cannot know its weight, mass distribution, or friction in advance, and acts on a wrong estimate and unreliable perception of them. The natural human remedy is trial and error: attempt, sense the outcome, and refine the estimate over a few tries. We give the character the same strategy, keeping its physical estimate in a latent space and optimizing it over several trials with Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) [17, 15], which casts policy improvement as a supervised regression. The result is simple and intuitive: the character improves the way a person would, turning a familiar coping behavior into a controllable source of expressive motion.

To verify the effectiveness of our novel paradigm for generating expressive human-object animations, we evaluate our method on representative object transportation scenarios. We name our full system ExpHOI (Expressive Human-Object Interaction), which couples a low-level object interaction controller with a high-level failure-aware planner. The object interaction controller is a physics-based policy conditioned on a latent code for physical properties. We train it on MDD (Massive-Diverse Object Dataset) with rich physical-property annotations. At test time, ground-truth physical properties of objects are unknown. The character initializes its latent embedding from a Gaussian distribution. Through a sequence of exploratory trials, our AWR scheme iteratively refines the latent estimation, during which, temporary discrepancies between latent codes and the real object dynamics drive latent optimization to produce an expressive behavioral progression: from hesitant, error-laden attempts to smooth, reliable object interaction. For this reason, we select representative intermediate latent outputs as the source of expressive motion animations and finalize the optimal latent parameters. Once the latent parameters are fixed, we integrate this low-level controller into our high-level task planner. Analogous to humans whose vivid behaviors stem from misestimation of object physical properties, expressive adaptive motions inevitably involve occasional failed attempts. Under such circumstances, the high-level planner is indispensable to activate a coherent give-up-and-retry behavioral cycle, ensuring physically complete and consistent animation sequences.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Latent test-time adaptation. We propose a method that optimizes a latent estimate of the object’s physical properties by advantage-weighted regression. The controllable intermediate trials are themselves expressive exertion.

The MDD dataset. We build Mass-Diverse Dataset, a large-scale dataset of over 40,00040{,}000 procedurally generated objects with 13 physical-property labels, which fills the gap of physical-parameter annotation in existing datasets.

Failure-aware high-level planner. We design a state-machine planner that coordinates the object interaction controller with a detouring controller, switching to a coherent give-up-adjust-retry cycle to ensure a complete animation system.

1. Latent test-time adaptation. We propose a method that optimizes a latent estimate of the object’s physical properties by advantage-weighted regression. The controllable intermediate trials are themselves expressive exertion.

2. The MDD dataset. We build Mass-Diverse Dataset, a large-scale dataset of over 40,00040{,}000 procedurally generated objects with 13 physical-property labels, which fills the gap of physical-parameter annotation in existing datasets.

3. Failure-aware high-level planner. We design a state-machine planner that coordinates the object interaction controller with a detouring controller, switching to a coherent give-up-adjust-retry cycle to ensure a complete animation system.

title: Adesktop learning factory for smart and resilient manufacturing based on digital twin and AI
authors: Wenxuan Hu,Zhuoxuan Cao,Achraf El Messaoudi,Peilin Li,Zhiguo Zeng
abstract: Learning factories have been increasingly applied in engineering research and education. In this paper, we develop a small-scale, low-cost, fully open-sourced learning factory that leverages AI and digital twins to demonstrate smart and resilient manufacturing. The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, two conveyors and their digital twins. Three typical use cases are designed to demonstrate the capabilities of the learning factory, i.e., material sorting through computer vision-based robot control, coordinating AGV, robots and conveyors for assembly, and digital twin-driven predictive maintenance. The results show that the developed learning factory can adequately support the teaching and research activities on digital twins and AI on manufacturing. Its fully open-source architecture and relatively low deployment cost make it an ideal solution for universities and research institutions.
introduction:
Learning Factory is an educational platform that closely integrates teaching with the simulation of real production environments [1]. For example, Free University of Bolzano developed a mini-factory to demonstrate modular reconfigurability through integrated robotics solutions [1] . EAFIT University’s learning factory [2] adopts comprehensive ICT(Information and Communication Technology) infrastructure to achieve Industry 4.0 compliance, enabling real-time data acquisition and analysis throughout production elements.

Existing learning factories, as reviewed before, share a few common challenges. First, most existing learning factories use industrial robots and controllers. These industrial equipment is usually expensive, which limits the applicability of the learning factory. Industrial equipment also takes up considerable space, making reconfiguration time-consuming and labor-intensive. Another significant drawback of the learning factories designed with industrial equipment is that, the industrial equipment is usually closed and it is difficult to design and implement new functions freely. Second, most of the existing learning factories still focus on traditional production processes. Emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digital twin are not well-integrated in the existing learning factories. Also, predictive maintenance and how to maintain a resilient production system, although important in practice, do not receive sufficient attention in the design of learning factories.

To address these issues, we propose a low-cost, fully open, "desktop-level" learning factory to demonstrate resilient production line operation based on AI and digital twins. The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, and two conveyors. The AGV and robotic arms are fully open and built on Robot Operating System (ROS), supported by a user-friendly graphical programming interface. This significantly lowers the entry barrier for beginners while leveraging open-source resources for rapid iteration. Additionally, this solution incorporates deep learning (e.g., image recognition and imitation learning) and digital twin technology, aligning closely with industry 4.0 trends.

title: S-BFM: A Behavioral Foundation Model for Humanoid Control from Sparse Spatiotemporal Goals
authors: Kun Yang,Xuanyu Chen,Jing Tan,Yanjing Liu,Yubo Zhao,Renjing Xu,Addison Lin Wang
abstract:
General-purpose whole-body trackers can execute diverse humanoid motions, but they require dense reference trajectories.
However, tasks usually specify only where, in which posture, and when the robot should arrive, leaving the motion in between to a separate planner.
Inspired by human motor coordination, our key idea is that a low-level controller can organize the intervening motion and its pace by itself from sparse goals with arrival times.
In this paper, we propose S-BFM, a novel behavioral foundation model superior in its autonomy: it generates whole-body transitions from target postures, poses, and arrival times alone.
Specifically, we first introduce Spatial Grounding, which adds world-frame position and heading to a forward-backward behavior representation through spatial reconstruction.
Then, Time-Conditioned Distillation is designed to learn transitions and pace from real motion through closed-loop imitation of a dense-reference teacher.
Lastly, Generative Fine-Tuning is introduced to broaden the covered distances and arrival times with a distilled motion generator.
In simulation, S-BFM lowers global joint-position error by over 32% relative to the best baseline under fixed and mixed horizons, and raises fixed-goal reach from 43.5% to 74.6% while cutting terminal position error from 1.67 to 0.26 m.
We further deploy S-BFM on the full-size AGIBOT A3 humanoid.
Sparse spatiotemporal goals thus suffice for natural, well-timed whole-body motion.
introduction:
Humanoid control is moving from task-specific skill policies toward general-purpose whole-body control.
Large motion datasets and physics simulation have enabled universal trackers that turn diverse motion references into executable joint commands.
These trackers connect motion generators and multimodal interfaces to the robot.
TextOp continuously generates short motion segments for a tracking policy to execute [39], SONIC links input modalities to control through a unified motion interface [21], and SuperMimic trains whole-body trackers efficiently with a shared differentiable world model [19].
These trackers can execute diverse humanoid motions, but they require dense reference trajectories.

However, task planning and interactive control require robots to organize motion around task goals and adapt as those goals change.
With dense-reference interfaces, this responsibility falls to a separate planner or generator.
It must supply the intervening motion and update future references when the task changes while ensuring a smooth transition from the motion already underway [21, 39].
Human movement instead combines goal-directed decisions with automatic coordination.
For example, when walking toward a table, the cerebral cortex helps select the goal and route.
Brainstem–spinal circuits support gait and posture while the cerebellum uses sensory feedback to coordinate movement.
Together, these mechanisms allow people to focus on their destination and surroundings without consciously controlling every step [6].
Inspired by this coordination, we ask a novel question: Can a low-level controller accept sparse goals with arrival times and organize the intervening motion from its current physical state?

Prior work provides foundations:
BFM-Zero supports goal reaching and motion tracking via a shared behavior space [18], and BeJEPA models whole-body posture together with world position and heading [41].
MaskedMimic and KINO produce physics-based motion from partial constraints or keyframes [32, 2], and BFMTrack tracks sparse timed goals by latent optimization [28].
Yet no existing method delivers all three sparse-goal requirements at once: accurate control of the world-frame pose, natural transitions between goals, and timing that adapts to the requested arrival.
A target state alone does not specify how the intervening motion should unfold, and imitating the pace of a demonstration does not adapt it to new distances and durations.

Inspired by human motor coordination, our key idea is that a low-level controller can organize the intervening motion and its pace by itself from sparse goals with arrival times.
In this paper, we propose S-BFM (Sparse Behavioral Foundation Model), which is superior in its autonomy: it generates whole-body transitions from target postures, poses, and arrival times alone ().
S-BFM is trained in three stages within a reusable forward-backward behavior space [34, 18, 8, 36].
Each stage targets one requirement.
Specifically, we first propose Spatial Grounding (Sec. 3.3), which adds world-frame position and heading to the behavior representation and uses spatial reconstruction to make the encoder retain them.
Then, Time-Conditioned Distillation (Sec. 3.4) is designed to learn transitions and pace from real motion: with the encoder and actor frozen, a controller conditioned on the remaining time imitates a dense-reference teacher in closed loop.
As real demonstrations cover only a limited range of distances and durations, Generative Fine-Tuning (Sec. 3.5) is lastly introduced to broaden this range with a lightweight motion generator distilled from Kimodo [25].
At deployment, S-BFM acts from robot observations, sparse goals, and the remaining time, without any intermediate reference.

We evaluate S-BFM in simulation on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 against SONIC, UFO, BeJEPA, and PLAT, and on the AGIBOT A3 humanoid.
Under both fixed and mixed command horizons, S-BFM lowers global joint-position error by over 32% relative to the best baseline.
For fixed goals, it raises the reach rate from 43.5% to 74.6% over BeJEPA, increases the rate of holding the goal for five seconds from 7.4% to 35.2%, and cuts terminal position error from 1.67 to 0.26 m.
At 3 to 4 m under lateral and downward pushes, it still reaches 68.0% of goals, against 23.6% for BeJEPA.
On the real robot, S-BFM moves from a shared start pose to five distinct goal postures ().
Sparse spatiotemporal goals thus suffice for natural, well-timed whole-body motion.

In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

1) We formulate sparse spatiotemporal goal control, in which a low-level policy, much like the cerebellum, generates natural whole-body transitions that reach target postures at prescribed world poses and times.

2) We propose S-BFM, trained through Spatial Grounding, Time-Conditioned Distillation, and Generative Fine-Tuning, which combines spatial goal reaching with the transitions and pace of real motion.

title: Where Delay Compensation Belongs in a Decentralized Mean-Field-Game Swarm with a Control-Barrier Safety Filter
authors: Jan Mikołajczyk,Igor Rostkowski,Bartosz Ogórkiewicz,Szymon Skierski,Sylwia Opat,Wojciech Rybak,Mikołaj Sczogiel,Radosław Pałys,Jan Gogulski,Bartosz Kościołek,Andrzej Pijanowski,Szymon Kowalski,Marcin Misiewicz
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
comment: . Submitted to the 8th International Workshop on Multi-Agent Path Finding (WoMAPF) at AAAI-27 (non-archival workshop)
abstract: Large robot teams are often run as a plan-then-execute stack: a routing layer tells each agent where to go, and a safety layer keeps agents apart. We study a decentralized instance for drone swarms, a mean-field-game (MFG) routing field with a per-agent control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter, when communication is limited by a shared TDMA channel. Agents know their neighbors only through noisy range and bearing measurements exchanged in round-robin slots, so the frame, and with it the age of every neighbor estimate, grows with the swarm size. We show in simulation that this delay reaches both layers but breaks only the safety layer. Without delay, swarms of up to 100 agents do not collide, even with the noise of each measurement held for a whole frame; with it, stale estimates at the CBF cause collisions beyond a frame period of 125 to 175 ms, or 75 to 100 ms at 100 agents with held noise, and the swarm size sets both where that limit lies and how steeply collisions rise beyond it. Stale estimates at the MFG distort the local density by which agents steer around congestion, but that density is an average over the crowd, which staleness makes noisier without biasing it, and throughput drops by at most a tenth. We then compensate the delay with lightweight on-board predictors, from constant-velocity fits to a small learned network, that estimate each neighbor’s current position from its last broadcasts. A layer-split experiment shows where the prediction is needed: at the CBF it restores safety and extends the frame period the swarm tolerates, by a factor of 1.4 to 1.7 with an untrained constant-velocity fit and about 2.3 with the learned network when the measurement noise is redrawn at every step; with the noise held for a frame, the two extend it about equally, while at the MFG it only refines the congestion correction. A constant wider safety margin, the simplest alternative, makes collisions more frequent in a bottleneck. With the routing solved offline, the routing layer is robust to the delay because it sees the neighbors only through a crowd average, and compensation belongs in the safety filter, switched on only when the frame period exceeds the uncompensated limit, since below it the predictor’s own error adds collisions.

authors: Jan Mikołajczyk,Jakub Bałenkowski,Maciej Borowiecki,Jan Ciecierski,Marcel Kolecki,Julian Maleta,Maksymilian Bernacki

abstract:
Persistent monitoring of large-scale subsea infrastructure, such as offshore wind farm foundations, export cables, and inspection corridors, remains a fundamental challenge for autonomous underwater systems.
The problem is
not solely spatial coverage, but rather temporal coverage: ensuring that all relevant regions of interest are revisited
within bounded time intervals under limited sensing, navigation uncertainty, and constrained vehicle resources.
We compare three specific classes of trajectory strategies:
introduction:
The rapid expansion of the offshore energy sector has increased the importance of the cost-effective subsea infrastructure maintenance. For offshore wind farms,
Operations and Maintenance (O&M) costs can account for up to 30% of the total life cycle
expenditure [1]. Efficient monitoring of export cables, turbine foundations, and inspection
corridors is therefore critical to reducing these costs and preventing catastrophic failures.
While Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) offer a scalable solution for these tasks, the fundamental challenge remains ensuring temporal coverage rather than mere spatial reach.
Effective persistent monitoring depends on regularly revisiting target areas within
specific time frames to guarantee the prompt identification of anomalies. Success in these
missions requires a careful synchronization of three core elements: AUV swarm coordination
and path-planning logic, the overall scale of the fleet, and the precision of the navigation
systems, which typically utilize dead-reckoning and acoustic beacons.
These challenges manifest differently depending on the operational objective: full workspace coverage versus targeted inspection of critical infrastructure such as turbine foundations.
Existing research frequently evaluates these parameters in isolation, often neglecting the
complex trade-offs that occur in dynamic underwater environments characterized by
stochastic disturbances and limited communication. This paper presents a quantitatively
grounded study that explicitly disentangles these dimensions. We test the hypothesis that
beyond a specific localization accuracy threshold, further hardware investment yields
diminishing returns compared to optimized trajectory design. Through the use of a lightweight 2D simulation framework equipped with spatial ocean current models, we provide actionable insights into the design of economically viable multi-AUV monitoring systems.
The primary contributions of this work are:

A systematic evaluation of trajectory, fleet, and localization effects on the primary temporal metric (AoI), with IVT as a secondary diagnostic indicator.

The identification of accuracy thresholds where localization improvements reach a point of saturation, depending on chosen path-planning strategy.

A cost-aware framework to optimize the balance between sensing infrastructure and
fleet size.

title: Ego4Gen: Generating Geometry-Grounded Motion Tokens as a World-Action Interface
authors: Yang Liu,Chao Ye,Jiahao Zhang,Zeyuan Hou,Ruijie Fang,Xiyin Ni,Xinyang Ren,Weiyang Lin
abstract: We present Ego4Gen (Egocentric 4D Future Generation), a world model for 4D future generation in robotic manipulation. Given a single egocentric image and a text prompt, Ego4Gen jointly generates temporally aligned RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow, explicitly predicting the evolution of scene appearance, spatial structure, and motion. Built on Cosmos3-Nano, Ego4Gen extends the pretrained generative backbone through modality-routed LoRA and asymmetric attention, using geometric pseudo-labels from MotionCrafter to learn to predict future geometry and motion latents. These latents can either be decoded into explicit 3D structure and motion or mapped to robot actions. To this end, we also introduce FlowInverse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network trained in two stages to translate predicted 4D latents into robot actions. Experiments show that these geometry and motion latents outperform the evaluated latent-action and video-latent baselines in out-of-distribution settings. Closed-loop policy evaluations further demonstrate their utility for translating predicted 4D futures into robot control. Together, these results support geometry-grounded motion tokens as a world-action interface, connecting 4D future generation with robotic manipulation and suggesting a path toward reduced reliance on action-labeled data.
introduction:
Visual world models offer a new way to learn interaction dynamics from large-scale video data for robotic manipulation. By predicting how a task may unfold, they support action planning and generation [7, 26]. However, RGB videos encode task-relevant state changes together with appearance factors such as color, texture, lighting, and background. Even scenes with similar spatial relationships and motions can differ substantially in pixel appearance, creating appearance shifts that a controller must accommodate. The representation connecting future prediction to action execution should therefore preserve control-relevant information while reducing interference from task-irrelevant visual variation.

Recent works explore latent-space interfaces between visual priors and robot actions. Some approaches perform planning with predicted video latent representations [1], while others use latent action models (LAMs) that compress inter-frame changes into compact action representations [8, 3]. However, these compact representations may still retain visual information unrelated to robot control. Prior analysis shows that latent action representations can encode exogenous noise alongside action-induced changes [28]. This suggests that compactness alone is insufficient to ensure robustness to appearance shifts.

Geometry offers a promising direction for reducing the influence of task-irrelevant visual appearance. Recent studies have explored mapping predicted geometry and motion to robot actions. Some methods use explicitly constructed geometric representations [25, 30, 31], while others extract features from within world models [29, 12]. The former introduces additional computation to construct and process explicit representations, while the latter can still be affected by shifts in the visual input distribution. We therefore seek an interface that contains as little task-irrelevant information as possible, motivating our focus on geometry-motion representations.

Our experiments show that the geometry-motion latents of MotionCrafter’s 4D VAE [32] are well suited to this role: they support both explicit 4D scene reconstruction and robust mappings to robot actions. Building on this finding, we develop Ego4Gen upon Cosmos3-Nano [18]. Given a single egocentric image and a text prompt, Ego4Gen jointly predicts future RGB video and temporally aligned geometry-motion latents, which can be decoded into dense point maps and dense scene flow. To connect these predictions to robot control, we introduce FlowInverse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network that enables closed-loop robot control with Ego4Gen through two-stage training: learning from real videos and adapting to predicted representations. We further show that adapting the world model with action-unlabeled videos can improve generalization in closed-loop control while keeping FlowInverse fixed, highlighting the potential to benefit from additional video data without additional action supervision.

Overall, our contributions are as follows:

We validate geometry-motion latents as a world-action interface. Through comparisons with latent action and video representations, we show that MotionCrafter’s 4D VAE latents support both explicit 3D structure reconstruction and robot action prediction, with strong robustness under the out-of-distribution conditions.

We introduce Ego4Gen, a 4D world model that jointly predicts temporally aligned future RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow from a single egocentric image and a text prompt.

We introduce FlowInverse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network that maps Ego4Gen’s geometry-motion latents to robot actions for closed-loop control. We also demonstrate that world-model adaptation with action-unlabeled videos can improve downstream policy performance, suggesting a way to reduce reliance on action-labeled data.

1. We validate geometry-motion latents as a world-action interface. Through comparisons with latent action and video representations, we show that MotionCrafter’s 4D VAE latents support both explicit 3D structure reconstruction and robot action prediction, with strong robustness under the out-of-distribution conditions.

2. We introduce Ego4Gen, a 4D world model that jointly predicts temporally aligned future RGB frames, dense point maps, and dense scene flow from a single egocentric image and a text prompt.

3. We introduce FlowInverse, a lightweight inverse dynamics network that maps Ego4Gen’s geometry-motion latents to robot actions for closed-loop control. We also demonstrate that world-model adaptation with action-unlabeled videos can improve downstream policy performance, suggesting a way to reduce reliance on action-labeled data.

title: NavRSI: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement for Vision-and-Language Navigation
authors: Guangzhao Dai,Guoxin Lian,Shuo Wang,Shengbin Yue,Qianru Sun,Xiangbo Shu,Bin Zhu
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) have enabled vision-and-language navigation (VLN) through direct closed-loop perception and action. However, navigation performance depends strongly on the harness governing LLM–environment interactions, while existing harnesses largely rely on manually designed navigation tools, memory, and agent roles. We introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric recursive self-improvement framework that optimizes the navigation behavior of frozen LLMs through closed-loop experience. In each round, NavRSI iteratively collects navigation trajectories and failure diagnostics, employs a designer agent to rewrite the harness, and retains the revisions that prove effective, while the designer accumulates experience from previous revisions so that the harness and this experience co-evolve. Privileged simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and remain inaccessible to the navigating LLM, enabling deployment with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, without task-specific model training or additional navigation tools. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across LLMs from four vendors, with 85.64% success rate on the full R2R-CE val-unseen split with GPT-6-Astra, surpassing the previously reported best by 4.13%. Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE, and a real humanoid robot further demonstrate its generalizability. Source code will be released.
introduction:
Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires a robot to follow language instructions and navigate to the target destination in an unseen environment [3, 16, 17]. Existing approaches either train specialized navigation models on large-scale embodied data [13, 1, 38, 8, 32, 41, 43] or construct explicit navigation workflows around general-purpose large language models (LLMs) [47, 4, 21, 23, 26]. Frontier LLMs such as GPT-6-Astra and Fable-5.2 have recently opened up a promising alternative, where the LLM directly perceives visual observations and executes primitive actions through closed-loop interaction [50]. This is enabled by a harness (such as Codex CLI and Claude Agent SDK), i.e., the program that connects the LLM to the environment and decides its context, tools, and feedback [46, 48]. The design of this harness thus becomes an important factor in translating the capabilities of LLMs into successful navigation [20, 7, 44, 25].

However, existing harness-based VLN methods [50, 20, 7, 44, 25, 48, 24] largely rely on human-designed assumptions about what an LLM needs to navigate successfully. They introduce auxiliary tools for depth estimation, waypoint execution, or learned navigation policies [20, 7, 48, 9], maintain explicit spatial or episodic memories [7, 44, 24], or divide navigation into specialized agent roles [25, 7, 48]. Although effective, these designs prescribe how the LLM should perceive, remember, and act, rather than identifying its limitations from actual interaction with the environment. Importantly, the same LLM performs very differently under different harnesses. As shown in Fig. 1(a), GPT-5.6-Sol achieves success rates of 56.7% and 58.7% with Codex CLI and Mini-swe-agent, but reaches 68.0% with our NavRSI harness on the same primitive actions. The harness itself can thus be a significant bottleneck, raising a fundamental question: Can we systematically improve the harness based on an LLM’s own closed-loop behavior, rather than relying on manually designed navigation mechanisms?

Answering this question is challenging because navigation failures emerge from long-horizon interactions between perception, reasoning, and action. An agent may repeatedly attempt blocked movements, lose track of its heading, revisit explored locations, or stop before reaching the destination. Such failures are difficult to anticipate through static prompt design, and an overall success score gives limited guidance on how the harness should be revised. Moreover, the simulator diagnostics that explain these failures are unavailable to the deployed robot, so the optimization must produce a harness that operates without privileged information. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) has recently shown promise for optimizing agent code and execution scaffolds [36, 40, 18], yet applying it to embodied navigation must account for the sequential, partially observable, and physically grounded nature of this interaction.

In this paper, we introduce NavRSI, a harness-centric RSI framework that keeps the LLM frozen and iteratively rewrites the executable harness around it from closed-loop navigation experience, instead of modifying the model or adding navigation tools. As shown in Fig. 2, NavRSI starts from a general-purpose Mini-swe-agent harness [50] and alternates between three steps: (1) running navigation episodes to collect closed-loop trajectories and failure diagnostics, (2) employing a designer agent to analyze them and generate revised harness candidates, and (3) evaluating the candidates to retain effective improvements. The designer also maintains a record of its optimization experience, including observed failure patterns, the hypotheses behind its revisions, and evidence of their effectiveness, so that the harness and this experience co-evolve across rounds. To bridge the gap between optimization and deployment, the designer, a separate LLM, reads execution logs and simulator diagnostics (e.g., distance to the goal) from training episodes, whereas the frozen LLM, as the navigator, never sees these privileged signals and relies solely on RGB observations and action feedback. Through this process, NavRSI discovers a lightweight harness that provides action feedback, progress tracking, and arrival verification, without requiring task-specific model training, additional navigation tools, or specialized agent roles.

Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of NavRSI. On R2R-CE-100, the NavRSI harness consistently improves navigation success rate across four LLM families, outperforming their native harnesses by up to 11.3 SR (Fig. 1(b)). With GPT-6-Astra, NavRSI sets new SOTA on the full R2R-CE val-unseen without training (85.64 SR), +4.13 SR over NavGPT-3, which pairs the same LLM with an 8B model additionally trained on 19.28M samples (Fig. 1(c), Tab. 1). Evaluations on RxR-CE, NavRAG-CE [29], and a Unitree G1 humanoid robot further demonstrate cross-dataset and sim-to-real transfer. Ablations show that its components are complementary and that closed-loop RSI outperforms one-shot writing.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We investigate the harness as an optimization target and introduce NavRSI, which improves the runtime interaction of frozen LLMs from their closed-loop navigation behavior, without task-specific model training.

We develop an iterative optimization framework in which a designer agent analyzes navigation failures, rewrites executable harness code, and accumulates experience from previous revisions. Simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and are never visible to the navigator, which bridges optimization and deployment.

NavRSI discovers a lightweight harness that operates with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, achieving strong performance across multiple LLM families, VLN benchmarks, and real-world environments, with competitive runtime efficiency.

1. We investigate the harness as an optimization target and introduce NavRSI, which improves the runtime interaction of frozen LLMs from their closed-loop navigation behavior, without task-specific model training.

2. We develop an iterative optimization framework in which a designer agent analyzes navigation failures, rewrites executable harness code, and accumulates experience from previous revisions. Simulator diagnostics guide only the designer and are never visible to the navigator, which bridges optimization and deployment.

3. NavRSI discovers a lightweight harness that operates with a single RGB camera and primitive actions, achieving strong performance across multiple LLM families, VLN benchmarks, and real-world environments, with competitive runtime efficiency.

title: ROSWORLD: When Digital Task Competence Meets Physical Execution
authors: Caoyuan Ma,Wendi Liu,Zhimin Zhang,Muyao Niu,Yujie Lu,Zengxi Zhang,Ji Zhao,Shuai Dong,Wenpu Liu,Ziyue Wang,Wenzheng Chang,Taiqiang Wu,Weichu Xie,Yuqi Xu,Haiyuan Wan,Xuehui Wang,Jiaqi Wang,Wenqi Shao,Yinqiang Zheng
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Computer-use agents now solve most desktop tasks through direct software input, but a robot using the same computer must turn GUI knowledge into physical contact with a keyboard and mouse. We introduce ROSWorld, a benchmark that couples a physically simulated robot workstation to a live OSWorld desktop, so that a robot and a desktop agent pursue the same goals under the same official evaluators. The evaluated model receives observations only from the workstation camera views and operates the peripherals through either a single-arm rigid probe or dual-arm dexterous hands. Across five frontier models and 40 tasks in ten applications, models that complete 31–39 tasks on the desktop complete at most 23 with the probe and 28 with the hands. Paired trajectory analysis shows that models adapt their interaction strategies toward keyboard input, yet physical execution frequently fails through missed presses, incorrect targets, and unintended contacts. ROSWorld makes the gap between knowing what to do on a computer and physically doing it measurable.
introduction:
Computer-use agents [45, 22, 44] can edit documents, manage files, and configure applications through software-issued keyboard and mouse input. These familiar tasks also offer a rich setting for evaluating models that control robots, where a small set of physical peripherals connects the robot to diverse application workflows, each with a concrete goal. When a model uses a robot to operate the computer, every intended input must be realized through motion and contact. Opening a menu requires locating and actuating the appropriate control; editing a document requires coordinating many such interactions while tracking changes in the application. A missed press or an unintended input can change what must happen next, requiring the model to recognize the discrepancy and recover. Physical computer use therefore brings visual understanding, task planning, precise manipulation, and feedback-based recovery together in sustained, goal-directed behavior. It provides a concrete setting for asking how well a model can turn its competence at desktop tasks into effective physical action.

Many existing embodiment benchmarks [23, 17, 35, 9] focus on assessing physical skills with bounded manipulation goals, such as grasping, placing, or actuating an object, while desktop benchmarks [49, 7] provide a rich set of computer-use scenarios with clearly defined, task-oriented purposes. To answer the question above, we propose ROSWorld, connecting these evaluation surfaces by preserving desktop goals and official outcome evaluators. Models need to complete various desktop applications selected from OSWorld [49] through robot controlling and contact with physical peripherals like keyboard and mouse within a simulated environment. Compared with an isolated manipulation goal, completing a computer task requires the model to maintain reliable physical control over a sequence of state-dependent operations. Closely spaced keys and small actuation travel demand precise contact; modifiers and mouse drags require coordinated holding and release; and the meaning of an input depends on the current window, focus, and editing state. The model must therefore connect the geometry and timing of its bodily actions to their changing effects in the digital world, recognize ineffective or unintended inputs, and recover while preserving progress toward the task goal.

ROSWorld evaluates end-to-end physical computer use under a fixed observation and action interface. Perception, action selection, robot control, physical contact, and feedback-based recovery are parts of a single embodied task rather than separately evaluated capabilities. This preserves the concrete challenges of physical computer use: reading the display from camera views, translating GUI intent into accurate 3D contact, and verifying state changes to recover over long horizons, while shared OSWorld tasks and evaluators allow direct comparison with software-based computer use.

We couple an Isaac Sim workstation to a live OSWorld desktop. The model reads camera views and robot status, then produces bounded motion sequences. Contact with the keyboard and mouse generates desktop input, and the updated desktop is rendered on the workstation monitor for the next observation.

We evaluate five models on 40 shared tasks across ten application domains with two embodiment configurations. Aligning each model’s desktop and physical trajectories shows that the task route is preserved, whereas the input modality changes. Models tend to convert mouse operations into keyboard operations in both embodiment configuration, and with the probe they look for single-key substitutes for key chords. Most physical failures arise from presses that do not reach the key, presses on the wrong target, and unintended contacts made by other parts of the robot. These unintended contacts reveal that some models fail to account for the robot’s full body during interaction. At the task level, most failed runs exhaust their step budget, some give up when they judge the task infeasible, and only a few wrongly declare the task complete without passing the evaluator.

Our contributions are:

A benchmark that couples simulation with a real system: input signals generated by robot contact with the keyboard and mouse in simulation drive a live VM, yielding long-horizon, fine-grained, and verifiable tasks.

A paired evaluation of five models on 40 OSWorld tasks under shared goals and official evaluators, comparing direct desktop input with two robot embodiments to quantify the gap between desktop competence and physical completion.

A trajectory analysis that links model plans, robot contact, device events, and application outcomes to characterize interaction strategies and identify failures at both the operation and task levels.

1. A benchmark that couples simulation with a real system: input signals generated by robot contact with the keyboard and mouse in simulation drive a live VM, yielding long-horizon, fine-grained, and verifiable tasks.

2. A paired evaluation of five models on 40 OSWorld tasks under shared goals and official evaluators, comparing direct desktop input with two robot embodiments to quantify the gap between desktop competence and physical completion.

3. A trajectory analysis that links model plans, robot contact, device events, and application outcomes to characterize interaction strategies and identify failures at both the operation and task levels.

title: Mechanism Parity for Simulation-Based Validation of Autonomous-Driving Perception
authors: Danial Safaei,Siddartha Khastgir,Matthew D. Higgins,Jeroen Ploeg,Mohsen Alirezaei,Son Tong,Paul A. Jennings,Xingyu Zhao
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: . Extended version of the authors' papers at IEEE IV 2026 and IEEE ITSC 2026. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
abstract:
Simulation is central to intelligent-vehicle validation, but visual realism or output agreement between a real scene and its synthetic counterpart does not prove that a perception system used the same evidence in both domains.
This paper addresses that mechanism-parity gap for paired real–synthetic autonomous-driving perception.
It unifies Decisive-Feature Fidelity, which compares decisive evidence maps in a frozen system under test (SUT), with Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity, which projects decisive evidence into semantic scene concepts for diagnosis.
The framework is a validation diagnostic rather than a standalone safety certificate: it asks whether output-consistent simulation also preserves the mechanism by which the perception model reaches that output.
The empirical evidence comprises ten retrained diffusion ControlNet generators evaluated on a deterministic exact-geometry KITTI–Virtual KITTI 2 subset.
Generated counterparts use a 1248-by-376-pixel padded inference canvas and are cropped back to the exact KITTI dimensions before evaluation.
The final benchmark reports target-image, output-consistency, and mechanism metrics recomputed from a single audited output set, then adds metric-disagreement cases, bootstrap uncertainty, threshold sensitivity, and concept/cache integrity audits.
Across the benchmark, output and appearance fidelity are at most weakly and inconsistently rank-correlated with decisive-mechanism distance for all three frozen SUTs, and a constructed positive control shows the estimator detects a known planted mechanism that output agreement misses, supporting decisive-evidence diagnostics for intelligent-vehicle simulation validation.
All numerical claims are restricted to the declared exact-geometry benchmark, ten generators, and three frozen SUTs.
introduction:
Simulation has become a core pillar of autonomous-driving development, testing, and safety assurance because it enables scalable experimentation over rare, risky, and difficult-to-reproduce traffic situations [1, 2].
However, a long-standing question remains unresolved in practical validation workflows:
when a real scene and its synthetic counterpart produce similar outputs, did the system under test rely on the same evidence to make that decision?

This question matters because output agreement alone can mask a failure mode that is especially problematic for safety-critical perception:
the system can produce a correct or near-correct output for the wrong reason.
For example, a steering model may retain the same steering angle across a paired real and synthetic scene while redistributing its reliance from lane boundaries and road texture toward spurious sky artifacts or background structures.
Likewise, a segmentation model may preserve mask overlap while shifting its decisiveness from road-aligned evidence toward scene content that does not reliably transfer across domains.
Such cases weaken the validity of simulation-based conclusions even when traditional fidelity indicators appear satisfactory [6, 7].

This paper builds on and unifies two complementary lines of work on that mechanism-parity problem.
The first [4] introduced Decisive-Feature Fidelity (DFF), a system-specific metric that compares decisive evidence maps extracted from a frozen system under test, and further proposed a DFF-guided generator-calibration objective.
The second [5] introduced Concept-Decisive Feature Fidelity (C-DFF), a concept-space diagnostic that aggregates decisive evidence over semantic scene concepts and identifies which concepts become more or less decisive in synthetic imagery.
Taken together, these two lines of work suggest that simulation fidelity should be assessed not only at the level of raw inputs, latent activations, and outputs, but also at the level of decisive evidence and semantic decisiveness.

This paper unifies, extends, and hardens those ideas into a single mechanism-parity framework for simulation-based validation of autonomous-driving perception; Section I-B states its specific contributions.

The central claim of the paper is simple:
output similarity is not enough.
What simulation-based validation requires is evidence that a frozen SUT processes matched real and synthetic scenes through sufficiently similar decisive mechanisms, and, when this fails, diagnostics that explain where the mismatch comes from in a way that can support debugging, calibration studies, and requirement-style monitoring.

This article reorganizes DFF and C-DFF around one intelligent-vehicle validation question: whether synthetic counterparts preserve the decisive evidence used by frozen vehicle-perception SUTs.
Table I delineates what is inherited from the prior conference-track work [4, 5] from what is introduced for the first time here, so the contribution is not mistaken for a re-presentation of the prior metrics.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows.

Unified mechanism-parity framework.
We integrate DFF and C-DFF into a common formal framework for paired real–synthetic evaluation of frozen autonomous-driving perception systems.

Decisive-feature mechanism metric.
We formalize DFF as a system-specific measure of whether matched real and synthetic inputs induce similar decisive evidence in the SUT, including estimator choices, threshold definitions, and implementation details.

Concept-level semantic diagnostic.
We formalize C-DFF as a concept-space diagnostic that aggregates decisive evidence over a shared semantic taxonomy and yields interpretable concept-shift summaries.

Calibration as an evaluated optional intervention (null on this benchmark).
We formulate a DFF-guided calibration objective that keeps the SUT frozen and uses decisive-feature mismatch as a feedback signal for synthetic-data generation, and we treat this loop as an optional layer rather than a headline result. We report the audited checkpoints it produces and state all outcomes explicitly, including where the paired comparison shows no advantage.

Audited benchmark on retrained models.
We generate all benchmark evidence from the ten retrained ControlNet generators and consolidate the run manifest, generated records, aggregate metrics, per-image metrics, and figures in one auditable directory.

Diagnostic hardening.
We add metric-disagreement, bootstrap-uncertainty, threshold-sensitivity, and concept/cache-audit outputs that test the diagnostic value and fragility of mechanism-parity evidence under the narrow final benchmark.

Held-out-scene replication.
We re-evaluate all ten audited checkpoints on Virtual KITTI scenes 18/20, held out from generator training, and show that the target-image parity ordering and the output/mechanism non-redundancy reproduce there—a within-corpus generalization check on two held-out scenes, not an independent-domain or corpus-wide claim.

Engineering guidance.
We distinguish framework claims from regenerated checkpoint evidence, report DFF/C-DFF only where recalculated from the final output cache, and state the exact empirical boundary of those claims.

1. Unified mechanism-parity framework.
We integrate DFF and C-DFF into a common formal framework for paired real–synthetic evaluation of frozen autonomous-driving perception systems.

2. Decisive-feature mechanism metric.
We formalize DFF as a system-specific measure of whether matched real and synthetic inputs induce similar decisive evidence in the SUT, including estimator choices, threshold definitions, and implementation details.

3. Concept-level semantic diagnostic.
We formalize C-DFF as a concept-space diagnostic that aggregates decisive evidence over a shared semantic taxonomy and yields interpretable concept-shift summaries.

4. Calibration as an evaluated optional intervention (null on this benchmark).
We formulate a DFF-guided calibration objective that keeps the SUT frozen and uses decisive-feature mismatch as a feedback signal for synthetic-data generation, and we treat this loop as an optional layer rather than a headline result. We report the audited checkpoints it produces and state all outcomes explicitly, including where the paired comparison shows no advantage.

5. Audited benchmark on retrained models.
We generate all benchmark evidence from the ten retrained ControlNet generators and consolidate the run manifest, generated records, aggregate metrics, per-image metrics, and figures in one auditable directory.

6. Diagnostic hardening.
We add metric-disagreement, bootstrap-uncertainty, threshold-sensitivity, and concept/cache-audit outputs that test the diagnostic value and fragility of mechanism-parity evidence under the narrow final benchmark.

7. Held-out-scene replication.
We re-evaluate all ten audited checkpoints on Virtual KITTI scenes 18/20, held out from generator training, and show that the target-image parity ordering and the output/mechanism non-redundancy reproduce there—a within-corpus generalization check on two held-out scenes, not an independent-domain or corpus-wide claim.

8. Engineering guidance.
We distinguish framework claims from regenerated checkpoint evidence, report DFF/C-DFF only where recalculated from the final output cache, and state the exact empirical boundary of those claims.

title: GenPA: Image Generators as Efficient Robot Policies
authors: Zian Deng,Tianyi Zhang,Zilong Zheng,Ziyu Liu,Tao Zhang,Yao Lyu,Shengbo Eben Li
abstract:
Pretrained visual generation models have shown great promise in robotic
manipulation. However, a representative line of work still treats future
visual prediction as the central link between visual generative pretraining and
action learning, retaining it as a training objective even when future scenes
are no longer generated at inference time. This paradigm organizes policy
learning around the proxy task of predicting future visual states. We argue
that the instruction-following, spatial understanding, and visual imagination
capabilities acquired through image generation pretraining can support
control without future visual prediction: image generation models themselves
can be directly adapted into powerful action learners. Building on this perspective, we propose
GenPA, which fine-tunes an image generation backbone with a lightweight
19M-parameter action regression adapter and reuses its native generative
objective for perception co-training. The native image-editing interface accommodates
different visual targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling
comparisons of current-scene perception, future prediction, and their
combinations within a common policy architecture.
At deployment, GenPA requires only
a single backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual
generation or iterative action denoising. Without additional large-scale
robot-data pretraining, GenPA demonstrates strong control performance and
robustness to perturbations across simulation benchmarks
(99.10% success on LIBERO and 83.79% on LIBERO-Plus)
and real-world manipulation tasks.
Under compiled inference, GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk on a single
H100 GPU, achieving 1.71.7–3.4×3.4\times speedups over strong VLA and WAM baselines.
Our latency analysis further highlights architectural advantages of
visual generation backbones for efficient robot control.
Ablations across visual tasks
and their combinations identify current-depth supervision as a simple,
effective training recipe. Together, these results show that image generators
can be directly adapted into strong, efficient robot policies without requiring
future visual prediction.
introduction:
Recent advances in image generation pretraining have yielded strong
instruction-following and visual understanding capabilities. Beyond
synthesizing realistic images, these models can identify objects referred to
in language, follow spatial constraints, and visualize instructed changes to
a scene (Xiao et al., 2025; Black Forest Labs et al., 2025; Zhao et al., 2026).
As illustrated in Figure 1(a), given a robot manipulation
instruction and a corresponding editing request, an image generation system
can depict the scene after task completion or sketch end-effector motion
paths on the current image. These behaviors suggest that the spatial
understanding and visual imagination capabilities acquired through
generative pretraining may provide valuable priors for robot action learning.

Pretrained image and video generation models have both been adapted for robot
control. A representative line of work treats future visual prediction as
the central link between generative pretraining and action learning,
using generated visual subgoals to guide goal-conditioned
policies (Black et al., 2024) or decoding actions from predicted visual
transitions through inverse dynamics (Li et al., 2026).
Several methods jointly predict future observations and actions within a
shared generative
model (Shen et al., 2025; Kim et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026b).
Recent approaches further reduce or bypass future visual generation at
deployment while retaining future prediction as a co-training
objective (Yuan et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026a; Ye et al., 2026a).
In the broader context of predictive policy learning, future supervision has
also been extended to depth, 3D pointmaps, and semantic
features (Zhang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2026).
Despite differences in architecture and deployment, these methods continue
to organize policy learning around the proxy task of predicting the future.

We argue that the control value of image generation pretraining need not be
realized through the intermediate objective of future visual prediction: image
generation models themselves can be directly adapted into powerful action
learners. Prior work demonstrates the value of features from frozen image
generators for control (Shin et al., 2026). We instead adapt the backbone
itself through action learning, with a lightweight adapter mapping its features
to actions. Meanwhile, direct action learning need not discard
the generator’s visual output capabilities. Research on generative perception
shows that depth estimation, surface normal prediction, and
segmentation can be learned as image generation tasks (Gabeur et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026).
Together with evidence that auxiliary depth and spatial
supervision benefit policy learning (Li et al., 2025b; Tu et al., 2026), these
findings motivate reusing the generator’s native interface for
current-scene perception co-training. Representing different targets through
this common interface also enables a systematic investigation of which visual
supervision benefits control, including comparisons with future prediction
and combinations of visual tasks.

Building on this perspective, we introduce GenPA (Generative
Perception for Action), an end-to-end policy that fine-tunes
the pretrained image generation backbone FLUX.2 klein Base
4B (Black Forest Labs, 2026) with a 19M-parameter action
regression adapter by default. During training, action and perception objectives jointly
update the backbone, with perception supervision reusing its native
image-editing interface and generative objective. Deployment requires only a single
backbone forward pass and action regression, without visual generation or
iterative action denoising. Figures 1(b)
and 2 provide an overview and the detailed
architecture, respectively.

Without additional large-scale robot-data pretraining, GenPA
achieves strong control performance on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and
RoboTwin 2.0. On real-world contact-rich manipulation, GenPA outperforms
π0.5\pi_{0.5}, Fast-WAM, and ImageWAM while demonstrating strong robustness
to visual perturbations. Under compiled inference on a single H100 GPU,
GenPA takes 20.9 ms per action chunk, achieving 1.71.7–3.4×3.4\times speedups
over the evaluated VLA and WAM baselines.
Our ablations further show that direct action regression achieves
better closed-loop control performance with lower inference latency than a
flow-based action head in our main evaluations. Compared with direct depth
regression, native flow-based depth supervision improves control robustness
at a higher training cost.

Our contributions are twofold. (i) We introduce GenPA,
demonstrating that an image generation backbone can be directly adapted into
a strong, efficient robot policy without a future visual prediction
objective. Its native visual co-training interface supports diverse
supervision targets without task-specific perception heads, enabling systematic
comparisons of visual tasks and their combinations within a common policy
architecture. (ii) Our controlled studies show that strong
closed-loop control can be achieved with direct action regression, without
iterative action denoising, and identify current-depth supervision as a simple,
effective training recipe. Our latency analysis further reveals
an architectural advantage of visual generation backbones for robot
control: lightweight observation encoding and independent language encoding
align computation with the different update frequencies of observations
and instructions.

title: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction
authors: GiHyun Kim,JinMo Yang,Hyung-Sin Kim
abstract:
Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur.
We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate’s depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints.
We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene–illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned Absrel\text{Abs}_{\text{rel}} by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.
introduction:
Monocular depth estimation (MDE) provides dense geometric cues from a single RGB image, making it attractive for mobile robots constrained by sensor cost, size, or payload [1].
Recent depth foundation models further expand the potential of RGB cameras as a source of geometry through improved generalization across diverse scenes [2, 3, 4]. Deploying these models reliably, however, depends on how RGB images are acquired as well as on the model that interprets them.

Camera settings determine the visual evidence available before inference begins. Saturation can erase intensity differences, while motion blur and low signal-to-noise ratios can obscure boundaries and texture [5, 6, 7, 8]. Learned priors can compensate for degraded observations, but faithful recovery of details lost during capture is not assured [9].
These effects are particularly important for moving robots: a long exposure that reveals a dark scene at rest can blur it during a turn, whereas shortening exposure limits the collected light. These tradeoffs motivate adapting acquisition to preserve evidence useful to the depth model as motion and illumination change.

The central challenge is obtaining feedback that distinguishes camera settings by their usefulness to the deployed depth model, without ground-truth depth online. Classical controllers optimize image statistics [5, 6, 7, 8], while learned approaches incorporate supervision from downstream perception tasks [10, 11, 12]. LENS [13] further uses a frozen model’s confidence to guide acquisition in quasi-static environments. These approaches establish the value of task-aware camera control, but feedback based on appearance, feature matching, or classification does not directly quantify capture quality for MDE. Depth uncertainty estimators provide relevant signals [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20], but their usefulness for ranking physical camera settings must also be established. On a moving robot, these rankings must be updated from successive observations as viewpoint and illumination change.

We introduce ADEPT, a framework that adapts exposure and gain using reference-relative disagreement (RRD) as learned feedback for a frozen MDE model.
During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of captures at approximately matched viewpoints and different camera settings. A compact predictor learns disagreement between each candidate’s depth prediction and the reference prediction (RRD), with an auxiliary ranking loss. RRD serves as a surrogate for relative capture quality, whose usefulness is evaluated through camera-selection experiments.
At deployment, the predictor scores observed captures using frozen MDE features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process (GP) controller uses recent scores to select the next exposure and gain under motion-dependent and photometric constraints.
We evaluate the resulting feedback across training and validation scene configurations and in online mobile-robot experiments.

Our contributions are threefold:

An acquisition-oriented supervision target (RRD), and a compact predictor that learns to compare camera settings for a frozen MDE model using ground-truth-selected references and a ranking loss.

A controller that integrates this feedback into sequential exposure and gain selection, using contextual Gaussian-process (GP) optimization with motion-dependent and photometric constraints.

An evaluation of camera-setting selection using relative and metric variants of Depth Anything v2, together with online control on a mobile robot. Across nine scene–illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean Absrel\text{Abs}_{\text{rel}} by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to Zhang et al. [11], with each condition weighted equally.

2. A controller that integrates this feedback into sequential exposure and gain selection, using contextual Gaussian-process (GP) optimization with motion-dependent and photometric constraints.

3. An evaluation of camera-setting selection using relative and metric variants of Depth Anything v2, together with online control on a mobile robot. Across nine scene–illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean Absrel\text{Abs}_{\text{rel}} by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to Zhang et al. title: Beyond Future Views: Exploring Future-State World Models for Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Kangyi Wu,Pengna Li,Yucheng Wang,Yance Fang,Xihan Ma,Zhizhong Su,Yang Wu,Ye Deng,Jinjun Wang,Jianyi Liu
abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.

title: AnyBodyCodec: A Shared Native Interface for Body-Model Conversion, Extension, and Humanoid Control
authors: Qianxing Li
abstract:
Parametric body models expose incompatible pose and shape controls, tying humanoid
policies to particular input formats. AnyBodyCodec learns a shared representation
through native conversion, then reuses it for new body models and control with its
core frozen. Encoders map MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA to aligned slots; native decoders
recover target controls. The 1.090M-parameter converter covers nine routes and reaches
16.801 mm input-reference MPJPE across six cross routes: the 2.887M Transformer bank
reaches 16.390 mm and its parameter-matched version 18.866 mm. Three measured routes
take 7.43–7.67 ms on an RTX 4090. Adding ANNY shows that comparable conversion accuracy can accompany
different action consistency under one frozen controller. Under a matched PPO budget,
aligned slots support 60.78% full-action success across three formats. Separate
160-hour training reaches 66.10% source-weighted validation success, and the controller
is deployed qualitatively on a physical G1 through three visual front ends. Together,
these results establish reuse through both native geometric fidelity and downstream
policy compatibility.
introduction:
A humanoid controller should be able to follow the same human motion when its
perception system changes the body model used to describe it. Yet parametric body
models expose incompatible pose and shape controls, tying conversion tools and policy
inputs to particular formats. We study whether native body-model conversion can learn
a shared motion representation that remains useful across changes in body-model
interfaces and downstream tasks.

Such reuse requires geometric fidelity and consistent interpretation. The representation
must retain enough information to recover target-native controls, while allowing a
fixed policy to interpret corresponding motions across formats. Geometric agreement
alone does not establish this compatibility: native decoders may recover similar poses
from features that elicit different actions from the same controller.

We introduce AnyBodyCodec as a shared native interface for MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA
(Fig. 1). Model-specific encoders map paired native fits to
aligned slots that constitute the shared representation; target decoders recover native pose
and shape controls. We then freeze the conversion-trained network and learn new
body-model interfaces or a control adapter around it. Our contribution is this reusable
representation and its evaluation across native conversion, frozen extension, and
humanoid control.

The experiments establish this reuse in three steps. Compact conversion approaches
the accuracy of a Transformer bank with 2.65 times as many parameters and improves
on a parameter-matched bank (Table I). Attaching ANNY tests whether
new interfaces can learn around the fixed representation. Similar conversion errors
but different frozen-policy action deviations reveal why downstream compatibility
needs its own evaluation (Fig. 5). Finally, matched-budget
PPO evaluates shared-policy learning across three formats (Table III);
separate 160-hour training tests larger-corpus learning (Table IV).
Qualitative G1 deployment through three visual front ends demonstrates reuse across
perception formats.
