title: FoRe: A Force-Guided Framework for Autonomous Grasp Recovery in Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Shuai Peng,Yongkai Liao,Yuxin Cheng,Haoyuan Wang,Jian Huang
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in grasp-based manipulation, yet reliable recovery from local grasping failures remains challenging. Specifically, in pick-and-place tasks, policies may continue transport after a failed grasp instead of retrying, potentially reflecting overreliance on proprioceptive cues for stage progression and limited retry supervision. Existing recovery approaches typically rely on deployment-time guidance or demonstration augmentation. We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures. Using force feedback, FoRe partitions demonstrations into approach–grasp and transport–placement stages to train separate policies. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach–grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. We also construct LIBERO-SUCTION, a force-augmented suction manipulation benchmark adapted from LIBERO, with complete demonstration trajectories for policy training. FoRe consistently improves task success rates for VLA-Adapter and π0.5\pi_{0.5} on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-SUCTION, average absolute gains are 18.4% and 6.5%, respectively. The corresponding real-world absolute gains are 25.0% and 21.7%. FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage pretrained visual-language knowledge and diverse robot data for generalizable manipulation [31, 12, 20, 25, 10], with advances in action generation, spatial understanding, reasoning, and long-horizon manipulation [2, 9, 11, 22, 30]. However, especially in pick-and-place tasks, reliable recovery from local execution errors remains challenging: an imitation-trained VLA policy may continue transport after a failed grasp, instead of retrying [17, 29]. Such behavior can turn a recoverable local error into overall task failure, motivating autonomous retries and task resumption.

Two related limitations may explain why VLA policies fail to recover after an unsuccessful grasp. First, as shown in Fig. 1, manipulation tasks can be viewed as sequences of stages, such as the approach–grasp stage and the transport–placement stage, each with its own distinct objective. Because robot proprioceptive states often correlate with task progress in successful demonstrations, a policy may rely excessively on these proprioceptive state cues to transition to the corresponding stage, regardless of the actual grasp outcome [4, 29]. Consequently, after a failed grasp, a robot proprioceptive state resembling those associated with transport may prompt the policy to persist in generating transport actions rather than retrying the grasp. Second, training dominated by uninterrupted successful demonstrations provides limited supervision for interrupting nominal execution and re-approaching the object after failure [29]. The policy may therefore lack an effective response even when failure cues are observable.

Recent studies have explored several approaches for robotic recovery. One direction uses human feedback [1, 23, 16] or vision-language model (VLM) guidance [5, 14, 28, 18] to monitor execution outcomes and guide stage progression. Another direction augments demonstrations [29] with varied robot poses and corrective trajectories to weaken correlations between pose and task progress and expand retry supervision. Force feedback provides direct physical cues about contact and load changes, making it an effective signal for detecting grasp failures. However, an explicit mechanism that uses such feedback to coordinate grasp retries and task resumption in VLA policies remains underexplored.

We introduce Force-guided Recovery (FoRe), a framework for autonomous recovery from local grasping failures in VLA-based manipulation. FoRe first uses force feedback to partition successful demonstrations into approach–grasp and transport–placement stages, training a separate policy for each. To supplement limited retry supervision, FoRe then initializes a dedicated retry policy from the approach–grasp policy and refines it through local reinforcement learning (RL) from post-failure states. To avoid inappropriate stage progression, a controller combines force feedback with grasp-command status at inference to coordinate the stage policies, detect grasp failures, and invoke the retry policy. FoRe thus mitigates the adverse effects of relying on proprioceptive cues for stage progression through explicit stage control, while local retry learning supplements limited recovery supervision. Our main contributions are threefold:

We propose FoRe, a framework that integrates independent training of two stage-specific policies, local refinement of a dedicated retry policy, and force-guided stage control to enable autonomous grasp recovery across VLA backbones.

The benchmark and demonstrations will be publicly released.

We demonstrate that FoRe yields consistent improvements in task success with VLA-Adapter and π0.5\pi_{0.5}, on LIBERO-SUCTION, LIBERO, and real-world tasks. Further evaluations show that FoRe also remains effective with only one demonstration per task on both simulation benchmarks.

title: PonderPounce-WM: When Does Predicting the Future Help Context-Dependent Robot Control?
authors: Jaeyoon Jung,Suhwan Choi,Yunsung Lee,Youngjae Yu
abstract: How does future prediction affect context-dependent robot control? We introduce PonderPounce-WM, extending PonderPounce with three future tokens supervised to predict visual-feature changes. Its pretrained MLLM, Ponder, integrates history and demonstrations into continuous cognition for the action model, Pounce. We investigate token ordering and delivery to distinguish predictive supervision from direct future conditioning. On RoboMME, cognition-first ordering with cognition-only delivery improves success from 60.83% to 67.42%. With the same ordering, direct future-token delivery yields 64.00% success. Probes show increased future information in cognition while the tested past-event attributes remain largely decodable. Across four real-robot tasks, PonderPounce-WM achieves 67.44% mean success under asynchronous execution, compared with 60.98% for PonderPounce. These results suggest that future prediction can improve context-dependent control through auxiliary supervision without delivering future tokens to the action model.
introduction:
Context-dependent robot control requires retaining past events that are no longer observable and using demonstrations to interpret the current task. Predicting future observations may help learn such control representations, but the information needed to anticipate visual changes need not coincide with what an action model needs to act. Prior work combines observation history or explicit memory with future prediction for control [10, 7, 4]. Building on PonderPounce’s use of a pretrained MLLM’s native causal context as episode memory [1], we investigate how predictive supervision shapes this continuous context representation, called cognition. This retains the MLLM context engine rather than introducing a video-generation backbone for pixel prediction.

Our focus is how predictive supervision changes a representation already responsible for episode memory: whether it improves control, whether direct future conditioning adds a benefit, and whether past-event information remains decodable. title: Geo-Force: A Theory of Force Sensing from Object Geometry
authors: Abdullah Ayad
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Robots need contact forces to handle delicate objects, but tactile sensors
are fragile and hard to integrate, whereas depth sensors, such as
RGB-D cameras, are widely available. A virtual touch sensor that keeps the
sensing surface of a tactile sensor but replaces its electronics with a touch
signal predicted from the target object’s geometry, as measured by a depth sensor,
could close this gap, yet it is unclear what such a virtual sensor computes
and when its output can be trusted. We give a formal answer. We define the
Geometric Force as the force on each taxel of a virtual touch sensor,
computed in three steps: rendering the surface to be touched as seen from the
virtual sensor, predicting the touch signal with a touch map, learned or
simulated, and estimating the force from that signal. We prove three
properties of the Geometric Force. First, its force vectors only rotate
under a change of coordinate frame. Second, it vanishes when the rendered
surface does not touch the virtual sensor. Third, it is stable: its error
grows at most linearly with the errors of the three steps for Lipschitz
maps. The
rendering error, in turn, depends on how well the surface is sampled or
reconstructed and how accurately the sensor is placed. We then show a
fundamental limit: geometry does not reveal the object’s stiffness, so no
touch map can predict touch exactly for objects of the same shape and different
stiffness. Under an elastic contact model, all object-specific knowledge
resides in the touch map. From these results, we derive requirements on the
depth sensor and the objects, design rules, and the conditions under which
such a virtual sensor fails.
introduction:
Touch-sensitive robotic tasks often rely on custom hardware such as
underactuated grippers, vacuum grippers, or fingertip tactile sensors, which
makes them system-specific. Compared to vision and language,
touch data in robotics remains scarce. Tactile perception is complicated by
the heterogeneity of sensor morphology, signal representation,
dimensionality, and processing pipelines [1].
Collecting consistent tactile data is hard as well: contact forces can
degrade both sensors and objects. Depth sensors, in contrast, are cheap,
standardized, and already mounted on most robots. We therefore ask:
what can a robot know about contact force from the geometry of an
object alone?

Touch sensors, regardless of their measurement principle (e.g., optics,
magnetism, capacitance), measure interactions between an external object and a
compliant sensing surface. Optical tactile sensors such as
DIGIT [2] have gained traction because they provide
rich spatial information, which motivated the notion of taxels,
analogous to pixels in images. Building, integrating, and calibrating such
sensors for every robotic platform remains a significant barrier to adoption.
Replacing them requires virtual alternatives of comparable fidelity, for which
physical simulators [3, 4] and cross-modal models
learned from easier-to-collect modalities [5, 6]
are candidate solutions. Cross-modal models that map vision or depth to touch
can, in principle, provide tactile feedback where only cameras are available,
which is attractive because RGB-D cameras capture 3D geometry directly.

A virtual touch sensor keeps the gel of a real touch sensor, so the object
still presses against the same soft surface, with the same force as on the
real sensor. Only the electronics that read the gel’s
deformation are replaced, by a touch signal predicted from the target
object’s geometry, as measured by a depth sensor. From this signal, a
pretrained decoder such as SPARSH [7] estimates the
force, just as it does from the signal of the real sensor. Unlike
methods that regress force or pressure directly from
images [8, 9], a virtual touch
sensor thus reports the force on the taxels of a real sensor. It can
therefore reuse the force decoder and the touch data recorded with that
sensor. Before such a virtual sensor can be trusted, e.g., to
grasp a raw egg, one must know what its force means, which depth sensors it
needs, which objects it works on, and when it fails. None of the four has a
formal answer yet.

We propose to reason about any such virtual touch sensor through one
quantity, the Geometric Force: the force on each taxel of a touch
sensor, predicted from the geometry of the object alone. The ideal
Geometric Force uses the touch map with the smallest mean squared error
between the predicted and the true touch signal. It thus marks the upper bound of what geometry
can reveal about touch, separating the errors that better geometry can remove
from those that only touch data can. In short, a virtual touch sensor sees
the shape of a surface, down to its texture, but not how it yields.

This work makes six contributions:

Formal definition. We define the Geometric Force as a composition of
three maps, rendering, touch prediction, and force estimation, on a shared
pixel grid. The touch map is either learned from real
tactile data or simulated.

Structural properties. We prove that the Geometric Force is
equivariant to the coordinate frame whenever rendering is frame-invariant,
and give conditions, met by any contact-gated touch map, under which
it vanishes exactly out of contact.

Stability bounds. For Lipschitz touch and force maps, the error of
the Geometric Force grows at most linearly with the errors of its three
maps. The rendering error, in turn, grows at most linearly with the fill distance
and sampling precision of the measured points and with the touch-sensor
pose error.

Stiffness limit. Shape alone cannot determine touch
for objects of unknown stiffness. The resulting irreducible touch error grows with
the range of the object-to-gel stiffness ratio. Under
an elastic-foundation model, only the touch map depends on the object.

Real-to-sim-to-real example. We realize rendering for a hidden surface by
shape completion and 6D tracking, and show that its completion and tracking
errors replace the sampling errors in the stability bounds.

Practical takeaways. We derive requirements on the depth
sensor and the objects. The depth sensor needs point spacing finer than
the surface detail and depth noise well below the gel indentation. The
objects should keep their shape until contact, have no sharp edges, and be
much stiffer than the gel or all about equally stiff. We
also state when a virtual sensor fails.

2. Structural properties. We prove that the Geometric Force is

title: RoboPRO: A Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-Aware Benchmark for Robotic Manipulation
authors: Zhiyuan Li,Charles Eret,Dingsheng Liu,Xuan Zhao,Joshua Choi,Yangzheng Wu,Tongtong Cao,Yingxue Zhang,Amir Rasouli
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? Some benchmarks evaluate isolated perturbations on uncluttered surfaces or use collision measures that do not capture contact severity. Others provide realistic environments but omit perturbation evaluation and safety metrics entirely. To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. The benchmark suite and data are available at https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/.
introduction:
Learning-based robotic manipulation policies have demonstrated impressive generalization on tabletop tasks in simulation [1, 2], yet deploying these policies in complex environments exposes two distinct failure modes that current benchmarks largely overlook. The first is perturbation fragility: policies that perform near-ceiling on the canonical evaluation regress sharply when camera pose, lighting, language phrasing, or object identity drift even modestly. The second is collision behaviour: a policy that completes its task by disturbing a non-target object or forcefully pushing through a cabinet door achieves a perfect score on the standard success rate (SR) metric even though it is unsafe to deploy [3]. Despite rapid progress in policy learning and evaluation, the existing benchmarks do not jointly stress both axes within the same set of obstacle-laden scenes.

Perturbation-robustness suites [4, 5, 6] omit the effect of camera vibration and bundle language factors, so individual perturbation factors are understudied. In addition, they report only success rate (SR) on clean tabletops with minimal surrounding geometry, so the contact events that would expose a brittle planner never occur. Conversely, the safety-oriented benchmarks that do instrument collision [7, 8, 9] use binary or count-based contact flags that conflate a 2 mm cup nudge with a sweep that knocks the cup off the table. In these benchmarks, the scene setups lack realistic, complex background, have limited diversity, and clutter perturbation is not systematic.

To this end, we propose RoboPRO, a safety benchmark that evaluates perturbation-resilience and obstacle-awareness of manipulation policies under a unified suite (see Fig. 1). RoboPRO consists of 60 atomic tasks and 20 compositional tasks performed in four distinct, realistically furnished simulated household environments under diverse configurations. Our benchmark extends upon existing perturbation protocols by modeling pixel shift, full OOD furniture texture and object diversification, and decomposes language perturbations along five axes, enabling more in-depth analysis of instruction diversity on performance. Moreover, we employ a clutter generation strategy to induce manipulation under different degrees of visual and operational complexity. To measure safety, we propose two novel metrics to determine hazardous contact between the robot and environment or distractors. In sum, our contributions are as follows: 1) A holistic safety benchmark that combines perturbation- and clutter-based challenges into a unified evaluation suite using diverse scenes, and atomic and compositional manipulation tasks; 2) Extended perturbation strategy for capturing real-world camera movement and per-axis analysis for measuring the impact of instruction diversity on performance; 3) A cluttering strategy allowing systematic scenario generation with different degrees of visual and operational complexity; 4) Safety metrics to quantify the hazardous actions of the robot with respect to the environment or non-target objects; 5) Extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art manipulation policies on RoboPRO, with in-depth analysis of the effect of perturbations and clutter, training data composition, and task complexity on performance.

title: RoboDyna: A Benchmark for Evaluating Robotic Manipulation under Physically Grounded Dynamics
authors: Zhiyuan Li,Rui Heng Yang,Xuan Zhao,Amir Rasouli
abstract:
Object manipulation in the dynamic real world requires understanding how the environment functions and evolves, and acting accordingly. Existing benchmarks, however, do not adequately address these needs. Physics-oriented benchmarks evaluate predictive fidelity but not closed-loop action. Dynamic robotic manipulation benchmarks often use simplified, physically implausible object motions, limiting evaluation of reasoning and action under realistic dynamics. Evaluation is also typically synchronized, freezing the environment during inference and making computation time irrelevant to task outcomes.
To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark for evaluating the physical understanding and action capabilities of manipulation policies in dynamic scenes. RoboDyna comprises 20 conceptual dynamic tasks spanning five capability categories, with simple objects and minimal scene clutter, under a two-factor difficulty design, and 10 household tasks that instantiate the same capabilities in visually and semantically richer simulated real-world environments. RoboDyna provides 3,500 expert demonstrations, paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocols, metrics for task success and partial completion, and interactive tools for human baseline evaluation.
Evaluating vision-language-action models and a world-action model across 5.4K episodes, we find that all policies achieve success rates below 20%, revealing substantial limitations in dynamic manipulation. The world-action model captures simple physical dynamics but struggles with complex interactions, and its prediction fidelity does not consistently align with task success. Sync–async comparisons show that inference latency flips 5–12% of episode outcomes while changing average success rates by at most 3%. Human baselines substantially outperform all policies under matched conditions.
The benchmark and complete results are available at https://robodyna.github.io/robodyna/.
introduction:
Recent robotic manipulation policies demonstrate impressive capabilities in static scenes [1, 2, 3, 4], but their physical competence in dynamic environments remains underexplored. Completing a task in a dynamic environment introduces two challenges [5, 6]. First, selecting the correct action may require integrating multiple observations to infer object motion and anticipate future states. Second, the correct action must be executed within a critical time window, as scene evolution can render an otherwise valid action ineffective [7, 8].

Evaluating such physical competence requires both anticipating how the scene will evolve and acting accordingly. However, current benchmarks do not jointly evaluate both. Predictive world-model benchmarks [9, 10] primarily evaluate physical consistency and the fidelity of predicted futures, with limited emphasis on closed-loop policy performance under realistic execution timing. Robotics benchmarks either contain no independent scene dynamics [11, 3, 4] or animate targets with scripted motion while pausing the world during inference [5].
Evaluating under the latter regime has several consequences. First, physically implausible dynamics limit transfer to real-world physics. Second, limited dynamic complexity restricts the range of physical capabilities tested. Third, synchronous evaluation makes inference cost-free: the environment is frozen during computation, whether a policy takes seconds per action chunk [12] or runs at tens of hertz [1].

To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a physics-governed, latency-aware benchmark for dual-arm manipulation in dynamic environments (see
Fig. 1). RoboDyna challenges policies to anticipate scene evolution, accounts for inference latency, and jointly evaluates physical understanding and action capabilities.
The proposed benchmark consists of 20 conceptual tasks, divided into five physical-understanding categories with varying difficulty levels to measure core policy competencies. An additional 10 complex household tasks are designed to evaluate transfer to realistic scenes. For evaluation, we use mixed metrics to record full and partial success under synchronous and asynchronous regimes. Moreover, our benchmark contains 3,500 expert demonstrations and tools for collecting human baseline performance under teleoperation and scene-interactive control.
In summary our contributions are as follows: (1) we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark suite of
physics-governed dynamic tasks, which consists of 20 conceptual tasks in five capability categories with four per-task difficulty designs and additional 10 household tasks; (2) We define a paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocol to isolate the effect of inference latency on task outcome and mixed success and partial-success metrics; (3) We conduct extensive evaluation of two state-of-the-art VLAs and one WAM on over 5400 episodes to characterize their physical competence under different dynamic conditions; (4) We report on 12-participant human baseline performance on proposed tasks using different control regimes.

title: RoboCap-10k: A Metrically Accurate Egocentric Dataset for Robot Learning
authors: Kheri Hughes,Qasim Ali,Nikash Bhardwaj,Owen Akhibi,Niresh Dravin,Vivek Sharma,Sam Cho,Ethan Lee,Paul Luo,Sunny Yu,Jonathan Victor,Amanda Young,Michael Cho,Ademi Adeniji,Vincent Liu
abstract: Egocentric video is the most scalable source of manipulation data for robot learning, but its difficulty lies in producing high-quality supervision. Existing large corpora lack metric 3D labels or rely on heterogeneous devices, motion-capture labs, or a headset’s built-in real-time tracker, whose accuracy is not reported for the released data. We introduce RoboCap-10k: 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation recorded during workers’ paid shifts in 11 countries, spanning 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks. Every hour is captured on one device, the RoboCap, a 250 g hat with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. Online calibration brings every device below 1 px of epipolar error, visual-inertial SLAM yields gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories, and a multi-view hand tracker yields metric cm-precise hand poses. Each episode is annotated with task and sub-task language captions. Project page: https://robocap10k.com.
introduction:
The pursuit of general-purpose robotics has exposed a data bottleneck: whereas foundation models for language and vision scale on internet text and imagery, robot policies remain starved for physical interaction data. Teleoperation provides demonstrations in the robot’s own embodiment, but it is slow, expensive, and hard to extend to the long tail of environments and tasks. The field has therefore turned to egocentric human video, which captures fluid, purposeful manipulation across thousands of real environments at a fraction of the cost.

Egocentric video becomes action supervision only through estimation. Recent scaling studies show that pretraining on large egocentric corpora improves generalization of robot policies, and that 3D hand pose labels are needed to extract most of that benefit [40, 4, 55]. The quality of those labels is set by the capture hardware. The largest corpora are recorded with monocular head-mounted cameras [23, 6], from which metric scale can only be inferred from learned priors. Calibrated stereo rigs measure scale directly, but are sensitive to calibration: on the RoboCap, one pixel of disparity error corresponds to roughly one centimeter of depth at 0.65 m, comparable to the grasp tolerance of a parallel-jaw gripper [3]. Research headsets paired with optical motion capture reach millimeter accuracy, but only within instrumented volumes and with small participant pools [5, 27]. Federated efforts scale by pooling heterogeneous devices [46], which introduces cross-rig variation in both appearance and 3D estimation quality. Datasets labeled by a headset’s own tracker inherit whatever that tracker outputs in real time, with no raw multi-view data to re-estimate from. RoboCap-10k instead releases the raw synchronized streams alongside offline labels whose accuracy is benchmarked (Section 5), so labels can be audited and regenerated as methods improve.

RoboCap-10k also standardizes the hardware: it contains a single device model collecting real paid work processed by a single 3D stack. All 10,000 hours are recorded on the RoboCap [3], a 250 g hat whose camera layout is designed based on the requirements of near-field metric estimation, and all are processed by the same Grounded API pipeline with per-session online calibration. Rather than scripted household chores or tabletop tasks, the corpus records occupational work, including bread and pastry production, industrial garment stitching, engine and motorcycle repair, circuit-board soldering, rebar tying, and onion harvesting, in workplaces across India, Nigeria, Colombia, the United States, the United Kingdom, Mexico, Chile, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, and Spain.

Our contributions are:

A 10,000-hour curated, single-device corpus of occupational manipulation. Every hour is bimanual manipulation with a clear task and passes SLAM and hand-tracking quality checks. RoboCap-10k covers 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 distinct tasks in 11 countries across five continents. Because every hour comes from the same hardware design with per-unit factory calibration, there is no cross-device domain shift in either imagery or 3D label quality.

A 10,000-hour curated, single-device corpus of occupational manipulation. Every hour is bimanual manipulation with a clear task and passes SLAM and hand-tracking quality checks. RoboCap-10k covers 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 distinct tasks in 11 countries across five continents. Because every hour comes from the same hardware design with per-unit factory calibration, there is no cross-device domain shift in either imagery or 3D label quality.

Metric 3D annotations for every frame. Online-calibrated, gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories from multi-camera visual-inertial SLAM and metric MANO hand poses from a multi-view hand tracker, expressed in the head-mounted rig frame and mapped to the world frame by the head trajectory.

A two-tier language layer. An episode-level caption (scene and high-level task) paired with dense, temporally segmented sub-task units, each carrying a high-level task and a low-level action.

title: Staleness Deadlines for Motion Plans during Onboard Reasoning
authors: Hassan Iqbal
abstract:
Language models may enable general autonomy in robot planning, but their reasoning on an onboard computer can run for most of a minute while the robot and nearby pedestrians keep moving.
The robot must then decide how long to keep following a plan that the language model’s answer may overturn.
Here we present staleness deadlines, which hand that decision to the robot’s clock.
Calibrated prediction regions for pedestrians and deviation tubes for the robot set the deadline.
When the language model answers, a graph planner rebuilds the route, and the robot switches to it only after the new plan passes the same clearance check against walls and predicted pedestrians.
We use exact binomial tests to determine which prespecified budget-selection policies keep close calls, wrong decisions and late arrivals below their targets at each inference profile.
Candidate policies either fix one budget or choose a budget for each query from how long the robot can continue its current plan before it must brake.
We study corridor signs that close routes and delivery requests whose destination the language model must infer.
In 81,000 simulated missions with recorded Qwen3-4B answers, full reasoning cuts wrong decisions about twentyfold, and tracking until the deadline cuts late arrivals by up to 64%.
The robot never collides while it moves, although pedestrians who never yield still walk into the robot once it has stopped, in 23% of offline and 32% of live missions.
On a Jetson AGX Orin under perception load, short budgets fail the wrong-decision target and full reasoning fails the lateness target.
Between these extremes, a fixed-budget policy passes for corridor signs and prespecified per-query policies pass for deliveries.
Live Orin missions agree with offline replay on all three losses in 24 of the 32 missions where either run records any of them.
The deadline turns slower reasoning into measurable mission outcomes, which let designers test how much reasoning can be supported under each inference profile.
introduction:
Mobile robots increasingly use natural-language information such as route restrictions and delivery requests to decide where to go and what to do (Figure 1a,b).
Language models supply the open-world knowledge needed to interpret such messages [1, 5], yet accurate interpretation and capable motion control do not automatically compose into safe, timely missions [12].
When Qwen3-4B [17] answers immediately, it sends our robot into a closed corridor in about one run in four.
Full reasoning cuts this to about one run in a hundred, yet the answer can take most of a minute on a Jetson AGX Orin.
During that minute the people around the robot keep walking, so how long it may keep following a plan that the answer may overturn becomes a control decision in its own right.

Existing systems allocate reasoning effort [6, 10, 4, 14, 15], accelerate inference [11, 18], or overlap inference and execution [3].
In the closest work [13], a vehicle falls back on a verified emergency maneuver whenever a new plan fails a check that finishes within milliseconds and covers every position other road users could legally reach.
Onboard reasoning allows neither luxury as the language model’s answer may arrive after most of a minute or never, and over such a wait the reach of a walking pedestrian spans the whole corridor.
We therefore bound pedestrians with calibrated prediction regions instead.

We present staleness deadlines for motion plans, which move the boundary between reasoning and control from the language model’s answer to the robot’s clock.
A plan grows stale as the people it was checked against move on, and the deadline marks the last moment at which the robot can still switch from the stale plan to braking without coming too close to anyone.
A clock monitor brakes at the deadline unless a plan built from the answer passes the same check in time (Figure 1c,d).
Our contributions are as follows.

Staleness deadlines (Section 3) that carry fail-safe planning [8, 16, 13] over to reasoning with no time bound.
The deadline plays the role of the time-to-react in [13], with conformal pedestrian regions and robot tubes in place of set-based reachability.

Mission-level reasoning-budget qualification that determines which prespecified fixed-budget and per-query policies keep close calls, wrong decisions and late arrivals below their targets with at least 95% family-level confidence within each task and inference profile.

Onboard evaluation showing inexpensive offline replay anticipates losses of live Orin missions.

title: Coherent Moment Propagation: Epistemic Uncertainty for Pre-trained Robot Policies
authors: Miguel Saavedra-Ruiz,Anqi Li,Claudia D'Arpino,Alperen Degirmenci,Tucker Hermans,Fabio Ramos
abstract: Flow matching policies underpin the state-of-the-art in robot learning, with impressive results ranging from long-horizon planning to dexterous manipulation. However, they provide no measure of whether their predicted commands can be trusted, particularly in novel situations outside their training set. Epistemic uncertainty reflects uncertainty about the model’s weights and quantifies this ignorance, but calculating it at inference time from a flow matching policy is not trivial. Actions are produced by an ODE solver, requiring uncertainty to be propagated through the entire integration process. BayesDiff addresses this problem for diffusion models by propagating the mean and variance of the state through the denoising chain under a last-layer Laplace posterior approximation, but it severely underestimates the epistemic uncertainty. In this paper we: i) prove that, for flow matching and diffusion ODEs, BayesDiff’s total variance decays at rate O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) as the number of Euler steps TT used by the solver increases; ii) introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters that fix this problem by carrying the cross-covariance between state and weights; and iii) widen the last-layer posterior with observation embeddings the policy already computes, improving uncertainty estimates without retraining for CoMP and several test-time estimators alike. We demonstrate these benefits on three manipulation benchmarks with applications in failure detection and demonstration selection for fine-tuning, where CoMP corrects BayesDiff’s variance collapse while matching or outperforming several uncertainty estimators.
introduction:
Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023b; Albergo et al., 2025) has become an integral component of robot stacks, powering action heads in state-of-the-art robot policies (Black et al., 2025b; Bjorck et al., 2025; Shukor et al., 2025). Despite their widespread success, these models lack an inherent mechanism to assess the reliability of their predictions. Epistemic uncertainty provides one such indicator, measuring how much predictions vary across parameter settings consistent with the training data (Kendall and Gal, 2017). However, obtaining this uncertainty at test time is increasingly important given the resources invested in foundation policies (Bjorck et al., 2025), whose reliability on unfamiliar tasks remains difficult to assess (Xu et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2026).

Uncertainty quantification of a flow matching-based policy is not trivial, as it requires propagating model uncertainty through the ODE solver that generates robot commands. A common technique to quantify uncertainty is to compare the predictions from an ensemble of policies, whether trained (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Pearce et al., 2020; Berry et al., 2024; Römer et al., 2026), generated by a hypernetwork (Chan et al., 2024) or drawn from a posterior fit after training (Jazbec et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2025). However, training and storing independent model copies is costly at the scale of foundation policies, motivating estimators that work from a single pre-trained policy.

Post-hoc Bayesian inference offers a way to obtain epistemic uncertainty from pre-trained models (Daxberger et al., 2021; Jazbec et al., 2025). Particularly, BayesDiff (Kou et al., 2024) combines a last-layer Laplace posterior with moment propagation, carrying the mean and variance of the denoised state through the sampling chain of a diffusion model (Ho et al., 2020), with extensions beyond the last layer (Gupta et al., 2026), to flow matching models (Han et al., 2026), and to multi-agent trajectory modeling (Capellera et al., 2025). However, we prove that BayesDiff exhibits variance collapse on flow matching and diffusion ODEs: under Lipschitz regularity and bounded predictive variance, its estimated total variance is upper bounded by O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) in the number of Euler steps TT, so it vanishes as the solver is refined; see Figure 1 (b) and (d). This creates an artificial tradeoff: finer integration better approximates the ODE solution, yet drives the reported uncertainty to zero.

To address this limitation, we introduce Coherent Moment Propagation (CoMP), a method that carries the cross-covariance between state and weights, yielding an upper bound on total variance independent of TT, see Figure 1 (c) and (d). We show that BayesDiff’s variance collapse results from treating the weights as independent of the state they generate, and derive two recursions inspired by the extended and unscented Kalman filters. Furthermore, to improve uncertainty estimates from a last-layer Laplace approximation (Deng et al., 2022; Calvo-Ordoñez et al., 2026), we draw inspiration from LULA (Kristiadi et al., 2021) and widen the last layer with observation embeddings already computed by foundation robot policies, without re-training or changing their action predictions.

In summary, our contributions are:

We prove BayesDiff’s variance collapse and show its total variance is upper bounded by O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) for flow matching and diffusion ODEs with the number of Euler integration steps TT;

We prove BayesDiff’s variance collapse and show its total variance is upper bounded by O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) for flow matching and diffusion ODEs with the number of Euler integration steps TT;

We derive two new uncertainty estimators, CoMP-EKF and CoMP-UKF, from a linearized sampler recursion that carries state-weight cross-covariance, with a constant total variance bound; and

We improve last-layer Laplace uncertainty estimates by widening the head with existing observation embeddings, without re-training the policy or changing its action predictions.

We demonstrate the practical utility of our uncertainty estimators in the problems of runtime failure detection (Römer et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025) and demonstration selection (Agia et al., 2025; Sirigiri et al., 2026) for fine-tuning (Bagatella et al., 2025; Römer et al., 2026). Across three robot policies and three manipulation benchmarks (robomimic (Mandlekar et al., 2022), LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023a), and RoboLab (Yang et al., 2026)), CoMP is better calibrated than BayesDiff and matches or outperforms several test-time uncertainty estimators for pre-trained robot policies. Lastly, we show that the augmented head further improves uncertainty estimates from CoMP and several baselines.

title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models
authors: Sheng Cheng,Deqian Kong
abstract:
World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history.
Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model.
We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length.
It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions.
The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window.
LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training.
Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks.
On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4 s of history matches one trained with 9.6 s, while a model with 4.8 s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points.
Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.
introduction:
Human behavior combines knowledge acquired over time with rapid learning from new experience, as described by complementary learning systems theory [35].
In motor control, discrepancies between predicted and observed sensory outcomes can drive adaptation during action [43].
These findings motivate learning during robot execution, where the outcomes of actions provide feedback for the predictions that guide subsequent behavior [37].

World-action models [13, 31, 24, 30, 21] provide a natural setting for such learning.
They predict future frames together with actions, drawing on video pretraining to learn how scenes evolve.
In the models we study, the imagined future guides action generation.
After the robot acts, the observed frames provide targets for the model’s own video loss.
As interactions within a task share objects, surroundings and dynamics, learning from these frames may improve predictions of what happens next.
The updated predictions can then guide subsequent actions.

This learning allows experience to influence behavior beyond a fixed observation window.
Most world-action models condition on a short history, which limits the past observations available at each decision.
Extending the history [21, 30] increases computation and can require a separately trained model.
Selecting or compressing the history requires components that are trained together with the policy [49, 54, 46].
Updating the model on the observed frames provides another way to use the past observations.
These updates are a form of test-time training, a family of methods that update a model on each test input with a self-supervised loss [40], which has been extended to language and video generation models [50, 17, 42, 41, 12].

We introduce LoCo-WAM, a test-time training method for world-action models, which trains the video expert during execution with its video loss on the observed frames.
At every decision, LoCo-WAM takes one gradient step on a low-rank adapter [18] of the video expert to predict the most recently observed frames from the history that preceded them.
It keeps the action expert unchanged and resets the adapter at the start of every episode.
Since the adapter accumulates these updates over the episode, the video expert is trained on frames that have already left its history.
The action expert then generates the next action from the imagined future and the features of the adapted video expert.
LoCo-WAM thereby requires no labels, rewards, additional data, new layers or meta-training, keeps the history length of the model, and can run its update while the robot executes the current action chunk.

We evaluate LoCo-WAM on two world-action models, Long-WAM [21] and LingBot-VA [30], and four simulation benchmarks: RoboCasa GR-1 [4], RoboCasa365 [36], LIBERO-Mem [11] and RoboTwin 2.0 [8].
LoCo-WAM improves the base model on all four benchmarks.
On RoboCasa GR-1, Long-WAM with 2.4 s of history reaches 73.6% with LoCo-WAM, on par with the base model trained with 9.6 s of history, at 0.76 s per decision compared with 0.67 s and without training a separate model.
With 4.8 s of history, it reaches 78.3%, 4.8 points above the 9.6 s model (Fig. 1).
On LIBERO-Mem, LingBot-VA with an 8-chunk history matches its default 30-chunk history.
On both benchmarks, LoCo-WAM also outperforms test-time methods for robot policies, including AdaWorldPolicy [55], which adapts the world model across the episodes of a task, and RoboTTT [23], which meta-trains fast-weight layers.

Our analysis on RoboCasa GR-1 examines what an update of the video expert learns from the observed frames, how it reaches the action, and how its effect develops over the episode.
The update improves the prediction of upcoming frames before they are used for training, with larger reductions in video loss for shorter histories.
Using the model’s own predictions as targets in place of the observed frames removes the gain in success rate.
The update affects the action mainly through the imagined future, since applying it only when the video expert predicts this future recovers most of the gain.
We further show that updating only the video expert performs better than also updating the action expert with the action loss.
Over the episode, the change of the action accumulates, and stopping the updates early removes most of the gain.

In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce LoCo-WAM, test-time training as long context for world-action models: the video expert is trained during execution with its video loss on the observed frames, without labels, additional data or meta-training.

On two world-action models and four simulation benchmarks, LoCo-WAM improves the base model on all four benchmarks, enables a model with a short history to match or exceed the base model with a longer history, and outperforms prior test-time methods for robot policies.

We analyze how the update of the video expert reaches the action: it improves the prediction of upcoming frames from the observed frames, affects the action mainly through the imagined future, and the change of the action it causes accumulates over the episode.

1. We introduce LoCo-WAM, test-time training as long context for world-action models: the video expert is trained during execution with its video loss on the observed frames, without labels, additional data or meta-training.

2. On two world-action models and four simulation benchmarks, LoCo-WAM improves the base model on all four benchmarks, enables a model with a short history to match or exceed the base model with a longer history, and outperforms prior test-time methods for robot policies.

3. We analyze how the update of the video expert reaches the action: it improves the prediction of upcoming frames from the observed frames, affects the action mainly through the imagined future, and the change of the action it causes accumulates over the episode.

title: Skill-JEPA: Learning Planner-Aligned Action Spaces for World Models
authors: Tomás Couso Coddou,Christ Devia,Rex G. Liu,Rodrigo Toro Icarte
abstract:
World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from pixels to predict the outcome of actions in a latent space. To reach a goal, a planner samples many candidate action sequences, uses the model to predict where each one leads, and executes the best one.
However, standard planners draw their candidates from a Gaussian,
while the model has only seen the structured, state-dependent actions of its training data. Its predictions for such candidates are unreliable, and planning fails more often as goals move farther away. We propose Skill-JEPA, which learns an action space aligned with the planner. A variational autoencoder conditioned on the current state encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. The world model predicts the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills starting from that same Gaussian, so its candidates resemble the model’s training data. Skill-JEPA adds a single module, trained end-to-end with the world model, and leaves the planner untouched, with no subgoals, hierarchy, or hand-designed skills. Across three JEPA world models and four benchmarks, average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% with raw actions to 62%; the gains grow with goal distance and hold across four planners. On AntMaze, a quadruped locomotion task, success on goals two maze cells away rises from 0.4% to 38%. This suggests that part of the difficulty of reaching distant goals lies in the action space, and can be removed without changing the planner.
introduction:
A world model predicts how an environment responds to an agent’s actions [10]. With such a model, the agent can plan before it acts [35]: to reach a goal, it imagines the outcome of many candidate action sequences and executes the most promising one. World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) [21] make these predictions in a learned latent space rather than in pixel space, and are trained on offline trajectories without rewards [45, 3, 33, 22, 17]. Nothing in this recipe is tied to a task. Once trained, the same model can pursue any goal given as an image, using an off-the-shelf sampling-based planner such as the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) [31]. Planning in this way has been found to generalize better than goal-conditioned policies learned from the same data [33].

The model and the planner, however, do not work with the same actions. The model learns from the actions recorded in its training data, which are structured and depend on the state: a walking robot moves its legs in coordination, and the right movement depends on its current pose. The planner knows none of this. CEM, like the other planners commonly used with these models, draws candidates from a Gaussian, scores them with the model, and refines its search around the best ones.
For the quadruped in Figure 1, a Gaussian candidate sends unrelated random commands to its eight joints at every step: a twitch, not a gait.

The model is therefore asked to predict the outcome of action sequences unlike those it has seen, and its predictions for them are unreliable. Because the planner chooses candidates by their predicted outcome, these errors mislead it, and they accumulate as the model is rolled out toward more distant goals. In our experiments, planning over raw actions reaches on average 87% of the goals that are 20 steps away, but only 42% of those 80 steps away. This gap between the actions a model is trained on and those it is queried with has been documented for latent world models [28, 40]. It echoes a long-standing observation in model-based reinforcement learning: optimizers exploit the errors of learned models [41, 18].

Existing remedies move one side toward the other. Some bring the model to the planner, by fine-tuning it on trajectories produced by planning or on adversarially perturbed data [28]. Others bring the planner to the data, by training a policy that proposes candidates [2, 5, 13]. Yet others shorten the problem itself, with a learned model that proposes subgoals [24] or a hierarchy of world models that plan at several time scales [43, 42]. These approaches help, but each adds a learned component, a training stage or a level of planning, and gives up part of the simplicity that makes the recipe attractive.

We take a different route: we change neither the planner nor the data, but the action space that connects them. Recent JEPA world models learn their state representation end-to-end [33, 22, 17]. We let them learn their action space as well, so that the planner’s samples fall where the model was trained. Our method, Skill-JEPA (Figure 2), adds a variational autoencoder [20] to the world model. Conditioned on the current state, it encodes short action sequences into latent codes with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. We call these codes skills, following Pertsch et al. [29]. The world model is trained to predict the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills, starting from that same Gaussian. Because the decoder sees the state, the same sample becomes a different action sequence in each state, one that resembles what the data shows there. The dependence on the state is thus handled by the decoder, and a single Gaussian can serve the planner everywhere.

Skill-JEPA is deliberately simple. Its only addition is the autoencoder, trained end-to-end with the world model, and the planner is used as is. In effect, the decoder teaches the planner what realistic action sequences look like, but without training a policy for any task: the knowledge is built into the action space itself. Skill-JEPA is also not hierarchical. Skills do not make the planner look farther ahead, since our raw-action baselines plan over action chunks of the same length, and there are no subgoals or higher-level models. Only the representation of each chunk changes, which makes the method complementary to the hierarchical approaches above.
Nor is the building block new: latent codes for action sequences are widely used in imitation and reinforcement learning (Section 2).

What we add is a precise role for the prior. We make it the distribution that a sampling-based planner starts from, so that the term that regularizes the autoencoder also limits how much worse the model can be on the planner’s initial candidates than on its training data (Section 3.3). We note that the prior is Gaussian because that is where such planners start, not because the idea requires it: the analysis holds for any initial distribution, and a planner that starts elsewhere would call for a different prior.

In summary, our contributions are:

Method. Skill-JEPA aligns the action space of a JEPA world model with its planner through a state-conditioned action autoencoder whose prior is the planner’s initial sampling distribution. The planner is left unchanged.

Analysis. We bound the model’s excess prediction error on the planner’s initial candidates through the autoencoder’s KL term, and show with controlled experiments that the gains vanish without this term.

Evaluation. On three JEPA world models, five tasks and four planners, the gains grow with goal distance and hold for every planner. Average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% to 62%, and on AntMaze goals two maze cells away, from 0.4% to 38%.

1. Method. Skill-JEPA aligns the action space of a JEPA world model with its planner through a state-conditioned action autoencoder whose prior is the planner’s initial sampling distribution. The planner is left unchanged.

2. Analysis. We bound the model’s excess prediction error on the planner’s initial candidates through the autoencoder’s KL term, and show with controlled experiments that the gains vanish without this term.

3. Evaluation. On three JEPA world models, five tasks and four planners, the gains grow with goal distance and hold for every planner. Average success on goals 80 steps away rises from 42% to 62%, and on AntMaze goals two maze cells away, from 0.4% to 38%.

title: Acoustic Markers of Engagement in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Their Caregivers
authors: Young Suh Hong,Kaleen Shrestha,Austin Joel Dympep,Maja Matarić
comment: Preprints allowed for IEEE paper submissions under review
abstract: Characterizing user engagement is essential for developing effective human-computer interaction (HCI) applications, particularly for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Because home-based HCI naturally involves caregivers as conversational facilitators, analyzing both child and caregiver vocalizations can provide critical insights into characterizing interaction dynamics. Using a dataset of home-based socially assistive robot (SAR) interventions, this work demonstrates how child and caregiver vocalization patterns can model engagement in HCI contexts. We employed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) with child and caregiver acoustic data to identify acoustic features that significantly differentiated engagement from disengagement. The results demonstrated that children and caregivers share three significant acoustic markers of engagement: mean Alpha Ratio (AlphaRatio), mean Harmonics-to-Noise Ratio (HNR), and mean Spectral Slope 500-1500 (SlopeV500-1500). This reflects cleaner and smoother vocalizations during engagement across both groups. Furthermore, we evaluated a State ×\times Group interaction model to compare the magnitudes of standardized state-dependent differences between children and caregivers. The results indicated that children exhibit significantly greater state-related variation than caregivers in three acoustic features: AlphaRatio, HNR, and SlopeV500-1500.
introduction:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition that influences how individuals communicate, behave, learn, and relate to others, affecting approximately 1 in 32 children in the United States [12]. Previous research suggests that common human-computer interaction (HCI) technologies, such as screen-based applications, robots, and virtual reality, have a positive effect on the social and emotional development of children with ASD[15]. For HCI interventions to be effective, participants must remain actively engaged. Therefore, characterizing engagement provides valuable insights in developing transparent and interpretable HCI interventions.
Vocal cues provide a non-invasive method for monitoring engagement in children with ASD. For example, Keerthana et al. [10] developed a speech-only engagement monitoring pipeline to guide personalized learning interventions, while Gupta et al. [7] demonstrated that vocal characteristics reflect engagement levels in children with ASD. Furthermore, in real-world and home-based environments, child engagement rarely occurs in isolation because caregivers actively participate as facilitators. Recognizing this dyadic interaction, prior work has incorporated caregiver audio alongside child vocalizations to model child engagement [9, 13, 3].
Despite the success of prior work in predicting child engagement using machine learning classifiers, existing approaches predominantly treat audio-based engagement detection as a classification task. As a result, limited work has examined which specific acoustic features systematically vary with a child’s engagement state or how these state-dependent acoustic differences compare between children with ASD and their caregivers. Understanding these acoustic differences provides insight into the vocal correlates of child engagement and supports the development of interpretable HCI interventions for children with ASD.
To address this gap, we conducted a systematic statistical evaluation of diarized speech segments from children with ASD and their caregivers during an in-home intervention with a Socially Assistive Robot (SAR). Using linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) with individual-level random intercepts, we first identified acoustic features associated with a child’s engagement state separately for child and caregiver speech. We then constructed a State ×\times Group interaction LMM to test whether the magnitude of state-dependent acoustic differences varied between child and caregiver speech. Together, these analyses characterized how the acoustic features of both children and caregivers varied with respect to a child’s engagement state.

title: TacHOI: Contact-Aware Object Reconstruction and Tracking for Egocentric Videos
authors: Jackson Codd,Haoyu Li,Xianyi Cheng
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Egocentric videos offer a scalable source of human demonstrations for robot learning. However, recovering metric object geometry and motion from monocular video is hindered by scale–depth ambiguity and hand-induced occlusion, while image-derived contact and shape priors alone cannot uniquely determine metric scale. We introduce TacHOI, a training-free framework that integrates tactile contact with monocular vision for joint hand–object reconstruction and tracking, without requiring object templates or depth sensors. Starting from pretrained visual estimates, TacHOI uses tactile contact to constrain object depth relative to the estimated hand, while spatially separated contacts on a metrically calibrated hand provide a physical ruler for object extent. It incorporates these constraints into a joint optimization of hand poses, object trajectories, and anisotropic object scale alongside visual alignment. Across 100 ARCTIC and HO3D sequences with synthesized tactile observations, TacHOI achieves the lowest median ADD-S* among the evaluated baselines, reducing error from 15.6 to 3.6 cm on ARCTIC and achieving 2.8 cm on HO3D. Additional experiments on OpenTouch demonstrate its applicability to measured tactile observations.
introduction:
Humans effortlessly manipulate objects in daily life, from pouring a drink to assembling a tool. The growing adoption of smart glasses [1] offers new opportunities to capture these everyday interactions at scale, turning daily activities into a rich source of demonstrations for robots to learn manipulation skills [2]. However, a key challenge of learning manipulation skills from egocentric videos is the ambiguity in estimating precise hand-object trajectories, especially for monocular observation. Hand-induced occlusion and self-occlusion further complicate accurate reconstruction and tracking [13].

A fundamental challenge in monocular reconstruction is scale ambiguity: an object scaled by a factor of kk and placed kk times farther from the camera produces the same image projection. Even accurate masks and 2D tracks therefore cannot uniquely determine its metric scale and depth. When demonstrations are retargeted to a robot, scale errors can lead to misplaced grasps and incorrect motion trajectories. Existing methods rely on additional information, including known instance-level 3D meshes [4], depth measurements [21], multiple camera views [6], object scans [7], or learned shape and grasp priors [8]. These requirements constrain their applicability to in-the-wild human demonstrations. Meanwhile, growing efforts to capture such demonstrations with tactile gloves [9, 10, 11] offer a complementary source of geometric constraints. Unlike contact inferred from vision, measured tactile contact provides direct physical evidence of hand–object contact, which can constrain reconstruction when paired with calibrated hand geometry.

To address these challenges, we introduce TacHOI, a training-free hand-object reconstruction framework that leverages tactile contact as an additional geometric constraint for hand-object reconstruction and tracking. Unlike contact inferred from vision, measured tactile contact provides physical evidence that is independent of the object’s image projection. TacHOI uses this evidence in two ways. First, tactile contact pulls the reconstructed hand and object together. Second, TacHOI uses the calibrated hand as a physical ruler. Spatially separated contacts provide a caliper-like measurement of the object extent between the contacting parts of the hand. This gives the optimizer a metric constraint on object scale without requiring a known object template or depth sensor. Based on the constraints, the framework jointly optimizes the object’s per-frame pose, anisotropic scale, and the hand pose. In summary, our main contributions are:

We present a framework that requires no task-specific training for jointly refining object reconstruction, metric scale, 6-DoF pose, and hand pose from monocular egocentric video and tactile contact.

We show that spatially separated tactile contacts on a calibrated hand act as a metric constraint, resolving the monocular scale-depth ambiguity without object templates or depth sensing.

We evaluate TacHOI on 100 ARCTIC and HO3D clips under a controlled tactile-synthesis protocol, showing consistent improvements in object scale and camera-space localization over vision-based initialization.

1. We present a framework that requires no task-specific training for jointly refining object reconstruction, metric scale, 6-DoF pose, and hand pose from monocular egocentric video and tactile contact.

2. We show that spatially separated tactile contacts on a calibrated hand act as a metric constraint, resolving the monocular scale-depth ambiguity without object templates or depth sensing.

3. We evaluate TacHOI on 100 ARCTIC and HO3D clips under a controlled tactile-synthesis protocol, showing consistent improvements in object scale and camera-space localization over vision-based initialization.

title: Search-Informed MPPI for Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Monte Carlo Tree Expansion
authors: Ihab S. Mohamed,Lantao Liu
comment: . Project page with videos:this https URL
abstract: Autonomous mobile robots in warehouses, factories, hospitals, and greenhouses must plan long routes through cluttered layouts while respecting how they can physically move. Widely used planners involve practical trade-offs: sampling-based planners such as the asymptotically optimal Rapidly-exploring Random Tree (RRT∗) and its variants may spend considerable computation exploring regions irrelevant to the task, grid-based planners depend on map resolution, and lattice-based planners often rely on predefined motion primitives. This paper presents SI-MPPI, a planner that uses tree search to decide which routes are worth exploring and MPPI to optimize many short, dynamically feasible motion candidates in parallel on a laptop-grade GPU, retaining low-cost candidates that satisfy collision-safety and progress checks. The planner operates directly on standard 2D occupancy-grid maps, using the robot’s motion model for trajectory generation and its footprint for collision checking. In simulations on four 100 m×100 m$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$\times$100\text{\,}\mathrm{m}$ cluttered maps, SI-MPPI consistently produced the smoothest steering commands under a common parameter configuration, potentially reducing actuator wear and payload disturbance. Averaged across these maps, it built search trees roughly 77–15×15\times smaller than those of the evaluated baselines and planned about 1010–27×27\times faster than the RRT∗-based planners, while maintaining comparable or shorter path lengths. Practitioners should note that the proposed framework currently targets static, known maps, does not guarantee the shortest route, and produces planned trajectories with relatively low speeds; for higher-speed execution, however, a separate receding-horizon MPPI controller can track the resulting waypoints, as illustrated in the supplementary video. Future work will extend the approach to robots with more complex dynamics and to speed-aware planning.
introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) are increasingly transitioning from controlled laboratory settings to large-scale, highly structured, and cluttered environments, such as manufacturing floors, warehouses, complex hospital layouts, smart farms, and greenhouses [1, 2, 3, 4], where they must navigate efficiently while avoiding obstacles and respecting their dynamic constraints. At the heart of this autonomy lies motion planning: the problem of computing a trajectory or path from one position to another while balancing reliability, computational efficiency, and trajectory quality [5, 6].
In these real-world scenarios, generating safe, dynamically feasible trajectories in real time is essential for reliable operation. Meeting this requirement through kinodynamic motion planning—wherein the robot must satisfy non-convex collision constraints alongside nonlinear dynamics—remains particularly challenging in complex, cluttered environments, as existing planners often struggle to efficiently couple high-level discrete decisions, such as selecting a narrow passage, with low-level continuous control under actuation limits [7, 8].

Conventional sampling-based algorithms, most notably Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRTs), have demonstrated remarkable success in geometric path planning by offering probabilistic completeness guarantees [9].
However, extending these methods to kinodynamic settings introduces substantial computational bottlenecks: generating dynamically feasible local connections typically requires either sequentially propagating control inputs through numerical integration [10, 11, 12], solving a challenging two-point boundary value problem (BVP) to connect exact states [13], linearizing the system dynamics around local operating points [14, 15], approximating steering or local path generation using learning-based methods [16, 17], or utilizing flat-output representations to derive algebraic trajectory rollouts [18, 19].
Yet, despite these alternatives, the underlying randomized sampling strategies can still expend substantial computation on regions irrelevant to the global task. This untargeted exploration can slow convergence in cluttered environments containing narrow passages [20, 21].
Consequently, although recent advances in learned, guided, biased, and bidirectional sampling improve exploration efficiency [22, 23, 24, 25], the computational cost of randomized global exploration and repeated kinodynamic edge generation can still hinder real-time performance in large-scale, obstacle-dense scenarios [26, 27, 28].

Search-based approaches offer an alternative by structuring motion planning as a search over long-horizon decision sequences and can be broadly divided into graph-search methods [29] and stochastic tree-search methods such as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) [30].
Within the graph-search branch, classical planners such as Dijkstra [31] and A∗ [32], their anytime and incremental/replanning variants [33, 34, 35, 36], and kinodynamic planners based on state lattices or motion primitives [37, 38, 39] reason over discrete state–action representations and can provide guarantees with respect to the chosen graph, lattice, or primitive set.
Their performance, however, depends strongly on graph resolution, lattice discretization, and primitive-set design; as the state dimension or planning horizon grows, the number of discrete states and admissible actions can increase rapidly, substantially increasing the computational burden of graph-based planning [8].
To mitigate this burden, recent methods have explored two complementary strategies: compact geometric representations of collision-free space [40, 41, 6] and hybrid search–optimization planners that combine discrete search with continuous trajectory refinement [42, 43, 44].
Yet such methods often rely on environment-specific structure, precomputed geometric or convex decompositions, simplified dynamics, analytical steering, or repeated trajectory optimization and repair, thereby limiting their direct applicability to large-scale, cluttered occupancy-grid environments, where planners must generate continuous, dynamically feasible motion segments under nonlinear dynamics.

Within the stochastic tree-search branch, MCTS offers a complementary mechanism for long-horizon planning by using tree-search statistics to adaptively allocate computation among promising decisions [45, 30].
Despite its success in large discrete decision-making domains such as Go and general game playing, its direct extension to continuous kinodynamic planning remains challenging: continuous control spaces induce large effective branching factors and rapid tree growth [46, 47]; stochastic rollouts introduce variance into finite-sample value estimates [48]; and unguided tree expansion can be inefficient for long-horizon planning and collision-aware robotic navigation [49, 50, 51].
Recent robotics work has addressed aspects of these challenges through specialized tree representations [52], task-specific formulations for constrained and multi-objective planning [53, 54], optimization-coupled MCTS for manipulation and locomotion [55, 56, 57], and continuous-space search mechanisms [46, 47].
In a separate line of work, Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has emerged as an effective sampling-based trajectory optimizer for nonlinear systems, leveraging massively parallel rollouts to optimize control sequences in real time [58, 59].
MPPI naturally accommodates nonlinear dynamics, state-dependent costs, and control limits, making it attractive for real-time local trajectory optimization in agile robot navigation.
Yet MPPI remains a local finite-horizon optimizer; without an informative nominal control sequence or reference trajectory, it can become trapped in obstacle-induced local minima or fail to make consistent global progress in cluttered, non-convex environments [60, 61].

Motivated by these complementary capabilities and limitations, we propose Search-Informed MPPI (SI-MPPI), a kinodynamic motion planning framework that tightly integrates MCTS-based tree search with GPU-batched MPPI optimization—an integration that, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, has not previously been reported for collision-aware kinodynamic navigation in cluttered environments. The key insight is to replace the conventional expansion and default-policy simulation stages of MCTS with a unified MPPI expansion stage guided by structured intermediate targets, termed baits (see Fig. 1). Within SI-MPPI, MCTS and MPPI serve complementary functions: MCTS adaptively allocates computation among competing long-horizon alternatives, whereas MPPI generates cost-informed local motion segments under the robot’s nonlinear dynamics.
The primary contributions of this work are as follows:

Unified search–optimization framework:
Rather than relying on exact BVP steering, predefined motion primitives, or purely random control propagation, our proposed framework constructs an asymmetric search tree from admitted MPPI-optimized motion segments, thereby coupling long-horizon global search with local nonlinear trajectory optimization.

Bait-guided MPPI expansion:
We develop a GPU-batched expansion mechanism that optimizes finite-horizon control sequences toward multiple retained baits in parallel and incorporates adaptive bait handling, feasibility gating, and top-kk selection, enabling computationally efficient, sparse, and directed tree growth in continuous state–action spaces.

ESS-guided adaptation and backpropagation:
We leverage the effective sample size (ESS) to adapt the MPPI nominal control mean, providing informed warm starts for subsequent expansions, while cost-based backpropagation updates the tree statistics to guide global search.

Comparative and ablation studies:
We evaluate our proposed framework through comparative simulations against three representative sampling- and search-based kinodynamic planners, complemented by an ablation study, with performance assessed in terms of mission success, search complexity, and trajectory quality in complex, large-scale, cluttered environments.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work, followed by the formal kinodynamic motion-planning problem formulation in Section III and an overview of MPPI and MCTS in Section IV. Building on these foundations, Section V presents the proposed SI-MPPI framework, detailing Upper Confidence Bound (UCB)-guided tree selection, bait-guided GPU-batched MPPI expansion, candidate admission, and ESS-guided adaptation with cost-based backpropagation. Section VI then presents the comparative offline planning evaluation, ablation study, and discussion, followed by the conclusions and future research directions in Section VII.
