title: MomentMem: Memorizing Key Moments for Robot Manipulation
authors: Guangyu Zhao,Yongchang Zhang,Ruizhang Jiang,Zhihong Yu,Yuhao Zhang,Tao Wu,Qimin Zhou,Kunsong Shi,Haoran Wen,Zeyu Zhang,Yin Li,Kun Zhan,Yiwu Zhong
abstract:
Robotic manipulation often requires remembering visual information that is no longer observable, such as the original location of an object.
Existing approaches typically rely on full observation histories, which become redundant over long horizons, or text summaries, which may omit precise visual details.
We study visual moment memory, the ability to retain such details from key moments for subsequent manipulation.
To support this study, we introduce VMBench, a suite of long-horizon manipulation tasks requiring memory of spatial locations, visual appearances, and their associations.
We further propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture in which a VLM-based memorizer selects keyframes and an executor predicts actions conditioned on the selected memories.
This separation enables us to evaluate memory selection alongside closed-loop task success and to study memorizer generalization independently of the executor.
On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points.
Moreover, we find that the memorizer transfers well to unseen appearances zero-shot. It can also adapt to an unseen task with only a few memory annotations, reaching 43.7% success, close to the 44.3% obtained with full memory supervision.
Further experiments show competitive performance on RMBench and improvements in real-robot manipulation. These results highlight the value of retaining sparse visual evidence for memory-dependent manipulation.
Our code is available at https://github.com/PKU-VaLuE-Lab/MomentMem.
introduction:
Recently, memory has increasingly become a key capability of multi-modal models [30, 18, 41, 37] and embodied models [28, 19, 31, 29]. Despite advances in embodied models [21, 4, 12], memory for robot manipulation remains challenging. As shown in Figure (a), existing approaches often focus on full observation histories [35] or text descriptions [5, 34].
Full observation histories are complete yet redundant, thus falling short when facing long-horizon tasks [38, 37].
Text captures abstract events, yet can omit visual details, or cannot fully describe certain information (e.g., “move the cube back to where it was”).
To this end, we study visual moment memory for robotic manipulation. It requires models to remember precise visual information at a key moment, such as texture patterns, spatial relations, and spatial locations. This type of memory is difficult to preserve in text.

As a first step, we propose VMBench, a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks that require visual moment memory.
Its key design principle is to make successful manipulation depend on remembering precise visual information.
Different from existing benchmarks [7, 10, 5, 22], our benchmark emphasizes tasks that cannot be well addressed by concise text memory.
Specifically, these tasks require remembering exact positions and visual patterns, rather than only object identities or task progress.
Concise text summaries may omit these details, as illustrated in Figure (b).
We organize the tasks around spatial locations, visual appearances, and appearance-location bindings.
For example, returning a cube to its original position requires remembering exactly where it was, rather than just knowing that it was moved.
Across these tasks, the key visual moment is only visible across a short period of time and the model has to capture such moments for successful task completion.
Together, these tasks provide a testbed for studying how robots memorize precise visual information for manipulation tasks.

Going further, we consider the modeling of visual moment memory for robot manipulation.
Task success alone does not reveal whether a failure comes from memory or execution [32].
Beyond overall task performance, we seek to examine two key capabilities: memory selection and action prediction.
To this end, we propose MomentMem, a hierarchical architecture that separates memory from action prediction.
This separation allows us to examine memory selection and action execution independently.
As shown in Figure (c) (top), a VLM memorizer selects keyframes, and then the executor predicts actions.
We observe that the key event often spans across several frames that show the same visual cue.
We annotate this span as a temporal segment.
We aim for the memorizer to select a keyframe in the segment as early as possible.
Also, if it misses an earlier frame, it should still try to capture the later frame in the same segment.
During inference, the executor predicts actions from the selected keyframes together with the current observation.
Details are provided in Section 4.

With our benchmark tasks and hierarchical model, we design metrics and protocols to evaluate end-to-end success rate and the generalization of memory capability, as shown in Figure (c).
As in most existing benchmarks, we test the models on our benchmark tasks and measure the success rate over closed-loop rollouts.
We evaluate how well the memorizer captures the relevant evidence.
We also test its transfer to unseen appearances and adaptation to new tasks.
As shown in Figure (c) (bottom), we vary the visual appearance and directly test the overall model, with the memorizer trained only on the original visual appearances.
Besides, we test the overall model for unseen tasks, allowing the memorizer to adapt to new tasks with a few memory annotations.
In both protocols, we train the executor on target-domain action demonstrations using memories predicted by the memorizer.
In other words, our protocols measure the generalization of the memorizer rather than the executor.

On VMBench, MomentMem achieves 49.9% average success, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 31.7 percentage points.
In addition, the memorizer transfers zero-shot to unseen appearances.
With only a few memory annotations, it adapts to an unseen task.
The resulting policy reaches 43.7% success, close to 44.3% with full memory supervision.
Beyond VMBench, MomentMem remains competitive on RMBench and improves task success in real-robot manipulation.
These results demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of MomentMem.

Our contributions are as follows:

We identify visual moment memory as a key research problem for robotic manipulation, focusing on remembering transient, precise visual information.

We introduce VMBench to evaluate and study this problem in closed-loop manipulation tasks. We also propose MomentMem, a hierarchical model that supports separate diagnosis of memory and action prediction.

Extensive experiments show that MomentMem exceeds the strongest baseline on our VMBench by 31.7 percentage points. Our analysis demonstrates that the memorizer can transfer to unseen appearance and task. Further, MomentMem performs well on RMBench and real-robot tasks.

1. We identify visual moment memory as a key research problem for robotic manipulation, focusing on remembering transient, precise visual information.

2. We introduce VMBench to evaluate and study this problem in closed-loop manipulation tasks. We also propose MomentMem, a hierarchical model that supports separate diagnosis of memory and action prediction.

3. Extensive experiments show that MomentMem exceeds the strongest baseline on our VMBench by 31.7 percentage points. Our analysis demonstrates that the memorizer can transfer to unseen appearance and task. Further, MomentMem performs well on RMBench and real-robot tasks.

title: FORTH: Grounding Tactile VLA Execution via Forward-Only Proxy-Control Pairing
authors: Junde Li,Wei-Han Yu,Xiangyi Chu,Yaoxin Li,Jiawei Xu,Ka-Fai Un,Pui-In Mak
comment: The code and models are open-sourced atthis https URL
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are widely credited with force control, operating on the unverified assumption that proxy loss minimization implies physical force grounding. In this work, we demonstrate that this assumption breaks down at three core deployment levels: frozen visual backbones discard contact geometry, downstream losses mask token-level gradient alignment, and discrete indicators trigger optimization collapse. To address these disconnections, we present forth, a forward-only measurement harness and execution framework that explicitly pairs the optimization objective at each level with its physical control observable. forth incorporates three grounded pillars: a layer-local, forward-only tactile encoder that preserves spatial contact geometry without backpropagation, a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter enabling activation-space updates, and SlipGuard, a continuous tactile verification gate that fires on incipient slip. On an elasto-plastic structural shell, the SlipGuard controller peaks at 29×29\times lower grip force than the reflex ramp of the same shell, preventing structural crush where the baseline leaves permanent deformation. Furthermore, forth matches state-of-the-art execution performance with a 97.6%97.6\% average success rate across three evaluated LIBERO suites, while reducing peak activation memory by 7.12×7.12\times compared to a backpropagated step on the same backbone. Enhanced perception enables deeper physical intelligence. The code and models are open-sourced at https://github.com/Jordanlllll/FORTH.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are rapidly advancing from tabletop picking to contact-rich manipulation. To
operate effectively under contact, state-of-the-art systems increasingly augment pretrained visual backbones with
tactile or force sensing modalities
[40, 41, 16, 87]. Concurrently, tactile
sensing hardware and representations have matured: optical tactile sensors, high-fidelity contact simulators, and
learned representations provide policies with spatially resolved contact maps rather than scalar load readings
[37, 71, 77, 20, 80]. While an emerging family of
tactile VLAs reports force-aware execution across tasks like insertion, wiping, and grasping
[11, 2, 8, 49, 90, 10, 84, 86, 52, 51, 35, 88],
performance across these systems is predominantly evaluated using a single proxy metric per task level. Such scalar
metrics obscure the underlying physical reality: the critical quantities governing whether an object survives an
episode are rarely measured or reported together. This discrepancy stems from a missing evaluation and reporting convention.

Existing research programs address isolated compute and memory bottlenecks without closing this measurement gap.
Layer-local learning objectives replace global backpropagation with forward-only computations
[23, 38, 44, 65, 29, 55, 63, 36, 17, 61, 1],
yet report performance strictly via local loss values. Zeroth-order (ZO) and gradient-free optimizers trade
memory-intensive backward passes for forward queries
[48, 46, 66, 32, 9, 19, 85, 67, 81],
evaluating only estimated gradient directional alignment. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and quantization
constrain these updates within frozen backbones [26, 13, 25], while
low-level controllers treat physical slip as a binary classification target scored by detection accuracy. Crucially,
an improvement in these algorithmic proxies can decouple from physical interaction quality—a lower local loss does
not inherently prevent object damage—and no current benchmark protocol
[42, 50, 30, 47, 91, 45, 57, 12, 58, 34, 79, 22, 74]
systematically measures and reports these paired dynamics.

To resolve this decoupling, we introduce forth, a unified harness governed by a paired metric convention across all
three execution levels: report the optimized algorithmic quantity alongside the physical quantity it aims to control,
accepting a policy level only when both metrics move in lockstep. Operating entirely forward-only and layer-locally on
frozen 4-bit backbones without global backward passes, forth integrates three key components: (1) a tactile feature trunk
composed of two Forward-Forward (FF) blocks; (2) a token-parallel zeroth-order adapter of
rank 8 attached to the action head; and (3) SlipGuard, a one-class shear-ratio gate with a bounded real-time
corrector. Rather than introducing a massive new backbone, forth makes tactile policy execution measurable and
correctable directly on edge deployment hardware, requiring only 16 forward passes per update (T=8T{=}8 tokens) instead of full
backpropagation.

This design yields a deployment-ready harness that acts dynamically before manipulation failure occurs. Empirically,
the forward-only tactile trunk matches backpropagated representation accuracy; the zeroth-order updater fine-tunes the
rank-8 adapter at a fraction of backward memory requirements; and SlipGuard converts incipient
slip into a recoverable interaction across three slip severity regimes, where standard hand-tuned force ramps result
in permanent object crush. Figure 1 illustrates our testbed for recording physical contact dynamics
across three material bodies driven past their friction limits.

title: Latent Space Planning with Sequential Monte Carlo
authors: Hrishikesh Viswanath,Anindita Ghosh,Uttaran Bhattacharya,Aniket Bera
abstract: Planning with learned world models amounts to finding action sequences whose predicted rollouts reach a goal. Sampling-based planners often struggle at longer horizons, while gradient-based methods can become trapped in local minima. Meanwhile, model predictive path integral control (MPPI), a complementary approach, alternates between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from samples and updating the plan from this estimate. Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian proposal and reach the target distribution only through importance weights. Moreover, a target distribution favoring goal-reaching trajectories can be difficult to define directly, motivating a sequence of intermediate distributions. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a natural mechanism for evolving such a sequence through importance weighting and resampling. Motivated by this, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by SMC, which moves a population of action sequences while a gradient-based optimizer updates the plan. Inspired by classical planning, we further introduce a PDE-derived cost-to-go that guides the evolution of the sample distribution using the structure of the latent state space. On navigation and manipulation tasks with visual and proprioceptive world models, our formulation outperforms gradient-based planners by 2929 and 5050, sampling-based planners by 3535 and MPPI by 77 percentage points in average success rate, while succeeding in fewer iterations than gradient-based planners and within 4% of MPPI.
introduction:
World models learn compact representations of environments from observations and predict how they evolve under actions, enabling inexpensive simulation for planning (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026; Terver et al., 2025). Planning with these models requires finding goal-reaching action sequences, typically by minimizing a cost that compares the predicted representations with the representation of a goal observation. Sampling-based planners, such as the cross-entropy method (CEM) (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026), draw action sequences from a Gaussian and refit it to the lowest-cost samples. While they require only cost evaluations, their performance degrades with longer planning horizons and higher action dimensionality (Psenka et al., 2026). Gradient-based planners, on the other hand, differentiate the cost through the world model and perform well on tasks where the goal is greedily reachable (Terver et al., 2025). However, they can become trapped in local minima (Terver et al., 2025). Additional strategies have been proposed to overcome this, including optimizing the intermediate states alongside the actions with Langevin-style perturbations of these states, as in GRASP (Psenka et al., 2026).

MPPI (Williams et al., 2016; Williams et al., 2017) takes a complementary approach, alternating between estimating an expectation under a cost-weighted distribution from these samples and updating the plan from this estimate. MPPI may thus be viewed as a form of expectation-maximization (EM), whose expectation step estimates the mean of the target from samples and whose maximization step moves the plan to this mean Cuin et al. (2025); Cuin et al. (2026). Its samples, however, are drawn afresh at every iteration from a Gaussian centered on the plan (Williams et al., 2016, Alg. 1) and reach the target only through importance weights. The target distribution that favors goal-reaching action sequences is generally intractable to construct directly. Instead, it can be approached through a sequence of intermediate distributions, beginning with a Gaussian centered at the initial plan and gradually shifting toward lower-cost sequences as the plan is updated. Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) provides a principled means of approximating such a sequence of distributions (Doucet et al., 2001; Del Moral, 2004). SMC samplers (Del Moral et al., 2006), extending annealed importance sampling (Neal, 1998), maintain a population of particles that is propagated between successive distributions using Markov kernels, with importance reweighting and resampling to maintain an approximation to each distribution (Arbel et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2025).

Our key insight is that latent-space planning can be formulated as optimization guided by SMC. The two methods complement each other, each carrying out one step of the EM view of MPPI. As the plan changes by one optimizer step per iteration, the targets of consecutive iterations form a sequence of evolving distributions. SMC carries a population of action sequences from one target to the next through sequential reweighting and resampling. The optimizer then updates the plan using this weighted population, thereby re-centering the target for the next iteration. This combines the population-based updates of MPPI with the gradient-based updates of conventional planners.

The tilting of action sequences toward the goal is determined by a cost function that assigns lower costs to more desirable sequences. A natural choice is the Euclidean distance between the final predicted latent and the goal latent, which is commonly used as an optimization objective in latent world-model planners (Zhou et al., 2025; Maes et al., 2026). Classical planning, however, often uses a cost-to-go, which quantifies the cost of reaching the goal from each state and can be obtained by solving a partial differential equation (PDE) over the feasible state space (Kimmel and Sethian, 2001; Mirebeau and Portegies, 2019). Inspired by this, we introduce a PDE-based cost-to-go over the latent space to capture connectivity between states. Since latent world models do not provide explicit access to physical states, we construct a roadmap over latent states using transitions observed between physical states in the offline dataset and solve the PDE over this roadmap.

Our contributions are thus summarized as:

In Section 3.3, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), combining population-based sampling with gradient-based plan updates through the world model.

In Section 3.4, we introduce a PDE-based cost-to-go over the latent space, inspired by classical planning. By accounting for connectivity between latent states through transitions in the offline dataset, this cost provides an alternative to the Euclidean distance commonly used in latent world-model planning.

In Section 4, we evaluate our planner on navigation and manipulation tasks using DINO-WM and LeWM. Across twelve settings, our planner achieves a success rate of 79.8%79.8\%, outperforming GD, GRASP, CEM, and MPPI by 28.828.8, 49.849.8, 34.534.5, and 7.47.4 percentage points, respectively, under a fixed budget of 150150 iterations. In seven of the twelve settings, we find that the PDE-based cost improves success over the L2L_{2} cost and in the remaining five, the difference stays within 88 percentage points.

1. In Section 3.3, we formulate latent-space planning as optimization guided by sequential Monte Carlo (SMC), combining population-based sampling with gradient-based plan updates through the world model.

2. In Section 3.4, we introduce a PDE-based cost-to-go over the latent space, inspired by classical planning. By accounting for connectivity between latent states through transitions in the offline dataset, this cost provides an alternative to the Euclidean distance commonly used in latent world-model planning.

3. In Section 4, we evaluate our planner on navigation and manipulation tasks using DINO-WM and LeWM. Across twelve settings, our planner achieves a success rate of 79.8%79.8\%, outperforming GD, GRASP, CEM, and MPPI by 28.828.8, 49.849.8, 34.534.5, and 7.47.4 percentage points, respectively, under a fixed budget of 150150 iterations. In seven of the twelve settings, we find that the PDE-based cost improves success over the L2L_{2} cost and in the remaining five, the difference stays within 88 percentage points.

title: One Behavior, Out of Order: Deterministic Execution and Parallel Simulation of ROS 2 Applications
authors: Chengzi Huang,Behnam Khodabandeloo,Duc Anh Nguyen,Chuanchao Gao,Wang Yi
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract:
System-level simulation is widely used to validate robotic applications before hardware deployment.
However, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2), a popular middleware for such applications, uses asynchronous publish-subscribe communication, which can make application behavior depend on scheduling and the platform.
The behavior can then vary across runs and machines even with the same inputs.
This nondeterminism makes faults hard to reproduce and tests unreliable.
In this paper, we first give ROS 2 applications a lightweight coordination scheme in which every component, including event-driven ones, reads its inputs and writes its outputs at predefined time instants.
By decoupling computation and communication, the scheme makes an application deterministic, that is, it always has one behavior for given inputs.
Tests are thus repeatable, but for large applications they still take a long time.
To speed up these tests, we then present an out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm.
From the predefined read and write instants, it knows before the run which activations of components depend on which.
It starts each activation as soon as those it depends on have finished.
Finally, we implement the algorithm in a simulator that runs existing ROS 2 applications without any change to them or to ROS 2.
We evaluate the simulator on industrial use cases and synthetic graphs.
On the industrial use cases, it is up to 2.6 times faster than synchronous parallel simulation and needs an order of magnitude less memory for messages than asynchronous parallel simulation.
introduction:
Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) [1] is widely used in research and industry to build robotic systems, from mobile robots to automated vehicles.
System-level simulation plays a pivotal role in their development, since developers can validate a whole application across many scenarios without the costly target hardware.
However, the components of a ROS 2 application execute asynchronously and communicate with each other.
The behavior of the application therefore depends on the execution times of its components, the communication delays and the scheduling.
Their variation makes simulation results differ across runs, even when the application code and inputs remain unchanged [2, 3].
In the example of Fig. 1, Planner computes a command every 20 ms from the latest objects that Detector found in the camera images.
In run 2, a variation in the execution time of Detector leads Planner to compute the command at 40 ms from image 2 instead of image 3.
If the command computed from image 2 causes a fault, the fault may not appear when the test is repeated, which makes it hard to reproduce.
Developers may therefore need to rerun the same test many times to reproduce and diagnose the fault.
This additional debugging effort slows development.

AUTOSAR solves this problem for automotive software with a rule by which every component reads its inputs and writes its outputs at predefined time instants, no matter when the computations run in between [4].
This separates computation from communication [5, 6], and the behavior of an application becomes independent of the scheduling and the platform.
Following the same principle, our first step gives ROS 2 a lightweight coordination scheme that fixes when each component reads and writes, including event-driven components.
Whenever a time-triggered or event-driven component is activated, it reads its inputs at that instant and writes its outputs after a fixed computation delay, even if they are empty.
Every output arrives after a fixed transport delay.
Since time-triggered components run periodically and the delays are fixed, all reads and writes happen at predefined time instants, as in AUTOSAR.
The application therefore becomes deterministic and exhibits one behavior.
Tests become repeatable, and application behavior can be validated independently of the target hardware.

However, system-level simulation still becomes time-consuming as applications and scenarios grow, slowing design iteration [7].
Even with one behavior, a recent simulator for ROS 2 applications runs all activations on a single thread, which its authors note increases the run time of complex simulations [8].
To further reduce the validation time, we therefore aim to exploit parallelism within a single simulation while preserving the application’s deterministic behavior.
Yet general parallel discrete-event simulation cannot assume that event dependencies are known in advance, so it must preserve causality during the run, either synchronously or asynchronously.
Synchronous parallel simulation stops all workers at a global barrier after each time instant or window [9], forcing fast workers to wait for the slowest one.
Asynchronous parallel simulation avoids global barriers, either through optimistic execution, which needs state saving and rollback [10], or through conservative execution with null messages [11].
When fast producers run far ahead of their consumers, it can accumulate large buffers of unconsumed messages.

Out-of-order simulation needs none of these mechanisms if the dependencies between events are known.
Existing out-of-order simulators derive them from a static analysis of the model or track them during the run [12, 13, 14].
Our key observation is that the coordination scheme already makes these dependencies known in advance, without any such analysis or tracking.
The predefined read and write instants determine which outputs each activation reads.
An activation therefore need not wait for all earlier activations.
Its computation depends only on the activations whose outputs it reads and on the previous activation of the same component, whose updated state it needs.
This allows activations of different components to run out of order and in parallel while preserving the one behavior of the application.
Building on this observation, we present an out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm for ROS 2 applications.
It computes the dependencies on demand from the application graph and the timing parameters, without constructing the full dependency graph.
Because a producer may run ahead of its consumers, several outputs may need to be retained at the same time.
To bound output buffering, the algorithm uses cyclic storage and allows a slot to be reused only after all readers of its previous contents have finished.

Together, the coordination scheme and the simulator make simulation-based validation of ROS 2 applications both repeatable and fast, which shortens each design iteration.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows.

A lightweight coordination scheme that makes ROS 2 applications deterministic, so that their behavior does not depend on the scheduling or the platform (Section II).

An efficient out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm that still computes the one deterministic behavior of an application (Section III).
We show how to integrate it into ROS 2 so that it simulates existing applications without changing their source code or the libraries of ROS 2 (Section IV).

We evaluate our simulator on industrial use cases and synthetic graphs.
On 256 cores, it is up to 228×228\times faster than sequential simulation, which is 91 % of the theoretical speedup bound.
Compared with synchronous parallel simulation, it is up to 2.6×2.6\times faster on the industrial use cases and about 2×2\times faster on the synthetic graphs.
Its message buffers stay much smaller than those of asynchronous parallel simulation (Section V).

2. An efficient out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm that still computes the one deterministic behavior of an application (Section III).
We show how to integrate it into ROS 2 so that it simulates existing applications without changing their source code or the libraries of ROS 2 (Section IV).

title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
authors: Chi Yan,Guoyang Zhao,Wentao Yuan,Yixiao Ge,Yanning Zhou,Dan Xu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints.
This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization.
We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations.
To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning.
StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning.
We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments.
To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning.
StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy (δ1\delta_{1}) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench.
Intervention results further indicate that the model’s performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors.
Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.
introduction:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in understanding and reasoning about visual content in the digital world (Alayrac et al., 2022). Building upon these advances, recent efforts have begun to extend such capabilities beyond the digital realm into the physical world, positioning VLMs as a key foundation for embodied AI (Driess et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2026).
However, extending VLMs from the digital to the physical world requires more than semantic understanding: it demands geometrically grounded spatial intelligence for reasoning and acting in 3D environments.

To extend VLMs beyond semantic understanding, recent studies have explored various ways to enhance their spatial reasoning capabilities.
SpatialVLM (Chen et al., 2024) learns qualitative and quantitative spatial concepts from large-scale spatial question-answering data, while SpatialRGPT (Cheng et al., 2024) augments region-level representations with monocular depth cues for object-centric reasoning. 3D-LLM (Hong et al., 2023), in contrast, grounds language models in reconstructed 3D scene representations. Despite these advances, spatial benchmarks such as VSI-Bench reveal persistent limitations in current models’ ability to construct and reason about 3D space from visual observations (Yang et al., 2025).
Moreover, the geometric information available to these models is typically inferred from monocular observations or supplied through estimated depth and reconstructed 3D representations, making it difficult to determine whether their spatial predictions are grounded in geometric evidence directly available from visual observations or primarily reflect learned priors—a concern reinforced by evidence-absent evaluations showing that VLMs can exploit scene- and category-level priors (Zhang et al., 2026).

Calibrated stereo provides explicit geometric constraints for metric 3D perception: cross-view correspondences determine disparity, which can be converted into metric depth using known camera intrinsics and baseline. Yet, providing binocular observations alone does not guarantee that a VLM will acquire geometric representations that generalize beyond the training distribution. Existing stereo methods primarily focus on geometric estimation, while VLMs typically treat paired images as generic visual inputs without explicitly learning the geometric relations between them. This raises a central question: How can a VLM learn transferable representations from binocular geometry that support metric 3D perception and high-level spatial reasoning?
To investigate this question, we introduce StereoVLM, a geometry-aware binocular VLM designed to learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated stereo observations.

To connect binocular geometry with spatial understanding, we organize the training supervision into a hierarchy of tasks spanning pixel-level correspondence, disparity estimation, calibration-conditioned metric depth, and object-level spatial reasoning. This hierarchy progressively connects cross-view matching to image-space geometric measurement and then to metric-scale estimation, before extending the learned geometry to language-referred objects and task-relevant 3D grounding.
Importantly, we find that disparity provides a substantially more generalizable supervision signal than direct binocular depth on unseen environments, motivating its role as an intermediate geometric representation between cross-view correspondence and metric depth. We further establish Stereo3D-Bench to evaluate this progression across point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning. Beyond conventional task accuracy, controlled right-view interventions and geometric out-of-distribution evaluation test whether model predictions genuinely depend on valid cross-view geometry. Compared with matched training without stereo instructions, hierarchical geometric supervision raises the five-benchmark spatial-reasoning average by 3.54 points and RoboCasa (Nasiriany et al., 2024) manipulation success by 4.3 percentage points.

Our contributions are:

We introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning, with hierarchical supervision that connects cross-view correspondence and disparity to calibration-conditioned metric depth and language-grounded spatial reasoning, yielding transferable 3D spatial representations.

We establish Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark spanning point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning, together with a verifiable evaluation protocol that uses controlled input interventions and geometric out-of-distribution evaluation to test whether predictions genuinely rely on binocular geometry.

We demonstrate that disparity provides a more generalizable geometric supervision signal than direct binocular depth on unseen environments, while hierarchical geometric supervision benefits broader spatial reasoning and downstream embodied control.

1. We introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning, with hierarchical supervision that connects cross-view correspondence and disparity to calibration-conditioned metric depth and language-grounded spatial reasoning, yielding transferable 3D spatial representations.

2. We establish Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark spanning point-level geometry, object-level geometry, and object-level spatial reasoning, together with a verifiable evaluation protocol that uses controlled input interventions and geometric out-of-distribution evaluation to test whether predictions genuinely rely on binocular geometry.

3. We demonstrate that disparity provides a more generalizable geometric supervision signal than direct binocular depth on unseen environments, while hierarchical geometric supervision benefits broader spatial reasoning and downstream embodied control.

title: Planar Formation Control with Minimal Sensing and No Common Orientation: An Almost-Global Result
authors: Jingyi Zhao,Hector Garcia de Marina
abstract: Formation control based on geometric constraints often requires either rigid interaction graphs or a common orientation reference. This paper shows that a prescribed planar formation can be achieved, up to translation and rotation, using the relative displacements measured over the N−1N-1 edges of any tree interaction graph, together with one scalar per edge direction exchanged between neighbors. Since a tree is the sparsest connected graph, any connected set of available sensing links suffices. Each internal agent of the tree parameterizes the positions of its tree neighbors on circles of the prescribed radii by means of virtual phases, and the relative phases within each neighborhood encode the internal geometry of the formation without fixing its orientation. The resulting distributed controller is a gradient flow. We characterize its complete equilibrium set: besides the desired formation, the only equilibria correspond to the collapse of a subset of internal tree edges, and every such equilibrium has exactly as many unstable directions as collapsed edges. Consequently, the desired formation is locally exponentially stable and almost globally attractive, and it is globally attractive when the tree is a star. The controller is implemented in mutually misaligned local frames, which only need to share the same handedness, i.e., the same sense of rotation.
introduction:
Formation control focuses on coordinating multiple agents to achieve and maintain a prescribed geometric configuration [1]. Depending on the geometric constraints used to specify the target formation, existing approaches are broadly categorized into distance- [2, 3], displacement- [4, 5], bearing- [6, 7], and angle-based methods [8, 9]. These geometric representations differ in requirements for inter-agent information and interaction topology, as well as in the degrees of freedom retained by the prescribed formation.

The interaction topology is particularly relevant when only limited relative measurements are available. For example, distance-based formation control typically requires a rigid interaction graph to locally determine the target formation up to rigid-body transformations, with a minimally rigid graph containing 2​N−32N-3 edges in 2-D. However, relative measurements obtained through onboard sensors, such as cameras and LiDAR, may be restricted by Line-of-Sight (LoS) obstructions, preventing the available sensing links from satisfying such rigidity requirements, as illustrated in Fig. 1. This motivates the investigation of formation control under sparse sensing conditions, where the available interactions may be insufficient to support conventional rigidity-based specifications.

Alternative geometric formation specifications offer different trade-offs under sparse sensing conditions, as summarized in Table I. Displacement-based approaches can achieve formation control over a spanning-tree interaction graph with only N−1N-1 edges, but they require a common orientation reference to specify the desired relative displacement vectors, either available a priori or estimated through additional orientation-alignment dynamics [10]. Bearing-based approaches preserve the formation scale as a free variable, but generally require bearing rigidity and a common orientation reference to determine the remaining geometric properties. In contrast, angle-based approaches do not require a common orientation reference and preserve global rotational freedom, but angle constraints alone cannot determine the formation scale. Existing distance–angle formulations further demonstrate that combining these constraints can determine both the shape and scale of a formation without requiring a rigid distance graph [11]. However, gradient feedback of subtended angles typically requires each agent to sense every vertex of the triangles in which it participates, involves configuration-dependent Jacobians that are undefined when the corresponding relative positions vanish, and its convergence guarantees are mostly local or limited to small formations [11, 12]. Table I also includes these distance–angle methods. Compared with them, the proposed method needs only N−1N-1 sensing links, at the price of exchanging scalars between neighbors, and its convergence is almost global for any NN without gain conditions, whereas the almost-global result of [11] is limited to three agents and [12] relies on state-dependent switching with shape-dependent gain conditions. These considerations motivate the exploration of an alternative formation-control architecture that exploits sparse relative measurements while preserving the desired formation scale and global rotational freedom.

Motivated by these considerations, we develop a formation-control framework inspired by parameterized Guiding Vector Fields (GVFs). In parameterized GVFs, a convergence component drives the physical state toward a prescribed manifold, while a virtual phase variable parameterizes its position along the manifold [14]. This mechanism has been primarily exploited in path-following and path-coordination problems [15, 14]. In this work, we extend the parameterization principle to formation control. Every internal agent of a tree interaction graph associates with each of its tree neighbors a circular manifold centered at itself. The convergence component regulates the radial deviation to establish the prescribed inter-agent distance, while the virtual phase describes the tangential degree of freedom along the circle. Coordinating the relative values of the phases hosted by the same agent establishes the internal formation geometry without imposing physical angle-gradient feedback or prescribing the global orientation.

The distributed implementation of the proposed framework introduces an additional challenge when agents operate in mutually misaligned local sensing frames. In particular, vector quantities expressed in one agent’s local frame cannot be directly used by another agent without knowledge of their relative orientation. Existing approaches typically address this issue by estimating inter-frame orientations [10] or by constructing orientation-independent feedback quantities [16]. Following the latter principle, we develop a local-frame implementation in which every agent integrates the phases it hosts using only its own measurements, and one scalar per hosted phase is sent to the corresponding neighbor, which reconstructs its control input from its own locally measured relative displacement.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A GVF-inspired formation-control framework is developed based on parameterized circular manifolds and virtual-phase coordination over an arbitrary tree interaction graph. The prescribed formation is achieved using exactly N−1N-1 sensing links, preserving the desired formation scale and global rotational freedom. Since a tree is the sparsest connected graph, any connected set of available links suffices.

The complete closed-loop equilibrium set is characterized. Undesired equilibria exist only in association with internal edges of the tree; they correspond to the collapse of a subset of such edges, and the Hessian of the associated potential has exactly as many negative eigenvalues as collapsed edges. Consequently, the desired formation is locally exponentially stable and almost globally attractive, and globally attractive when the tree is a star. An explicit energy level that excludes all undesired equilibria is also given.

The controller is implemented under mutually misaligned local frames using locally expressed relative measurements and a single scalar per edge direction. The frames only need to share the same handedness, which is necessary for any method that, like ours, resolves the mirror-image ambiguity.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II gives the preliminaries, and Section III formulates the problem. Section IV develops the geometric representation and the graph condition, while Section V presents the controller, the convergence analysis, and the local-frame implementation. Section VI gives simulations, followed by conclusions in Section VII.

The prescribed formation is achieved using exactly N−1N-1 sensing links, preserving the desired formation scale and global rotational freedom. Since a tree is the sparsest connected graph, any connected set of available links suffices.

title: Self-Supervised Continuous-Time Depth Learning and Ego-Motion Estimation from Asynchronous Events
authors: Sadiq O. Macaulay,Dipon Kumar Ghosh,Hadfield Simon
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Event cameras register brightness changes pixel by pixel with microsecond precision, whereas the dense depth that could supervise them is costly to acquire and exists only at isolated instants. Condensing the stream into frames eases learning, but at the expense of the very timing that sets event sensing apart. We propose a self-supervised approach in which each event is assigned its own depth in continuous time, and the camera motion is recovered from the same observations. Supervision arises from geometry: lifted into 3D by its predicted depth and displaced by the camera motion at the instant it fired, an event should coincide with others produced by the same edge, so any misalignment exposes an error in depth or motion. Differentiable rendering then turns these per-event estimates into dense depth maps at target times within each window, faithful to the events behind them. On MVSEC, the approach outperforms prior event-only self-supervised methods in most sequences and depth ranges, with the widest margins at night, and recovers camera rotation more accurately than an earlier unsupervised event-based method. Ablations isolate the roles of local spatiotemporal context, the temporal backbone, and the alignment objective. These results position motion-compensated event alignment as a principled source of supervision for continuous-time depth and ego-motion estimation.
introduction:
Each pixel of an event camera fires independently the moment its brightness changes, producing a sparse stream with microsecond temporal resolution and high dynamic range that is well suited to depth estimation in high-speed and low-light regimes [5]. In this setting, scene structure and camera motion are coupled prediction problems: each event must be assigned a depth, and the continuous camera motion that carries the same 3D point across the sensor must be known at each event’s own timestamp.

The difficulty is that event streams are irregular in time and sparse in space, whereas dense metric depth is usually available only at image timestamps. Assigning the same endpoint depth map to every event ignores the fact that the camera and the visible geometry evolve within the interval. Most learning pipelines respond to this mismatch by converting events into event frames, voxel grids, or recurrent frame surrogates before estimating geometry [6, 18, 12, 7, 13]. This suits standard backbones but discards the fine-grained timing that is the main advantage of event sensing.

We instead derive supervision from the geometry of the measurements themselves. A predicted depth and the camera motion together allow each event to be back-projected at its own timestamp and transported to a common instant. If both are correct, events generated by the same edge arrive at the same place with consistent timestamps. If either is wrong, the events smear across the image. Sharpness after motion compensation is therefore a measure of geometric quality that requires no depth label.

Our method (Figure 1) learns per-event depth from motion-compensated event alignment using a local-global event-state encoder trained by dual-anchor alignment losses. A selective state-space model captures temporal context across the time-ordered events of each window, and a multi-scale local branch captures image-plane neighbourhoods. An occlusion-aware renderer then combines the per-event depths into a target-time map while preserving event-time geometry and gradients to the contributing depths. It anchors each pixel on its most recent observations and combines samples through smooth weights, allowing the rendered map to enter the training objective. A camera-motion head predicts each window’s motion, which is also estimated by aligning its events under the predicted depths.

A self-supervised formulation at event-time granularity: per-event depth, camera motion evaluated at each event timestamp, and dual-anchor motion-compensated alignment in place of dense depth labels.

A local-global event-state encoder that pairs bidirectional Mamba temporal modelling with multi-scale local spatiotemporal aggregation returned to the original event order, a head that predicts a bounded depth per event, and a camera-motion head for the window. Ablations confirm the contributions of the local branch, the state-space backbone, and the alignment objective.

Geometrically consistent dense depth from per-event depth: a differentiable occlusion-aware renderer transports each event depth to the target time. A recency-anchored log-depth consensus suppresses older samples that disagree with the most recently observed surface, limiting foreground-background mixing. The target-time map remains consistent with its contributing event depths and passes gradients to each of them. On MVSEC, the rendered depth is the most accurate among event-only self-supervised methods at every 20 m cut-off and at three of the four 10 m and 30 m cut-offs.

title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
authors: Oliver Schön,Adrien Banse,John Lygeros,Lars Lindemann
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
abstract:
Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language.
Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax.
We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all.
For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers.
We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction.
On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.
introduction:
Symbolic control methods compute, from a model of a system and a task description, a controller that carries out the task
by construction (Belta et al., 2017). This guarantee has a price: the task must be stated in a
formal language, such as a temporal logic. Consider a mobile robot that receives
the instruction “Visit street 5 while ensuring you never enter parking lot 2”. In linear temporal
logic (LTL), it reads
“◇​street_5∧□​¬parking_lot_2\Diamond\,\texttt{street\_5}\;\wedge\;\Box\,\neg\,\texttt{parking\_lot\_2}”,
where the atomic propositions street_5 and parking_lot_2 hold when the robot is at the
corresponding location. Writing such formulas takes expertise that most users do not have and is, together
with scalability, one of the two main bottlenecks in applying formal methods (Rozier, 2016). This makes
automatic translation of natural language (NL) into a formal language important.

Many recent translators from natural to formal language rely on the most powerful language models available,
from Codex to GPT-5, Claude Opus, and the latest Gemini models
(Cosler et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Sundarsingh et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Bayat et al., 2026; Newcomb and Ochoa, 2026). Such translators have outperformed earlier translation methods on
shared benchmarks (Pan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023) and are therefore considered the state of the art
(Appendix A provides a literature review).
Most of these models are proprietary and behind an API, or too large
to be run on a single computer, and only a minority of translators run entirely on local, open-weight models.
On a robot, however, the translator must run onboard. New instructions may arrive during operation and require translating and replanning in real time,
with limited compute and energy resources, and often without access to the cloud, e.g., for security or reliability reasons
(Kehoe et al., 2015; Firoozi et al., 2025).

We ask whether such generative models are needed at all for physical AI applications. Indeed, translators can identify a formula by asking a model a few simple questions; for the running example, four questions suffice (Figure 1). The two “yes” answers select the operators ◇\Diamond (eventually) and □¬\Box\neg (never), and the two choices fill them with
street_5 and parking_lot_2. Recently, general-purpose frontier classifiers were introduced with TypeSafe’s model Jev (Almeida, 2026). These recent models read unstructured text together with a question and return a probability for each of its possible answers, instead of generating text. These System-One models are particularly cheap and fast: they answer a
question in a single forward pass instead of one per generated token, and the open-weight model Laya (Convai Innovations, 2026) has
421 million parameters, orders of magnitude fewer than state-of-the-art LLMs and small enough to run locally on a robot.

We introduce the first family of translators from NL into LTL built on a System-One model rather than on a generative
language model. Its questions are designed for each system’s fragment of possible requirements and atomic propositions, so the same
architecture serves different control systems (Section 3). By construction, its number of forward passes per instruction is bounded in
advance, and every output is a well-formed formula; generative
models lack both properties.
We compare our translators with 20 off-the-shelf and 5 fine-tuned local language models on three benchmarks, including a new
Mine Rover benchmark, measuring accuracy, runtime, and energy consumption on a laptop and a Raspberry Pi 5
(Section 4); to our knowledge, no prior study of translation into temporal logic measures energy.
Their accuracy matches or exceeds that of language models with the same characteristics, i.e., local
and fine-tuned on the same data, at a much lower cost.
Beyond that, our translators generalize to atomic propositions and temporal patterns unseen in training and, on the Mine
Rover, make 3.6 times fewer errors than the most accurate fine-tuned language model at an order of magnitude lower
runtime and energy (Section 4.3).
This is the first approach that enables efficient NL to formal language translation for real-time physical AI that uses embedded hardware such as a Raspberry Pi 5.

title: Ego2Ego: Generative Visual Perspective Taking Across Collaborators
authors: Chuhan Jiao,John Gideon,Anshul Gupta,Guy Rosman,Andreas Bulling
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration.
However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person.
We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person’s egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator’s camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator’s perspective.
This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap.
We address these challenges with Ego2Ego– a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants.
Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person’s current view from the ego person’s visual memory.
Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone.
By generating the collaborator’s egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.
introduction:
Perspective taking is the mental and emotional ability to step outside one’s own frame of reference and understand a situation from another person’s point of view.
Its visual form is visual perspective taking: The task of determining whether another person can see an object (Level 1) or how the visual scene looks from their position (Level 2) [13, 40, 42, 50].
Humans rely on this ability during collaboration [51], for example when handing over an object, when referring to an object only visible to the collaborator, or when avoiding obstruction of another person’s view or motion.
Consequently, robots collaborating with humans were argued to require similar abilities [57, 5, 25, 12].
Prior work
reduced visual perspective taking to estimating symbolic or geometric states [57, 5, 29], reconstructing the visual scene from another viewpoint [25, 12], or answering spatial questions [30, 15].
We explore the significantly more challenging task of visually synthesising what the collaborator actually sees.

Existing cross-view video generation methods do not address this task:
Novel view synthesis [60, 80, 22] and camera-controlled video generation [3, 33, 83] only re-film an input video along a new camera trajectory and infer unobserved regions from source observations and learned priors, while exo-to-ego methods [55, 26, 35, 39] require one or more third-person cameras that observe the target person and their workspace.
These assumptions break down in collaborative perspective taking: Two collaborating individuals often face each other or attend to disjoint regions of the workspace, so much of what one person sees is not currently observed by the other, and the collaborator whose view is to be generated is frequently outside the ego person’s field of view (see Fig. 1).

In this work we study generative visual perspective taking between two human collaborators:
Given the posed egocentric video of one person, the ego person, with access to earlier frames of the same recording, a scene point cloud, and the camera trajectory of the other person, the collaborator, the task is to generate the egocentric video that the collaborator sees at any point in time.
While pretrained video diffusion models provide strong priors over scene appearance and human motion, they cannot directly relate two views separated by large viewpoint changes.
Our key insight is that collaboration takes place in a shared workspace: its static 3D geometry, together with the collaborator’s camera trajectory, determines which surfaces the collaborator sees and where, while the ego person’s observations provide appearance cues that the video prior can build on for many of these surfaces.
We thus propose Ego2Ego– a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that ground video generation in this shared geometry and visual memory.
First, to handle extreme viewpoint shifts and dynamic occlusions, dense geometric rendering rasterises the point cloud into a scene coordinate map for every view, so that the same 3D point receives the same value across views and serves as a shared spatial reference.
Second, to relate two independently moving cameras, relative geometric attention extends single-trajectory ray-aligned attention [82] to align tokens between the ego person’s and the collaborator’s views, pairing token-wise ray-frame transforms with shared temporal encodings.
Third, to handle sparse visual overlap, the ego person’s visual memory selects earlier ego-person frames that best cover the collaborator’s view, recovering regions outside the current clip.

We evaluate Ego2Ego on CoMind [14] across three backbones: the general-purpose video models Wan2.2-5B and Wan2.1-14B [61], and AnyView [60], which is pretrained for dynamic view synthesis.
Besides visual quality, we evaluate whether the generated video reproduces the scene layout from the collaborator’s viewpoint (Level-2 perspective taking) and captures the collaborator’s head and hand motions, which matter for learning manipulation policies from human videos [47, 62, 27].
Ego2Ego consistently improves all three backbones and outperforms the baselines built on the same backbone on all metrics, including Level-2 scene layout, and also on commonly used video quality metrics when the collaborator’s head stays outside the ego person’s view.
Notably, Ego2Ego on general-purpose backbones without cross-view pretraining surpasses AnyView on most metrics despite AnyView’s large-scale multi-view pretraining, while adding Ego2Ego to AnyView brings further gains.

In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

We introduce the task of generative visual perspective taking between collaborators, and evaluate existing novel view synthesis, camera-controlled, and exo-to-ego video generation methods on the CoMind dataset.

We propose Ego2Ego, a backbone-agnostic geometric method that combines shared 3D scene coordinates, relative ray-space attention, and the ego person’s visual memory.

Across three video diffusion backbones, Ego2Ego consistently outperforms the cross-view video generation baselines built on the same backbone in visual quality, Level-2 scene layout, and collaborator motion.

Because its inputs require only a wearable camera, a one-time scene scan, and a camera trajectory, Ego2Ego is promising for human-robot collaboration in two complementary ways:
When the ego person is a robot collaborating with a human, visual perspective taking could allow the robot to infer what its human collaborator sees from their head trajectory, helping the robot plan complementary next actions and avoid redundant work.
Conversely, when training a robot policy to act as the collaborator, Ego2Ego can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos, which are costly to capture [70, 14] but valuable for visuomotor policy learning [10, 27].

1. We introduce the task of generative visual perspective taking between collaborators, and evaluate existing novel view synthesis, camera-controlled, and exo-to-ego video generation methods on the CoMind dataset.

2. We propose Ego2Ego, a backbone-agnostic geometric method that combines shared 3D scene coordinates, relative ray-space attention, and the ego person’s visual memory.

3. Across three video diffusion backbones, Ego2Ego consistently outperforms the cross-view video generation baselines built on the same backbone in visual quality, Level-2 scene layout, and collaborator motion.

title: BladeR: Scalable, Shape-Guided 3D Reconstruction of Wind Turbine Blades from UAV Imagery
authors: Jonathan Sterckx,Michiel Vlaminck,Hiep Luong
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: The structural integrity of wind turbine blades is critical for safe, efficient energy production. Accurate 3D reconstruction allows precise localization and quantification of wear and early damage detection. While drone-based inspections are standard, their high-resolution imagery poses challenges such as weak texture, lighting variability, and high computational cost. We present BladeR, a scalable pipeline for high-quality 3D reconstruction from inspection imagery. A hierarchical sparse reconstruction strategy leverages GPS/IMU data and blade shape priors to guide advanced keypoint matchers on full-resolution images. For dense reconstruction, a tiled Gaussian Splatting framework processes 45 MP images at native resolution, isolates the blade from background, and adaptively enhances detail recovery along the leading edge. Validation against commercial and open-source baselines shows significant improvements in model completeness and detail.
introduction:
Wind energy is a critical component of the global transition to renewable energy [Global Wind Energy Council, 2024]. The operational efficiency and lifespan of wind turbines depend heavily on blade integrity. Leading edge erosion, for example, degrades aerodynamic performance, reduces energy output and shortens blade lifespan [Herring et al., 2019], [Özçakmak et al., 2024], making regular inspections essential [Shafiee and Sørensen, 2019].

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have revolutionized turbine inspections by providing safer, faster, and more cost-effective alternatives to manual methods [Poleo et al., 2021]. While 2D drone images are useful for detecting surface defects [Xu et al., 2019], [Memari et al., 2024], full 3D reconstructions offer richer insights by enabling precise volumetric quantification, defect localization, and differentiation between true damage and surface artifacts [Sterckx et al., 2025b]. They also support defect tracking and blade deformation analysis, enabling more comprehensive digital twin models, with room to advance beyond current 2D techniques [Hu et al., 2025].

Prior studies demonstrate the feasibility of photogrammetry for blade reconstruction [Nielsen et al., 2020], [Zhang et al., 2020], but often rely on decommissioned blades under controlled conditions, without a scalable pipeline. [Sterckx et al., 2025a], proposed a custom reconstruction pipeline with improved accuracy, yet it does not leverage domain-specific knowledge and its applicability remains limited to small datasets.

To address these limitations, we present a pipeline tailored to real-world inspections and validated on a new UAV dataset. Our contributions are:

A high-overlap UAV dataset of two operational blades captured with a 45 MP camera under varied conditions.

A scalable preprocessing pipeline that uses automated segmentation and blade-centered tiling to enable full-resolution image processing without exceeding memory limits.

A robust two-stage sparse reconstruction that leverages GPS data and a blade-geometry prior to concentrate keypoint matching along the leading edge, reducing the number of required image-matching operations.

A custom Gaussian Splatting framework with soft background masking, blade-specific adaptive densification, and tiled full-resolution processing, allowing reconstruction at resolutions significantly higher than those supported by standard dense reconstruction methods.

Our method produces more complete and detailed 3D models than leading commercial and open-source software, while scaling effectively to high-resolution imagery and large inspection datasets—providing a solid foundation for improved damage assessment and maintenance planning.

1. A high-overlap UAV dataset of two operational blades captured with a 45 MP camera under varied conditions.

2. A scalable preprocessing pipeline that uses automated segmentation and blade-centered tiling to enable full-resolution image processing without exceeding memory limits.

3. A robust two-stage sparse reconstruction that leverages GPS data and a blade-geometry prior to concentrate keypoint matching along the leading edge, reducing the number of required image-matching operations.

4. A custom Gaussian Splatting framework with soft background masking, blade-specific adaptive densification, and tiled full-resolution processing, allowing reconstruction at resolutions significantly higher than those supported by standard dense reconstruction methods.

title: InterBand-EMG: A Cross-Band Foundation Model for Generalizable Hand-Pose Estimation
authors: Zongheng Guo,Tao Chen,Dalong Du,Yijian Yang,Heng Liu,Lun Shu,Chen Luo,Junhao Tu,Lei Shu,Mingzhou Wu,Yifan Liu,Yu Zhang,Zhenqiang Liu,Shilei Wen,Jie Zhou,Manuela Ferrario
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO); Image and Video Processing (eess.IV)
abstract:
Surface electromyography (sEMG) enables continuous hand-pose
estimation, but learning representations that generalize
across users and movements remains challenging.
We introduce InterBand-EMG, which combines band-specific
quantization with cross-band reconstruction and structured
masked code prediction to learn transferable EMG
representations for hand-pose tracking.
We also introduce SynapMyo, an eight-channel EMG-to-pose
dataset comprising 1,227.74 hand-hours from 499 users
across 68 movement categories.
Experiments on emg2pose and SynapMyo show that InterBand-EMG
outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in joint-angle accuracy
across all three generalization settings on both datasets. The source code and the SynapMyo dataset will be publicly
released upon acceptance of this paper.
introduction:
Continuous hand-pose estimation recovers the joint-angle trajectories
that describe finger articulation during hand movements. It supports
applications such as demonstration capture, teleoperation, and human–robot interaction. Vision-based approaches provide accurate hand pose estimates (Banerjee et al., 2025; Han et al., 2022),
but their availability can be limited by objects occlusion and movements outside the camera’s field of view (Salter et al., 2024).
Surface electromyography (sEMG) offers a complementary sensing modality: skin-mounted electrodes record electrical activity associated with muscle activation, providing information for movement decoding without requiring the hand to remain visible.

Learning a transferable mapping from sEMG to hand pose is challenging
because anatomy, electrode placement, and sensor contact vary across
participants and recordings. The emg2pose benchmark provides approximately 370 hours of paired 16-channel sEMG and hand-pose data from 193 participants, with separate evaluations on held-out users,
movement stages, and both (Salter et al., 2024). This benchmark
establishes a basis for studying generalization in continuous pose
decoding. Alongside task-supervised learning, an important question
is how pretraining on EMG without pose labels can produce
representations that improve subsequent pose estimation under
these generalization conditions.

Self-supervised biosignal learning addresses this question through
a range of prediction targets and training objectives. Some
approaches first discretize continuous signals using
vector-quantized (VQ) autoencoders, then learn representations by
predicting masked or future codes (Jiang et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2026a; Barmpas et al., 2025). Others learn continuous
representations through signal reconstruction, latent prediction,
or contrastive objectives, without a separately pretrained discrete
tokenizer (Yang et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a; Wang et al., 2025).
For continuous EMG-to-pose estimation, EMG-GPT predicts future codes
from a frozen tokenizer and transfers the resulting representations
to pose decoding (Magni et al., 2026). Its locally matched tracking
evaluation reports higher mean angular errors than the supervised
vEMG2Pose baseline across all three generalization splits, although
the models retain different input-processing pipelines. These
findings motivate further investigation of how EMG pretraining
targets influence downstream pose estimation.

Frequency-aware tokenization offers one way to structure these
targets. Surface EMG reflects the superposition of action potentials
from multiple motor units, with spectral characteristics influenced
by muscle properties, tissue filtering, and electrode
configuration (Muceli and Merletti, 2024). Allocating separate
codebooks to different frequency bands may help retain signal
features that a single broadband vocabulary underrepresents.
BandVQ follows this principle for EEG by training an independent
VQ-VAE tokenizer for each frequency band and using the resulting
codes for shared-encoder pretraining (Sukhbaatar et al., 2026).
However, its band tokenizers are learned independently: each
reconstructs its own band without access to features from the
others. This leaves open whether interaction during tokenizer
training can produce more useful discrete targets while retaining
separate vocabularies for individual bands.

We investigate this question through InterBand-EMG, a
self-supervised pretraining framework that combines band-specific
quantization with cross-band reconstruction. Our central hypothesis
is that coupling reconstruction across bands improves the
usefulness of the resulting codes as targets for representation
learning. Three encoders with separate codebooks tokenize the low-,
mid-, and high-frequency components of EMG. We compare independent
reconstruction with three interaction strategies: feature
concatenation, band-query attention, and concatenation followed by
attention (Figure 1). Our main model uses each band’s quantized features as queries to retrieve context from all bands before reconstruction. Reconstruction losses therefore couple the learning of the band-specific codes while each band retains its own discrete vocabulary.
After tokenizer training, we freeze its parameters and use its
band-specific code indices as prediction targets. A shared encoder
receives masked broadband EMG and learns to predict the codes of
all three bands at masked positions. The encoder’s continuous
representations are subsequently fine-tuned for hand-pose
estimation. This two-stage design allows us to examine whether
cross-band interaction during target construction improves
downstream representation quality.

To support larger-scale pretraining and evaluation, we also
introduce SynapMyo, an eight-channel EMG-to-pose dataset
intended for public release. SynapMyo contains 81,564 single-hand
recordings, totaling approximately 1,228 hand-hours across
499 participants and 68 annotated gesture and movement categories.
The collection includes glove-based recordings acquired using
Waveletech EMG wristbands and Manus motion-capture gloves, alongside
recordings annotated through vision-based hand reconstruction.
Both annotation sources are mapped to a common 20-dimensional
UmeTrack joint-angle representation and temporally aligned with
EMG. Hand-hours count each hand separately. We establish fixed
evaluation splits for held-out participants, held-out movement
tasks, and both. Recordings from the same acquisition episode,
together with temporally overlapping episodes from the same
participant, remain within a single split.

Our contributions are as follows:

We propose InterBand-EMG, a self-supervised framework that learns band-specific EMG codebooks through cross-band reconstruction and uses their discrete codes to retrain
a broadband encoder for continuous hand pose estimation.

We introduce SynapMyo, an eight-channel EMG-to-pose
dataset comprising approximately 1,228 hours of hand data with a common joint-angle representation and fixed evaluation splits for held-out participants and movement tasks.

We achieve state-of-the-art joint-angle accuracy on
both emg2pose and SynapMyo across all three generalization
settings, reducing MAE by 0.3–4.2% and 16.2–24.2%,
respectively, relative to the strongest evaluated baseline
on each dataset.

1. We propose InterBand-EMG, a self-supervised framework that learns band-specific EMG codebooks through cross-band reconstruction and uses their discrete codes to retrain
a broadband encoder for continuous hand pose estimation.
