title: AceVLN: Asynchronous Cloud Edge Deployment of VLNs via Latent Scheduling and Compensation
authors: Zihao Zheng,Hangyu Cao,Yulong Han,Xichang Wu,Zhihao Mao,Maoliang Li,Jiayu Chen,Hailong Zou,Donggang Cao,Xuanzhe Liu,Hong Mei,Xiang Chen
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Cloud–edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors.
Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate.
We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation.
Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift.
Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes.
AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation.
Experiments show that AceVLN improves success rates by 1.7–2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7–10.0% and FLOPs by 18.4–22.3%.
introduction:
Streaming Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) enables robots to generate real-time navigation actions from continuous visual observations and language instructions [1, 2, 3].
To balance high-level reasoning and real-time control, recent models adopt an asynchronous dual-system architecture, where a slow system performs low-frequency reasoning and a lightweight fast system generates high-frequency actions [4, 5].
However, the substantial computational and memory demands of the slow system hinder its deployment on resource-constrained robots [6]. Consequently, practical systems commonly adopt edge-cloud collaboration (ECC), deploying the slow system in the cloud and the fast system onboard to leverage cloud computing resources while preserving real-time local control [7, 8, 9].

In dual-system VLN, the latent serves as an intermediate representation that transfers multi-step navigation guidance from cloud-side reasoning to edge-side control.
Specifically, the slow system encodes uploaded visual observations and navigation instructions into a latent containing guidance for subsequent navigation steps, which the fast system combines with real-time observations to generate actions [10, 7].
However, cloud inference and communication delays cause the robot to continuously move while the fast system reuses a latent generated from historical observations [11].
As the robot’s position and navigation requirements change, the historical latent becomes increasingly inconsistent with the ideal latent that would be generated from current observations, resulting in latent mismatch.
Its severity depends on both edge-cloud latency and the rate of navigation-state changes, causing outdated guidance to induce action deviations and accumulated trajectory errors, ultimately degrading navigation accuracy.

Existing methods mitigate latent mismatch through adaptation. AsyncVLA [8] employs an onboard Edge Adapter to refine actions using real-time observations, while TIC-VLA [5] incorporates delayed semantic features and latency metadata into action generation. CloudEdgeVLA [7] further improves tolerance to stale guidance through training with paired fresh and delayed observations. However, these methods primarily improve action or representation-level adaptation to historical guidance, rather than explicitly assessing action-relevant mismatch to schedule new latent generation or compensate during delayed updates. When historical guidance no longer reflects current navigation requirements, adaptation alone cannot provide updated guidance.
These limitations motivate Active Latent Refresh, which proactively requests updated navigation guidance based on runtime mismatch.

However, achieving efficient and reliable refresh requires addressing three key challenges:
Challenge ①: Latent Mismatch Is Hard to Model.
A single latent entangles guidance for multiple navigation steps, whose mismatches have different impacts on current actions. Consequently, overall latent differences conflate action-critical deviations with less relevant future-step changes, obscuring their actual impact on current actions.
Challenge ②: Latent Refresh Timing Is Hard to Determine.
Different navigation states have varying tolerances to action deviations. Similar deviations can lead to substantially different navigation errors, making fixed refresh intervals prone to unnecessary cloud updates or delayed refreshes that degrade navigation accuracy.
Challenge ③: Latent Mismatch Is Hard to Handle under Latency Spikes.
Even when refresh timing is accurately determined, unexpected latency spikes can delay updated latents [12, 13], leaving the edge system without fresh navigation guidance as a reference for tracking and correcting mismatch during the refresh wait.

To address these challenges, we analyze latent mismatch and its impact on actions, deriving three key insights:
Analysis ①:
We examine latent variations across subspaces, action deviations, and feature responses in the fast system, revealing that changes in a compact Critical Subspace dominate action deviations and can be tracked through fast-system features for lightweight runtime mismatch assessment.
Analysis ②:
We investigate error tolerance and directional drift distributions across navigation steps, revealing that higher Critical Feature Drift Entropy indicates greater navigation sensitivity, guiding dynamic latent refresh scheduling.
Analysis ③:
We analyze critical drift evolution and latent update dynamics under delayed refreshes, revealing short-term continuity in latent updates under consistent drift directions, motivating adaptive compensation on the edge through extrapolation of consistent historical updates.

Guided by these insights, we propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and compensation in cloud–edge streaming VLN.
Method ①: Subspace-Decoupled Latent Mismatch Modeling isolates the Critical Subspace and tracks its mismatch through fused features of the fast system for lightweight runtime assessment.
Method ②: Drift-Distribution-Guided Latent Refresh Scheduling combines critical feature drift with its directional entropy to adapt latent refresh timing to navigation sensitivity.
Method ③: Continuity-Guided Latent Compensation extrapolates recent critical latent updates, using drift continuity and magnitude to control compensation scope and strength during pending refreshes and latency spikes.
Together, these mechanisms reduce cloud updates while preserving navigation accuracy.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We reveal that latent mismatch affects actions primarily through a compact critical subspace, uncovering new insights into navigation error tolerance and temporal mismatch evolution.

Based on these insights, we propose AceVLN, a training-free framework that combines adaptive latent scheduling and complementary edge-side compensation through unified mismatch modeling, enabling efficient and reliable VLN deployment.

On A100 with Jetson Orin/Thor, we quantify the trade-off between cloud calls, total compute, and edge response time. Relative to Bridge, AceVLN cuts FLOPs by 18.4%–22.3% and amortized compute by 2.7%–10.0%, with 5–13 ms higher mean response time. Success rate improves by 1.7–2.4 percentage points over the best baselines, and compensation adds 2.7 points under latency spikes.

1. We reveal that latent mismatch affects actions primarily through a compact critical subspace, uncovering new insights into navigation error tolerance and temporal mismatch evolution.

2. Based on these insights, we propose AceVLN, a training-free framework that combines adaptive latent scheduling and complementary edge-side compensation through unified mismatch modeling, enabling efficient and reliable VLN deployment.

3. On A100 with Jetson Orin/Thor, we quantify the trade-off between cloud calls, total compute, and edge response time. Relative to Bridge, AceVLN cuts FLOPs by 18.4%–22.3% and amortized compute by 2.7%–10.0%, with 5–13 ms higher mean response time. Success rate improves by 1.7–2.4 percentage points over the best baselines, and compensation adds 2.7 points under latency spikes.

title: SCAP: Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining
authors: Xiao Lin,Yaoxu Lyu,Ronghao Dang,Zhili Liu,Kaijing Ma,Yang Zhou,Dingning Liu,Runzhe Teng,Jun Cen,Shanghang Zhang,Chengju Liu,Qijun Chen
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Single-modality action-expert pretraining controls competition from visual shortcuts before vision–language–action (VLA) adaptation.
Yet single-modality pretraining can impair the vision–language interactions needed for subsequent joint prediction.
We construct a diagnostic model in which VA or LA pretraining can disable an initially active pathway for joint vision–language modeling.
In this model, subsequent training with complete visual and language inputs cannot restore the pathway, even with unlimited adaptation.
We therefore introduce Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP), a new action-expert pretraining stage that precedes full-input training.
During this stage, visual and text tokens are randomly masked before entering the VLM.
In this unified diagnostic model, SCAP can preserve the joint vision–language modeling pathway during pretraining and subsequent full-input training.
Compared with direct full-input training, it can also reduce reliance on visual shortcuts and increase reliance on language instructions.
SCAP consistently improves performance across four different VLA architectures.
In real-robot experiments, it achieves 76.67% average success across three instruction-conditioned manipulation tasks, outperforming full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points.
introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models build robot policies on pretrained vision–language models (VLMs), using an action expert to turn the observed scene and the instruction into continuous actions [3]. However, scene–instruction correlations in demonstrations can encourage visual shortcuts, allowing policies to ignore language [17, 38]. Because the action expert is randomly initialized, it can readily inherit these biases and may, in turn, degrade the pretrained VLM’s representations through backpropagation during joint fine-tuning. Action expert pretraining is thus worth exploring to foster language dependence.

Existing recipes counter visual shortcuts by controlling which modality the expert sees. APT [34] and BayesVLA [35] adopt vision–action (VA) pretraining, first learning a visuomotor prior and then introducing language. Conversely, LA4VLA [18] uses language–action (LA) pretraining without vision to learn instruction–action associations, exploring both sequential and mixed LA–VLA training. Despite their differences, these methods follow the same paradigm of incorporating a unimodal pretraining stage preceding full pretraining.

However, single-modality staging can damage the pathway needed to combine vision and language. For an instruction such as “pick up the cup that is the same color as the plate,” VA pretraining provides the scene without the instruction specifying color matching, while LA pretraining provides the instruction without the visual evidence needed to identify the matching cup. Neither stage directly supervises this joint computation, yet the parameters supporting it continue to change. The risk is therefore not merely that joint modeling is left untrained, but that its pathway can be shut down.
Under the specified population gradient flow, subsequent full-input training cannot reopen it, even with unlimited adaptation. This raises a question: can action expert pretraining mitigate visual shortcuts while preserving joint vision–language modeling?

We answer with Stochastic Context for Action Expert Pretraining (SCAP). SCAP follows a two-stage training scheme: we first pretrain the action expert by randomly masking both visual and text tokens, then continue training with full visual and language inputs. By varying the visibility of both modalities, this pretraining exposes the expert to diverse combinations of visual and linguistic cues, discouraging visual shortcuts while retaining joint supervision whenever complementary cues remain visible (Fig. 1). VA, LA, and full-input pretraining are special cases of SCAP obtained with different mask distributions.

In the same construction, SCAP meets both requirements. First, if masks retain both joint cues sufficiently often, the joint modeling path never closes (Sec. 3.3). Second, random masking gives cues from either modality a chance of being hidden, reducing overreliance on a single modality. This advantage persists through subsequent full-input adaptation (Sec. 3.4).

Experiments demonstrate that SCAP outperforms alternative pretraining methods, with consistent gains across four VLA architectures and multiple model scales. By intervening on test-set instructions, we further show that SCAP improves robustness to paraphrasing and sensitivity to changes in task intent. On three real-robot manipulation tasks, SCAP achieves an average success rate of 76.67%, exceeding full-input pretraining by 25 percentage points.

In summary, our contributions are:

We identify a key limitation of unimodal action expert pretraining: it can shut down certain pathways for joint vision–language modeling.

We propose SCAP, which randomly masks visual and text tokens during action expert pretraining to address visual shortcuts while preserving vision–language modeling.

We establish a controlled evaluation protocol spanning multi-task simulation, paired language interventions, and real-robot joint grounding to test instruction reliance and the preservation of joint conditioning.

1. We identify a key limitation of unimodal action expert pretraining: it can shut down certain pathways for joint vision–language modeling.

2. We propose SCAP, which randomly masks visual and text tokens during action expert pretraining to address visual shortcuts while preserving vision–language modeling.

3. We establish a controlled evaluation protocol spanning multi-task simulation, paired language interventions, and real-robot joint grounding to test instruction reliance and the preservation of joint conditioning.

title: Mem-X: A Memory-Dependent Cross-Episode Benchmark for Vision-and-Language Navigation
authors: Zhikang Shi,Yuk Tung Samuel Fang,Hongyu Ding,Zixuan Chen,Yujin Wang,Junhui Guo,You Wu,Jieqi Shi,Jing Huo,Yang Gao
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: . Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027)
abstract:
Long-term memory enables embodied agents to reuse past observations across tasks. However, existing cross-episode vision-and-language navigation (VLN) benchmarks often leave it unclear whether successful navigation relies on historical memory or current exploration. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark designed to evaluate memory-dependent cross-episode VLN. Mem-X organizes episodes into sessions in which subsequent instructions refer to objects or routes encountered in earlier episodes. Its three levels evaluate historical-object recall, in-memory localization and episodic indexing, and off-memory relocalization and historical-route reproduction. For the latter two levels, agents receive episode-local poses but no transformations between episode frames, requiring them to establish spatial correspondence with historical memory. Mem-X comprises 2,071 episodes across 710 sessions in 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes. We also provide MemBridge, a modular baseline that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval to support existing VLN agents. Experiments with state-of-the-art VLN methods demonstrate the benefits of MemBridge while revealing substantial room for improvement on memory-dependent navigation. The benchmark and baseline code are available at
https://github.com/NJU-R-L-Group-Embodied-Lab/Mem-X.
introduction:
Embodied agents that operate in real environments over long horizons need to
retain and use observations and experience from past tasks
 [1, 2].
When an agent continuously executes tasks in the same scene, different tasks
usually share the same locations, and historical memory from preceding
episodes can often assist later tasks [1].
Cross-episode memory is therefore necessary.

Traditional VLN
benchmarks [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] usually evaluate each episode independently, and an
agent’s historical information is used only within the current task, making it
difficult to exploit the associations across tasks.

Existing cross-episode VLN
benchmarks [1, 9] and lifelong navigation
benchmarks already allow agents to retain and use historical information.
However, these benchmarks usually do not make historical memory necessary for
completing later tasks.
Relying only on the spatial relations and actions suggested by the current
instruction, exploration can achieve the same effect.
We therefore consider this task design not tightly coupled with the memory
mechanism, and it cannot truly evaluate an algorithm’s cross-episode memory
ability.

To address this issue, we construct Mem-X, a cross-episode VLN benchmark for
memory-dependent tasks, as shown in Figure 1.
Its three levels of increasing difficulty are detailed in
Section III-A.

Unlike existing work, we design Mem-X for tightly coupled memory
evaluation.
Through memory recall, in-memory and off-memory localization, episode
indexing, and historical-path reproduction, it forces the agent to use memory
to complete the related tasks.
Table I compares Mem-X with existing related
benchmarks.

To provide a reference baseline for Mem-X, we introduce MemBridge, a modular approach that combines semantic scene memory, cross-episode localization, and coarse-to-fine retrieval. MemBridge connects historical observations to current navigation tasks and can be integrated with different VLN agents, providing a practical starting point for studying memory-dependent navigation.

The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark that makes historical experience an explicit part of VLN task specification through references to previously encountered objects and traversed routes. It comprises 2,071 episodes organized into 710 sessions across 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes.

We establish an evaluation protocol that controls access to cross-episode coordinates and assesses both memory-related capabilities and task completion, revealing navigation failures that endpoint-based metrics alone overlook.

We provide MemBridge, a modular reference baseline that enables existing VLN agents to use historical memory across episodes. Experiments with four representative agents demonstrate its effectiveness while highlighting substantial room for improvement on Mem-X.

1. We introduce Mem-X, a benchmark that makes historical experience an explicit part of VLN task specification through references to previously encountered objects and traversed routes. It comprises 2,071 episodes organized into 710 sessions across 34 scenes, including 1,204 memory-dependent episodes.

2. We establish an evaluation protocol that controls access to cross-episode coordinates and assesses both memory-related capabilities and task completion, revealing navigation failures that endpoint-based metrics alone overlook.

3. We provide MemBridge, a modular reference baseline that enables existing VLN agents to use historical memory across episodes. Experiments with four representative agents demonstrate its effectiveness while highlighting substantial room for improvement on Mem-X.

title: Simulation-Based Testing of RCM-Constrained Robotic Software via Task Manifolds
authors: Zhenyu Jiang,Yanlin Li,Rongjie Yan,Rihui Song,Kai Huang
abstract:
System-level testing of surgical robots requires generating executable test scenarios that exercise diverse, safety-critical behaviors. However, remote-center-of-motion (RCM) surgical manipulators operate within tightly constrained workspaces governed by coupled task geometry, inverse kinematics, and motor limits. Direct sampling in motor-command or Cartesian spaces frequently wastes testing budgets on physically unfeasible configurations. To address this limitation, we present a manifold-centered testing framework that decouples feasible test-domain construction from downstream test-generation strategies. Candidate inputs are generated directly within this constructed feasible domain and mapped to lower-level joint commands for simulation execution. Offline trajectory safety oracles and a spatial reference grid then evaluate failure yield and coverage.
We compare our task-manifold representation against Cartesian XYZ and principal component analysis (PCA) under random testing, systematic traversal, and genetic search strategies.
Results demonstrate that the feasible task domain improves test-generation efficiency and enables systematic reference-cell coverage.
Crucially, random and genetic search strategies detect a broader spectrum of failure patterns than baseline representations, revealing that complete reference-cell coverage alone does not exhaust intra-cell behavioral dynamics.
Furthermore, differential testing between defective and patched controller versions reveals that targeted evolutionary search detects aggregate failure-rate shifts from software repairs. Finally, a cross-platform study on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 arm in MoveIt 2 confirms workflow transferability to kinematically redundant manipulators. Together, these findings highlight the necessity of combining feasibility-aware domain modeling with complementary search strategies for systematic testing of robot software.
introduction:
Surgical robots support precise manipulation in confined workspaces
(Taylor and Stoianovici, 2003; Chatterjee et al., 2024). For example, in ophthalmic
microsurgery, instruments maneuver through a narrow entry port while avoiding
damage to delicate intraocular tissue
(Thirunavukarasu et al., 2024). Recent autonomous platforms have demonstrated closed-loop needle navigation and targeted retinal injections (Zhang et al., 2023; Bian et al., 2026). Executing these delicate interventions reliably demands tightly coupled perception, trajectory planning, and low-level control to reach surgical targets while strictly adhering to kinematic and safety constraints.

Comprehensive system-level testing is essential to ensure the operational safety of surgical robotic platforms. However, physical hardware experiments are prohibitively expensive, time-consuming, and incapable of exhaustively evaluating the vast space of feasible states and boundary conditions. Simulation-based testing offers a scalable, repeatable framework for evaluating closed-loop system dynamics and detecting safety violations. Nevertheless, the validity of simulation-derived evidence critically depends on which inputs are selected and how thoroughly they cover the underlying input domain (Bresolin et al., 2015; Araujo et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2025).

Remote-Center-of-Motion (RCM) constraints serve as a fundamental mechanism to ensure a surgical instrument remains aligned with a fixed anatomical entry port. Systematic safety testing of an RCM-constrained surgical robot requires both a valid test domain and an effective testing strategy. The domain defines which physical configurations constitute distinct test inputs, whereas the testing strategy determines how a finite simulation budget is partitioned—whether toward broad coverage, unguided exploration, or focused evaluation of high-risk operational regions.

Because motor commands directly govern robot actuation, the Cartesian product of valid joint parameters constitutes an input domain for test case generation. Nevertheless, this joint-space domain does not reflect task-level semantics.
Independently selected motor commands can violate
coupled kinematic constraints, distinct motor commands can represent the same
task-relevant state, and Euclidean distance between motor vectors does not reflect
whether the corresponding tool poses exercise different safety conditions.
Another common test domain is the tool pose in Cartesian space, which introduces a complementary drawback: it describes spatial locations without guaranteeing that they are task-compatible or kinematically realizable by the robot. Consequently, exhaustive or uniform sampling across either domain risks expending substantial test budget on unreachable or redundant inputs while leaving critical, feasible task states unexplored.

This paper encodes test inputs using physically meaningful coordinates of
a task manifold, which describes states satisfying structural task
constraints. Workspace and robot constraints further restrict these
coordinates to a feasible test domain. Selected inputs are mapped
to motor commands for simulation, and their outcomes are associated with
the inputs’ reference-grid cells for coverage and failure analysis.
Consequently, the test domain establishes the boundaries of valid execution and the reference framework for evaluation, while the testing strategy independently governs the allocation of the simulation budget across this domain.

We evaluate the method on an RCM-constrained surgical needle-withdrawal
task. Each test case specifies an initial needle configuration from which the
robot must withdraw through a fixed entry port, respecting the RCM
constraint (Aghakhani et al., 2013; Taylor and Stoianovici, 2003). The initial task state is fully parameterized by two orientation variables and an insertion depth, subject to physical workspace, inverse-kinematic, and motor-limit constraints. These three task coordinates directly substitute for the raw motor variables of the robot under evaluation.

We compare three input representations—Cartesian XYZ, our
task-coordinate representation with feasibility filtering (labeled as Manifold), and
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) (Abdi and Williams, 2010)—under random, traversal, and genetic search. This setup decouples valid input generation from search-driven failure discovery and coverage. We further classify failing trajectories by their first safety violation and the preceding geometric states to examine which failure behaviors each representation reveals.
Subsequently, a comparative evaluation between a defective and a patched controller assesses practical defect detection capabilities, followed by a MoveIt 2 case study to verify the transferability of our framework.

In summary, the paper makes three contributions:

We introduce a task domain modeling method that embeds task-space and kinematic constraints directly into a minimal task-coordinate representation, eliminating invalid test candidates and maximizing execution throughput under a fixed sampling budget.

We propose a testing framework that explicitly decouples the generation of valid test domains from the search strategies used to explore them, enabling independent analysis of input validity, spatial coverage, and failure detection.

We evaluate the Manifold representation against Cartesian XYZ and PCA baselines, showing its benefits for feasible test generation, systematic reference-cell coverage, and failure-pattern diversity. We further assess practical defect detection through controller variants and workflow transferability through a MoveIt 2 (Coleman et al., 2014) planning pipeline.

title: Portable Active Recovery under Timed and Position-Dependent Visual Outages
authors: Jinyuan Zhang,Shengshuo Jiao
abstract: When a camera blackout depends on physical position rather than elapsed time, stable hovering prevents visual recovery and mission completion. On stereo visual-inertial quadrotors without external localization, an exogenous timed blackout and an endogenous position-dependent dark zone appear identical at loss onset yet require opposite responses: hover-and-wait completes 93/96 timed blackouts but 0/96 spatial outages (13 hard failures), whereas blind continuation traverses many spatial zones yet fails heavily during timed blackouts. We formulate visual-outage recovery as a worst-condition active-observability problem and introduce a portable recovery module at the reference interface of an unchanged host controller with zero retraining. Using deployable telemetry alone, the module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing, settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional gated prior-map branch. On a preregistered 48-scene benchmark (1,920 flights), our full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition completion, outperforming development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2+29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] and exceeding all six external baselines after Bonferroni correction. Attached without retraining to SimpleFlight, the module lifts worst-condition completion by +17.7+17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0×/1.25×1.0\times/1.25\times speeds, 0/80 hard failures). Trace diagnostics reveal that survival hinges on visual-inertial re-acquisition asymmetry at vision return—not blind IMU drift suppression—and uncover a bias–drift map crossover confirmed on 72 held-out EuRoC windows.
introduction:
When a stereo visual-inertial quadrotor loses usable camera frames, stable hovering is not task recovery. Modern learned and adaptive flight controllers track agile trajectories with high accuracy while pose estimates remain available (Kaufmann et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; O’Connell et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025), yet multi-second visual blackouts force open-loop inertial propagation while the tracker keeps acting on drifting states.

Under deployable onboard telemetry, two outage regimes are observationally aliased at loss onset yet impose opposite recovery laws. In an exogenous timed blackout (T8, 8 s), camera frames return automatically once the interval expires; stopping on inertial propagation preserves local visual context and completes 93/96 flights (Section 5). In an endogenous position-dependent dark zone (Slong, 1.35 m arc), frames return only after the vehicle physically leaves the unobservable region; hovering inside the zone completes 0/96 flights (13 hard failures). Conversely, continuing blindly along the schedule traverses many spatial zones yet incurs 7–12 timed-outage hard failures across external trackers. Completing missions reliably when the outage mechanism is undisclosed requires an active-observability decision layer (Bajcsy, 1988; Kaelbling et al., 1998) above low-level tracking, analogous to Simplex runtime assurance (Sha, 2001).

We decouple active recovery from low-level actuation at the reference interface, enabling zero-retraining deployment above unchanged host controllers. Beyond closed-loop recovery performance, trace-level diagnostics overturn a widely held intuition: stopping succeeds not by slowing open-loop IMU drift—which grows at a similar quadratic rate across actions and hosts (≤1\leq 1 cm difference at 4 s despite 4.4×4.4\times higher body-rate excitation on MPPI)—but by governing visual-inertial re-acquisition when stereo frames return. Stopping or probing back into previously observed texture enables Basalt’s KLT optical flow to collapse accumulated blind error to 2–8%, whereas forward traversal onto unseen far-side texture induces host-dependent re-acquisition jumps that a gated prior-map branch corrects on MPPI.

Contributions. This paper makes three contributions:

Worst-condition aliased-outage formulation and kinematic analysis (Section 3): We formalize timed versus position-dependent visual-outage recovery under parallel physical (CphysC_{\mathrm{phys}}) and localization-qualified (CctrlC_{\mathrm{ctrl}}, CVIOC_{\mathrm{VIO}}) task-completion criteria scored by worst-condition completion WW, accompanied by a 1D kinematic lemma establishing exact quintic stopping depth, probe-budget feasibility, and two-segment blind-exposure reduction.

Portable reference-interface recovery module (Section 4): Operating solely on deployable telemetry and references without altering host weights, our module coordinates visual-loss detection, jerk-limited braking, bounded backward probing (0.50 m planned budget), settled rejoining, height-integral trim, and an optional support- and consistency-gated ORB-SLAM3 translation branch across three distinct flight controllers.

Preregistered benchmark, cross-host transfer, and mechanistic diagnostics (Section 5): Across 48 fresh scenes (1,920 flights), the full MPPI configuration reaches 88.5% [81.2, 94.8] worst-condition CctrlC_{\mathrm{ctrl}}, beating development-selected DATT-L1 by +29.2+29.2 pp [17.7, 40.6] (H1) and all six external baselines under Bonferroni correction (99.17%). Without retraining, the module lifts T8 completion across MPPI, SimpleFlight, and DATT-L1, raises SimpleFlight worst-condition completion by +17.7+17.7 pp [7.3, 28.1] to 86.5% (and 90% across 1.0×/1.25×1.0\times/1.25\times speeds with 0/80 hard failures), and uncovers the re-acquisition asymmetry and bias–drift map crossover confirmed on real EuRoC data.

title: EgoSurgHands: An Egocentric 3D Hand Pose Dataset & Benchmark for Open Surgery Training
authors: Ankit Pal,Guillaume Kugener,Sofia Volpi,Joshua Schwartz,Alex Idarraga,Pranav Rajpurkar,Gabriel A. Brat
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code, dataset, and benchmark leaderboard available atthis https URL
abstract: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon’s hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels are sensor-fused with human-validated pseudo-ground truth: every evaluation frame passes human review with examiner cross-review and surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an external multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18% and 40% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1% of evaluation rows. As a lightweight diagnostic baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://huggingface.co/datasets/surgicalinformatics/EgoSurgHands and https://github.com/monk1337/egoSurgHands.
introduction:
Egocentric 3D hand pose is a key perceptual signal for surgical skill assessment, AR-guided training, and robot learning from demonstration: in suturing, a surgeon’s hands encode grip choice, suture tension, needle trajectory, and the sequencing of one-hand and two-hand ties. Large egocentric hand datasets now support robot learning of dexterous manipulation from human video Hoque et al. (2026), but none covers surgery, and progress there is limited by data. Hand-pose backbones are largely trained on kitchens, factories, sports, or assembly tasks and do not transfer reliably to surgical settings, where colored gloves, surgical drapes, occlusion, and metallic instruments degrade the visual cues that vision-only models depend on.

Existing egocentric hand-pose datasets do not cover surgical training. EgoExo4D Grauman et al. (2024), ARCTIC Fan et al. (2023), AssemblyHands Ohkawa et al. (2023), and HOT3D Banerjee et al. (2025) capture skilled activities, toy assembly, and object manipulation, while surgical datasets are non-egocentric (AIxSuture Hoffmann et al. (2024); the multi-view replica-operating-room benchmark of Fischer et al. (2026)), synthetic (POV-Surgery Wang et al. (2023)), or limited to wrist and palm tracking (EgoExOR Özsoy et al. (2025a)). No public benchmark is simultaneously real, egocentric, sensor-grounded, and human-validated for open surgery training tasks.

We introduce EgoSurgHands, the first benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with Meta Project Aria glasses, it provides 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings (PRs) and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, from four trainees in three experience tiers (junior pre-resident, senior pre-resident, surgical trainee), three glove colors, and 13 surgical training tasks on synthetic-skin pads.

What makes the release unique. Each frame includes the multi-sensor sensor stack (camera intrinsics, MPS hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, with SLAM extrinsics for the recordings where SLAM succeeded). Evaluation labels are initialized from Aria Machine Perception Services (MPS), whose visual-inertial SLAM, multi-camera stereo, and online calibration are unavailable to monocular RGB models, so the reference comes from analytics that the evaluated models cannot access. The labels are sensor-fused, human-validated pseudo-ground truth: every evaluation frame passes primary review, with examiner review and surgeon adjudication of flagged cases. We quantify human correction and inter-annotator agreement (§3.4), characterize label-model mismatch (§6.2), and validate the labels against an external multi-view triangulated reference (§6.3).

What the benchmark reveals. We evaluate eight methods under zero-shot transfer: six MANO-based Romero et al. (2017) reconstructors, the two-hand IntagHand, and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands (§4.1). Three findings stand out. (i)  Backbones pretrained using egocentric data are associated with stronger zero-shot transfer, and the ego-pretrained JointTransformer is best at 14.95 mm PA-MPJPE. (ii) A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detects a hand on only 24.1% of evaluation rows. (iii) Aligned-pose accuracy is inadequate; most backbones do not predict where the hand is in the camera frame, which AR overlay and robot learning from demonstration require (§6).

As a lightweight diagnostic baseline, we developed JRN (Joint-Residual Network), a 58K-parameter two-headed (pose + translation) residual corrector trained on the PR-disjoint training split with the backbone frozen. Its gains persist under a leave-one-wearer-out protocol (10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE for the two ego-pretrained backbones) and reach the benchmark’s empirical label resolution scale of about one centimeter. Methods are compared on the zero-shot table, whose 15 to 30 mm spread lies well above that scale. Its translation head supplies the camera-frame root that most backbones lack, and measuring the remaining placement and fingertip error is a central purpose of the benchmark.

title: Many Plans at Once: Diverse Top-Quality Planning in Continuous Time
authors: Mahyar Jahani-nasab,Hamid Rezatofighi,Mor Vered,Buser Say
abstract:
Planners for physical systems usually return a single trajectory, which leaves no alternative when an unmodeled constraint invalidates the chosen route or downstream preferences change. A set of plans computed in advance provides ready-made alternatives and warm-starts for fast adaptation, but only if the plans are both low-cost and mutually distinct. Discrete planning addresses
this with top-quality and diverse planning, but these ideas do not transfer to
continuous time, where every valid trajectory has infinitely many valid
near-copies, and existing trajectory planners converge to one or a few
solutions. We present Many Plans at Once (MPAO), which treats every plan
it finds as a reason to search elsewhere: it samples untrained neural networks
whose outputs meet the boundary conditions by construction, trains corrections
shared by networks from the same distribution, stores every validated plan, and
adapts its sampling to what it has found, which makes it anytime. We define
the goal by bringing the cost bound of top-quality planning and the
distinctness threshold of diverse planning to continuous time. Under equal
budgets against five baselines, MPAO is the only method that solves all
40 instances across four domains. On contact-rich manipulation, it is the only
method with plans within 25% of the best known cost on one task, and returns
about ten times as many such plans as the strongest baseline on the other two.
introduction:
Trajectory planning for physical systems computes a plan that satisfies the system’s differential dynamics and
constraints, and typically returns a single trajectory that is optimal, or
locally optimal, with respect to a cost (Betts 1998; Zucker et al. 2013; Morari et al. 2015). This paradigm is effective when the environment and objective are fully known, but brittle when new constraints emerge or task preferences shift. If an unexpected obstacle obstructs the chosen route or a secondary preference rules it out, the single plan is unusable and no alternative is available (Otte and Frazzoli 2016). Local feedback control and trajectory deformation can absorb only small deviations around a single nominal path (Tedrake et al. 2010), whereas replanning from scratch across different homotopy classes or contact modes is computationally expensive (Posa et al. 2014). Computing a set of plans in advance addresses both limitations: downstream execution or local replanning can fall back on or warm-start from an unobstructed mode (Magdici and Althoff 2016), and an operator can select among qualitatively different options (Nguyen et al. 2012). However, such a set is only useful if its plans are both low-cost and mutually distinct: an expensive plan is a poor choice (Katz et al. 2020), and a plan close to an obstructed one is likely to share the same obstruction (Srivastava et al. 2007).

Returning multiple plans is well studied in discrete planning: top-kk
planning returns the kk cheapest plans (Katz et al. 2018), top-quality
planning returns all plans within a cost bound (Katz et al. 2020), and diverse
planning returns plans that differ by a given
distance (Nguyen et al. 2012; Katz and Sohrabi 2020), often by forbidding
each plan found and searching again. These ideas do not transfer directly to
trajectory planning, where a plan is a function of continuous time rather than
a timed sequence of discrete actions, as in PDDL+
planning (Cashmore et al. 2020). Shifting a valid path by a fraction of a millimetre yields another valid plan that passes every obstacle on the same side. Consequently, a valid plan has infinitely many valid near-copies. Because these plans cannot be enumerated, forbidding one plan simply leaves all of its near-copies available.

Existing continuous methods fall into three groups, none of which is designed
to return such sets. Trajectory optimizers, whether gradient-based or
sampling-based such as CEM and MPPI, converge to a single local optimum or
mode, and restarting them tends to return the same few
optima (Martí et al. 2025; Kobilarov 2012; Williams et al. 2017).
Multi-modal methods such as Stein variational MPC maintain several
trajectories, but provide neither cost bounds nor an explicit distinctness
criterion (Lambert et al. 2020). Quality-diversity algorithms keep archives
of diverse solutions, but measure diversity over predefined behaviour
descriptors and bound no solution’s cost relative to the
best (Cully et al. 2015). Because no method targets sets that are both
low-cost and distinct, continuous planning also lacks a measure for them:
benchmarks report success rates, mode counts or
coverage (Chamzas et al. 2021; Cully et al. 2015), none of which
combines a cost bound relative to the best plan with a distinctness threshold
on dynamically feasible, constraint-satisfying trajectories.

We address this gap with Many Plans at Once (MPAO), which returns large
sets of distinct, low-cost, validated trajectories in a single run
(Fig. 1). We formalize the goal as (q,δ)(q,\delta)-plan sets (Sec. 3),
bringing the cost bound of top-quality planning and the distinctness threshold
of diverse planning to continuous time, and measure them by their size
N⋆​(q,δ)N^{\star}(q,\delta). Unlike optimizers, which stop once they converge,
MPAO treats every plan it finds as a reason to search elsewhere. It samples untrained neural networks whose outputs meet the boundary conditions by construction, and trains a correction shared by networks from the same distribution so that progress on one candidate carries over to others. MPAO then stores every validated plan, replaces most successful candidates with fresh samples, and continuously adapts its sampling distributions to what it has found. Because
stored plans are never discarded, it is anytime. Under equal budgets against
five baselines, MPAO is the only method that solves all 40 instances of
four domains and the only one with any plan within 25% of the best known cost
on Pick, one of three manipulation tasks (Sec. 5.1). On the
other two, Push and Slide, it overtakes the strongest baseline’s final count
within a tenth of the budget and ends with about ten times as many such plans,
and about 200 times as many within twice that cost.

title: Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Stefan de Lasa,Mohammadreza Mofayezi,Gennady Pekhimenko,Nandita Vijaykumar
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [1, 2, 3] are an emerging paradigm in robotics that aim to learn generalizable robotics behavior. They leverage internet-scale vision encoders (ViT) and vision-language models (VLM) as backbones to understand image observations and user text-prompt instructions. A subsequent “action expert” (AE) stage generates a series of actions to achieve the text-prompted goal (see Figure 1).

Unlike stand-alone VLMs, VLAs typically follow the ViT encoding and VLM prefill stages with a constant-step diffusion-based action policy [1, 2], rather than a variable-length auto-regressive decode [4, 5].
The VLA “action chunking” paradigm entails that multiple action tokens are generated per inference pass, instead of a single decoded language token like with large-language models (LLMs) or VLMs. As a result, VLA workloads alternate between GPU inference and on-robot action execution (see Figure 2).

While VLAs have improved robotic generalizability [1, 6], we find they severely under-utilize GPU compute. Action chunking leaves the GPU idle between inference passes for >>80% of total task completion time while the robot executes generated actions. We also observe under-utilization during inference passes: streaming multiprocessor (SM) throughput averages 21-27% across models, with the AE’s utilization being the lowest of all three stages (5-19%). Given the high cost of GPUs, VLA operators are economically motivated to maximize hardware utilization [7]. Since single-robot scenarios leave hardware idle, multi-client VLA serving – scheduling inference for multiple robotic clients on one device – is a natural setting to study. This setting is most applicable to warehouse and factory deployments where robot fleets communicate with an on-premises server [8].

Multi-client serving enables techniques such as batching [5, 4] and stage co-execution [9, 10] to improve inference-time utilization, but these have not been characterized for VLAs. Prior LLM/VLM serving work [5, 4, 10, 9] does not account for the VLA’s AE or action chunking, and prior multi-client VLA work [8, 11] details neither the heterogeneous behavior of VLA stages nor stage co-execution.

We profile popular VLA models [1, 2, 3], spanning key VLA architectural axes, to highlight fundamental challenges with these serving techniques applied to VLAs. Our analysis of batching shows that it alone cannot improve utilization across all stages due to the VLM’s and ViT’s compute-bound matrix-multiplication (GEMM) kernels. Furthermore, intuitions from LLM serving do not transfer directly to VLAs, since the latter cannot easily amortize the increased latency incurred from a batched VLM and ViT. Stage co-execution yields modest speedups as VLM GEMM kernels block AE kernel dispatching or slow substantially on partitioned SMs.

Therefore, in this characterization study, we make the following contributions:

We explain VLA GPU compute under-utilization, both between and during inference passes, motivating the multi-client setting we characterize.

We analyze VLA per-stage hardware utilization, power usage, and latency under batching, quantifying trade-offs and fundamental challenges for multi-client VLA serving.

We explain the behavior of VLAs under stage co-execution, highlighting the limitations of co-execution techniques.

1. We explain VLA GPU compute under-utilization, both between and during inference passes, motivating the multi-client setting we characterize.

2. We analyze VLA per-stage hardware utilization, power usage, and latency under batching, quantifying trade-offs and fundamental challenges for multi-client VLA serving.

3. We explain the behavior of VLAs under stage co-execution, highlighting the limitations of co-execution techniques.

title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
authors: Qiang Zhou,Jianing Deng,Siyan Dong,Jingxian Chen,Han-Yi Lin,Jingtong Hu
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one.
Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost.
We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model’s visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history.
Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own.
A map trained to reproduce the large model’s cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone.
Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model’s own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame.
Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model’s layers.
On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28–47% less compute, and 8×\times less per escalation at 64 frames.
Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model’s headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.
introduction:
An embodied agent that acts over minutes must remember what it saw: where an object was hidden, which button was pressed, what changed since the last step.
Running a large vision-language model (VLM) over the whole visual history at every decision is too expensive, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only the decisions it is unsure of to a large one [9, 23, 18], much as a robot asks an expert for help when it is uncertain [25, 28].

Escalation has a hidden cost.
The large model has never seen the history, so it must re-encode every frame before it can answer, and this re-encoding, not the answer, dominates its compute (Fig. 1): at 64 frames it takes nine tenths of an escalation.
Yet the small model has already perceived the same history: its key-value (KV) cache over the video is a visual memory that exists for free at the moment of escalation.
A transformer reads its past only through this cache: later tokens attend to its keys and values alone.
Describing that memory in words loses most of it; the cache keeps what the small model saw, in a form another model can attend to.
This raises a critical question (Fig. 2): can the large model read that memory instead of watching again?

The natural way to hand over a cache is to translate it: fit a map from the small model’s KV to the large model’s own KV over the same history, as has been done between text language models [19, 26].
On video this fails in an instructive way.
The fitted maps reproduce the large model’s cache more closely than any other map we train, and a large model reading them answers no better than the small model alone.
What it reads from them is almost what it reads from its own cache, and it still gains nothing.
Matching a representation and matching its function are different things [11], and here the difference is the whole effect.

We find that the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own.
Baton therefore does not regress the cache.
It distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model’s own answers, through the path in which the map is deployed: the history comes from the small model’s memory and the large model encodes only the current frame.
The resulting memory is farther from the large model’s native cache and carries the whole gain.
By what the large model reads from it, it is eleven times farther than the fitted maps.

Because the map is linear, we can test this directly.
A random step with exactly the norm of the gap between the fitted and the distilled map costs nothing; the same step along the gap costs the whole gain.
The gain sits in the middle third of the large model’s layers, which alone are necessary and sufficient, in two model families.
The correction is mostly in the keys, in where the large model looks, and sits where the distilled map departs least from the large model’s own cache.
Handing off a memory is thus not a reconstruction problem but a search, among many nearby memories, for one the reader can use, and only the reader’s own answers say which (Sec. 6.6).

On RoboMME [13], a large model reading the small model’s memory beats the small model alone, a closed-form KV regression, a pruned or shortened re-watch [10, 2], and a text memory.
As the escalation channel of a cascade, Baton matches re-watching to within about one point at 28–47% less compute, and its cost stays nearly flat as the history grows.
At 64 frames an escalation needs 8×\times less compute and runs 2.6×\times faster on one RTX 4090.
The gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model’s headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA [22].

In summary, we (1) pose the handoff of visual KV memory as the escalation channel of a small-to-large VLM cascade (Sec. 3), (2) introduce Baton, a label-free linear handoff distilled from the large model’s answers (Sec. 5), and (3) show by intervention why a usable memory, not a faithful one, is what the large model needs (Sec. 6.6).

title: FlowScope: 3D Scene Flow Pretraining Improves Surgical Robot Policies
authors: John J. Han,Adam Schmidt,Jingpei Lu,Zooey He,Muhammad Abdullah Jamal,Jie Ying Wu,Omid Mohareri
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Imitation learning for surgical robots is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations.
Meanwhile, many robot-assisted procedures are recorded as stereo video, yet policies cannot learn from them directly; clinical video carries no action labels.
We present FlowScope, which pretrains a surgical policy network on unlabeled clinical video by forecasting scene flow, the metric 3D motion of scene points, with labels computed by off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models.
We pretrain the trunk of an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) on a dataset of 1,149 clinical procedures (1.35M clips) and discard the flow head afterward, so the deployed policy is a standard ACT with no added inference cost.
On a real surgical robotic system, FlowScope raises needle pickup success from 54% to 90% and first-handover success on needle regrasp from 4% to 52% (full task: 2% to 14%) over training from scratch (n=50n=50 trials each), and retains its gains with a generative flow-matching action head.
Ablations indicate that metric 3D motion is the strongest pretraining signal among those tested; kinematics, 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow, each paired with kinematics, yield smaller or no gains.
Representation analyses suggest that scene-flow pretraining encodes metric needle depth more accurately, that kinematics pretraining increases reliance on the robot state, and that needle-depth probes follow the ordering of real-robot success where offline validation error does not.
introduction:
Robot-assisted surgery is a promising but underexplored frontier for robot learning.
Automating even routine suturing subtasks, such as needle pickup or needle handover, could reduce surgeon fatigue and ultimately improve patient outcomes.
Imitation learning has recently made dexterous behaviors like these tractable in general-purpose manipulation [48, 11, 3], following a simple recipe: collect more demonstrations, train better policies.
In surgical robotics, the first half of this recipe is the bottleneck.

Surgical demonstrations are scarce and expensive.
Each one requires an expert operator, often an experienced robotic surgeon, a carefully prepared physical setup, and time on a costly system.
Simulation offers a potential alternative, but accurately modeling deformable tissues and realistic endoscopic scenes remains challenging, limiting reliable transfer of learned policies to physical surgical robots [19, 28, 39].

Pretraining offers another way to reduce the demonstration burden.
It has transformed language [36, 37, 14] and vision [20, 31, 41]. Robotics has followed, from the RT series [5, 4, 32] to vision-language-action models built on web-scale data [3, 35].
The natural next step is to fine-tune these generalist models on surgical tasks.
Yet vision models pretrained on general-domain images transfer poorly to surgical scenes [18, 34, 13], and the robot data behind generalist policies looks nothing like the inside of a patient.
Indeed, in our experiments, a fine-tuned π0.5\pi_{0.5} trails FlowScope on both surgical tasks (Sec. 4).
Surgical policies need surgical pretraining data.

Such data already exists at scale.
Many robot-assisted procedures are recorded through an endoscope, producing a large and growing corpus of video from the domain a policy will be deployed in.
This video, however, cannot serve as demonstrations directly.
Imitation learning needs action labels, but clinical video carries none; the kinematics of clinical systems are rarely available outside the manufacturer.
Even when they are available, they are offset from where the instruments appear in the image, due to errors in the forward kinematics and calibration [47, 26].
Actions recovered from them do not match what the policy sees.

What, then, should a surgical policy learn from unlabeled stereo video?
Our answer is motion.
What a surgeon does is visible in how the scene moves: the instruments sweep toward the needle, the needle lifts from the tissue, and the tissue deforms under traction.
Because the endoscope is stereo, this motion can be estimated in metric 3D with off-the-shelf stereo depth and optical flow models.
The resulting scene flow is an action-like signal that is read directly from the pixels, needs no robot labels, and does not inherit the errors of the kinematics.

We present FlowScope, a pretraining recipe for surgical policies built on scene flow.
Using off-the-shelf stereo depth [43] and optical flow [42] models, we convert raw surgical video into metric 3D trajectories of points on tissue, needles, and instruments.
We then pretrain the trunk of an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) model to take the endoscope image as input and predict the 3D positions and future trajectories of queried points.
Pretraining adds only a set of point queries and a lightweight flow head, both discarded afterward, so the fine-tuned model is a standard ACT policy and FlowScope requires no changes at deployment.

We pretrain FlowScope with 1,149 clinical procedures, about 1.35M training clips, and fine-tune it on two subtasks on a minimally invasive surgical robotic system: needle pickup and needle regrasp.
On both tasks, FlowScope substantially improves real-robot success over training from scratch: from 54% to 90% on pickup, and from 4% to 52% on the first handover of regrasp.
It also outperforms Diffusion Policy [11] and the finetuned vision-language-action model π0.5\pi_{0.5} [35].
The gains are not tied to ACT’s regression head; they persist when we replace it with a generative flow-matching head.
Pretraining also improves data efficiency: with half of the demonstrations, FlowScope matches a policy trained from scratch on all of them on needle pickup (52% vs. 54%) and surpasses it on needle regrasp (32% vs. 4% first-handover success).

Two findings stand out.
First, scene flow alone is a better pretraining signal than robot kinematics for surgical robot learning.
We expected the kinematics recorded alongside the video to be useful supervision, since they describe exactly what a policy must output.
Yet pretraining on kinematics gives little to no gain over training from scratch, and sometimes hurts; adding kinematics to scene-flow pretraining lowers success.
Second, metric 3D scene flow outperforms its alternatives based on 2D point tracks, depth-only supervision, and scale-free 3D flow. Metric scale, which the stereo endoscope provides, is what makes FlowScope work.

To understand why, we look inside the policies.
Kinematics-pretrained policies devote nearly three times as much visual attention to the robot-state input as other policies, and keep doing so after fine-tuning.
Flow-pretrained policies instead encode the needle’s metric depth more accurately than any other initialization.
FlowScope teaches the policy to locate what matters in 3D from visual input only.

In summary, our contributions are:

FlowScope, a recipe that pretrains surgical policy networks to forecast metric 3D scene flow from unlabeled clinical stereo video, requiring no robot labels and no changes to the deployed policy.

A real-robot evaluation on two surgical tasks, showing that FlowScope improves success and data efficiency over training from scratch, kinematics pretraining, and strong baselines, with both regression and generative heads.

Controlled ablations showing that the benefit comes from metric 3D motion: 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow give smaller or no gains when added to kinematics, and kinematics alone are a weaker signal than scene flow.

Representation analyses showing that flow pretraining improves the policy’s encoding of metric needle depth, that kinematics pretraining shifts attention toward the robot state, and that such probes, unlike offline validation error, track real-robot success.

1. FlowScope, a recipe that pretrains surgical policy networks to forecast metric 3D scene flow from unlabeled clinical stereo video, requiring no robot labels and no changes to the deployed policy.

2. A real-robot evaluation on two surgical tasks, showing that FlowScope improves success and data efficiency over training from scratch, kinematics pretraining, and strong baselines, with both regression and generative heads.

3. Controlled ablations showing that the benefit comes from metric 3D motion: 2D tracks, depth alone, and scale-free 3D flow give smaller or no gains when added to kinematics, and kinematics alone are a weaker signal than scene flow.

4. Representation analyses showing that flow pretraining improves the policy’s encoding of metric needle depth, that kinematics pretraining shifts attention toward the robot state, and that such probes, unlike offline validation error, track real-robot success.

title: 3D Open-Vocabulary Detection via Visual Alignment and Generative Captions
authors: Thomas E. Huang,Alex Zihao Zhu,Hao Xiang,Tianyi Cai,Jingwei Ji,Yuliang Zou,Jiafan Yu,Xin Huang,Mingxing Tan
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
abstract:
Open-vocabulary 3D object detection remains a significant challenge for outdoor scenes, with existing methods often struggling to effectively transfer the rich semantic knowledge from powerful 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into a 3D context.
We propose a novel, two-part framework for this task.
First, we introduce a direct, object-level distillation method.
We generate class-agnostic 3D proposals to source regions from the entire scene, without relying on any manual labels.
We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal’s projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis.
Second, to enhance zero-shot capability and inject domain-specific information, we employ a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner to generate rich textual captions for each of these proposals.
These captions are integrated into the training objective to directly align the 3D features with these rich semantics, creating a composite loss that combines direct feature distillation with caption-based semantic enrichment.
Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, establishing a new state of the art in 3D open-vocabulary detection on the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.
introduction:
Accurate 3D object detection is foundational for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving.
Current state-of-the-art 3D detectors, which rely on LiDAR point clouds [1, 2] and multi-view images [3, 4], have achieved remarkable performance on challenging benchmarks [5, 6].
However, these methods are fundamentally limited: they can only identify and localize objects that belong to a pre-defined set of categories seen during training.
In real-world environments, systems constantly encounter novel objects and long-tail concepts, rendering closed-set detectors unreliable.
When a closed-set detector fails to identify a novel obstacle such as debris or an unconventional vehicle, it poses a direct threat to downstream motion planning and collision avoidance systems.

The emerging field of open-vocabulary 3D object detection addresses this limitation by aiming to detect arbitrary objects described by natural language.
To achieve this open-set capability, prevailing approaches typically rely on knowledge distillation from large-scale pre-trained 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [7].
These methods transfer the VLM’s rich semantic features to the 3D detector, either by projecting 2D features to 3D points/voxels for alignment [8], or by using 2D open-vocabulary detections [9, 10] as pseudo-labels for 3D localization [11, 12].
This enables the 3D model to predict an embedding vector that can be compared against arbitrary text queries (e.g., object names) at inference time.

The primary challenge in this domain is bridging the knowledge gap between the feature-rich 2D domain, where vast Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like CLIP [7] have acquired broad open-world knowledge, and the sparse, 3D domain.
Directly aligning sparse, unorganized, 3D features with dense, pre-trained 2D image features is notoriously noisy.
Additionally, the 2D VLMs are pre-trained on web-scale data, which are general, but may create significant domain gaps when applied to specific domains.
3D autonomous driving environments are often cluttered, occluded, and have highly varied-perspective views.
Relying solely on this visual-only alignment is insufficient; the 2D visual features are often semantically ambiguous and lack the granularity to distinguish between fine-grained categories (e.g., ‘trailer’ vs. ‘truck’).
This forces the 3D model to learn a similarly coarse representation, limiting its generalization.

In this work, we introduce a novel, end-to-end framework that effectively transfers and grounds open-world semantic knowledge to a 3D detector.
First, our Visual Alignment stage (Section III-B) creates a robust visual foundation.
To overcome the noise and sparsity of 3D-to-2D projection, we distill knowledge in an object-centric manner.
We first generate class-agnostic 3D box proposals using DBSCAN [13] on the raw point cloud, allowing us to source distillation targets from all regions of the scene, including background and potential novel objects, without relying on any ground-truth labels or prior knowledge.
We aggregate 2D VLM features at the object level and use this stable visual signal to supervise the underlying 3D voxel features.
This efficiently distills the VLM’s rich visual knowledge into the 3D backbone, creating a feature space that is visually discriminative.

While this VLM distillation provides general open-world knowledge, the original image embeddings are pre-trained to cover a broad range of captions, and may miss domain specific context. To this end, we propose a second Language Alignment stage (Section III-C) which complements this visual-alignment and instills fine-grained semantic understanding.
We leverage a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner and domain adapter.
Using the same DBSCAN-generated 3D regions, we generate high-fidelity, descriptive captions directly from the 3D dataset’s image patches. These captions are then embedded into the VLM embedding space with the VLM text encoder.
By aligning the visually-grounded 3D features (from Stage 1) to these domain-specific text embeddings, we overcome the semantic ambiguity of 2D visual features and explicitly force it to learn the nuanced semantics of the 3D environment (e.g., “a white sedan stopped in traffic”).
In short, our loss combines the breadth of pre-trained image embedding distillation with the depth of per-object caption embedding distillation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a Visual Alignment strategy that uses class-agnostic proposals to distill object-level 2D VLM features into their corresponding 3D voxels, enabling robust feature learning from the entire scene without manual labels.

We propose a Language Alignment strategy that uses an MLLM to generate high-fidelity, contextual text captions for these same scene regions, grounding the 3D features in rich, descriptive language.

We achieve state-of-the-art results for open-vocabulary 3D object detection on the challenging Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes benchmarks.

title: SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
authors: Ilya Zaychuk
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting.
However, current approaches are each tailored to one sensor type: point density differs by more than ten times between devices, public datasets are labeled with incompatible body models, and LiDAR approaches need long input sequences to offset sparse scans.
In this work, we present SparseHPS, a novel sensor-agnostic network that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global translation from a human point cloud with one set of weights, for single frames and streams alike.
Specifically, SparseHPS encodes the cloud with a LitePT backbone over sparse voxels, represents every joint by a learnable query decoded with one common head, localizes the body by voting over voxels, and draws temporal context from a causal memory of tokens from the seven preceding frames.
A single model is trained on ten datasets that mix rendered clouds with real depth-camera and LiDAR captures, all converted to one body model.
Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the SLOPER4D and FreeMotion LiDAR benchmarks, where SparseHPS lowers the root-relative joint error by 22% and 11%, respectively, compared with the strongest prior method, which needs 32 frames.
On real Azure Kinect captures of held-out HuMMan subjects, SparseHPS attains a joint error of 34.7 mm.
Moreover, the current frame alone already yields the bulk of this accuracy.

introduction:
Estimating the 3D pose and shape of the human body is a long-standing task in computer vision that underpins motion capture, robotics and autonomous driving.
Unlike RGB images, depth cameras and LiDARs deliver metric 3D measurements of the body: they remove the ambiguity of depth and scale, are unaffected by illumination, and place the person in world coordinates.

However, existing point-based methods are designed around one kind of sensor.
Depth-camera approaches [21, 55, 31, 8] expect dense inputs of several thousand sampled points, while LiDAR approaches [28, 45, 44, 46, 1] operate on sparse scans with only hundreds of points and recover the missing geometry by aggregating long point sequences, up to 32 frames in the latest methods.
Each sensor has its own models and benchmarks, and the data are not interchangeable: after 2 cm voxelization, the median person has 2.3k points in the Azure Kinect views of HuMMan [9] but about 100 for the most distant LiDAR in FreeMotion [45]; in addition, labels come in different body models.
Image-based mesh recovery, by comparison, has gained substantially from training one model across many datasets [19, 10].
We are not aware of any model that serves both sensor families with one set of weights.

To bridge this gap, we present SparseHPS (Fig. 2), a novel network that estimates human pose and shape from point clouds, frame by frame or over a stream.
Its encoder is LitePT [61], a point transformer over sparse voxels that uses convolutions at the fine levels and attention at the coarse ones.
Specifically, 24 learnable query tokens, one per body joint plus one for shape and one for translation, cross-attend to voxels from the two coarsest stages of the encoder, and all joint tokens share one linear head.
Instead of predicting the global position directly from a token, each voxel votes for the pelvis location, weighted by the translation token.
In addition, a causal memory lets each token attend to its own states in the seven previous frames; for a frame with no history, the computation reduces exactly to the single-frame model.
We refer to the single-frame variant as SparseHPS-S and to the variant with memory as SparseHPS-T.

To train one model for all sensors, we bring ten sources into a common label space, the neutral SMPL-X model with 16 shape coefficients: three LiDAR datasets (SLOPER4D, FreeMotion, RELI11D), four depth-camera datasets (HuMMan, BEHAVE, EgoBody, FORM-HOI), and renderings of synthetic and scanned humans (AMASS, BEDLAM2, CAPE).
Per-source quotas keep large datasets with many views from dominating training, and a rotation augmentation that respects gravity retains the vertical direction on which sparse scans depend.

Extensive experiments on the full mixture support every design decision.
Over seven consecutive single-frame models, each changing a single component, the vertex error averaged over nine test sets falls from 43.3 mm to 36.0 mm (Tab. 4); a data ladder further shows that every sensor family needs data of its own, whereas adding the other families comes at almost no cost (Tab. 5).
The memory leaves the mean single-frame accuracy intact and cuts acceleration error by 5% (Tab. 6).
On the LiDAR benchmarks, SparseHPS sets a new state of the art: with a history of seven frames, its root-relative joint error is 28.6 mm (SLOPER4D) and 41.8 mm (FreeMotion), whereas the strongest published method obtains 36.5 mm and 47.2 mm from 32 frames (Fig. 1).
Notably, a single frame already reaches 28.9 and 42.9 mm, since the encoder sees every point of the scan.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce SparseHPS, a novel one-stage model that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global position from single-frame or sequential point clouds, using per-joint query tokens with a shared decoding head, a voting scheme over voxels and a causal memory of tokens.

We develop a training recipe that spans range sensors: ten sources mapped to one label space, per-source quotas and a gravity-preserving augmentation, yielding shared weights across depth cameras and LiDARs.

We provide controlled ablations on the complete training mixture and reach state-of-the-art accuracy on LiDAR benchmarks with one quarter of the frames that sequence-based methods take.

1. We introduce SparseHPS, a novel one-stage model that recovers SMPL-X pose, shape and global position from single-frame or sequential point clouds, using per-joint query tokens with a shared decoding head, a voting scheme over voxels and a causal memory of tokens.

2. We develop a training recipe that spans range sensors: ten sources mapped to one label space, per-source quotas and a gravity-preserving augmentation, yielding shared weights across depth cameras and LiDARs.

3. We provide controlled ablations on the complete training mixture and reach state-of-the-art accuracy on LiDAR benchmarks with one quarter of the frames that sequence-based methods take.
